gods.description: Enormous, near-perpetually sleeping brother of Ravana, roused to fight Rama's army and slain in the war.

gods.name: Mandodari
gods.description: Chief queen of Ravana, remembered for wisdom and virtue despite her husband's ruinous course.

gods.name: Vishrava
gods.description: Brahmin sage, son of Pulastya; father of Kubera by one wife and of the rakshasa line of Lanka by Kaikasi.

gods.name: Daksha
gods.description: A Prajapati and patriarch of the Puranic genealogies, whose many daughters wed gods and sages. His slighting of Shiva drove Sati to self-immolation.

gods.name: Diti
gods.description: Daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa; mother of the Daitya asuras, including Hiranyakashipu.

gods.name: Kadru
gods.description: Daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa; mother of the nagas, the serpent race.

gods.name: Vinata
gods.description: Daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa; mother of Garuda. A lost wager with Kadru bound her to servitude.

gods.name: Sati
gods.description: Daughter of Daksha and first wife of Shiva; she cast herself into her father's sacrificial fire and was later reborn as Parvati.

gods.name: Anasuya
gods.description: Wife of the sage Atri, exalted for her chastity and virtue; mother of Dattatreya, and in Puranic accounts of Chandra.

gods.name: Rukmini
gods.description: Princess of Vidarbha and chief queen of Krishna, worshipped as an avatar of Lakshmi; mother of Pradyumna.

gods.name: Satyabhama
gods.description: Fiery queen of Krishna and daughter of Satrajit; she fought at his side in the campaign against Narakasura.

gods.name: Jambavati
gods.description: Daughter of the bear-king Jambavan and a queen of Krishna, wed after Krishna's contest over the Syamantaka jewel.

gods.name: Pradyumna
gods.description: Son of Krishna and Rukmini, held to be the god Kama reborn; a leading warrior of the Yadavas.

gods.name: Revati
gods.description: Wife of Balarama and daughter of King Kakudmi; in a famed tale she returned from Brahma's realm to find ages had passed on earth.

gods.name: Ugrasena
gods.description: Yadava king of Mathura, deposed by his son Kamsa and restored to the throne by Krishna.

gods.name: Shurasena
gods.description: Yadava king of the Vrishnis; father of Vasudeva and of Kunti, and thereby grandfather of Krishna.

gods.name: Devaka
gods.description: Yadava noble, father of Devaki and brother of Ugrasena.

gods.name: Padmavati
gods.description: Queen of Ugrasena and mother of Kamsa in the Puranic Yadava genealogy.

gods.name: Narakasura
gods.description: Asura king of Pragjyotisha, son of the earth-goddess Bhudevi; slain by Krishna. Also called Bhauma.

gods.name: Rohini
gods.description: Yadava wife of Vasudeva who bore Balarama. In the Bhagavata tradition, the embryo carried by Devaki was transferred to Rohini's womb, giving rise to Balarama's name Sankarshana.

gods.name: Chhaya
gods.description: Personified shadow of Saranyu, left in her place as Surya's wife; mother of Shani.

gods.name: Shachi (Indrani)
gods.description: Queen of Indra and of Svarga, also called Indrani; a Matrika goddess. Mother of Jayanti.

gods.name: Svaha
gods.description: Goddess of the sacrificial oblation, invoked as 'svaha' when offerings are cast into the fire; consort of Agni.

gods.name: Angiras
gods.description: Vedic rishi and seer of hymns, father of Brihaspati; distinct from the Angirasa clan of sages descended from him.

gods.name: Durvasa
gods.description: Short-tempered sage, son of Atri and Anasuya and held to be a portion of Shiva; his curses set many Puranic and epic events in motion.

gods.name: Mena
gods.description: Wife of the mountain-king Himavan and mother of Parvati.

gods.name: Jayanti
gods.description: Daughter of Indra and Shachi; she attended the sage Shukra through his penance and became his consort.

gods.name: Kacha
gods.description: Son of Brihaspati who studied under Shukra to obtain the Sanjivani lore of reviving the dead.

gods.name: Svayambhuva Manu
gods.description: The first of the Manus, mind-born from Brahma and paired with Shatarupa as a primordial progenitor of humankind. The Manava Dharmashastra presents its teachings as a discourse associated with Manu and transmitted through Bhrigu.

gods.name: Shatarupa
gods.description: Primordial first woman associated with Brahma's creation; wife of Svayambhuva Manu and, with him, a progenitor of humankind.

gods.name: Ghatotkacha
gods.description: Half-rakshasa son of Bhima and Hidimbi; a giant warrior who fell to Karna's celestial spear at Kurukshetra.

gods.name: Hidimbi
gods.description: Rakshasi who wed Bhima during the Pandavas' exile; mother of Ghatotkacha.

gods.name: Ulupi
gods.description: Naga princess, a wife of Arjuna and mother of Iravan.

gods.name: Iravan
gods.description: Son of Arjuna and the naga princess Ulupi; he offered himself in sacrifice at Kurukshetra and is venerated in the Kuttantavar tradition.

gods.name: Chitrangada
gods.description: Warrior princess of Manipura and a wife of Arjuna.

gods.name: Vrishasena
gods.description: Son of Karna and a warrior at Kurukshetra, slain by Arjuna.

gods.name: Balandhara
gods.description: Princess of Kashi and a wife of Bhima; mother of Sarvaga.

gods.name: Sarvaga
gods.description: Son of Bhima and the Kashi princess Balandhara.

gods.name: Kaikasi
gods.description: Rakshasi wife of the sage Vishrava; mother of Ravana, Kumbhakarna, and Vibhishana.

gods.name: Vali
gods.description: Mighty vanara king of Kishkindha and elder brother of Sugriva; slain by Rama.

gods.name: Tara
gods.description: Vanara queen, wife of Vali and later of Sugriva; renowned for her wisdom.

gods.name: Ruma
gods.description: Vanara queen, wife of Sugriva.

gods.name: Lopamudra
gods.description: Learned wife of the sage Agastya, credited with hymns of the Rigveda.

gods.name: Arundhati
gods.description: Wife of the sage Vasistha, upheld as an ideal of devotion and identified with a star of the Great Bear.

gods.name: Dridhasyu
gods.description: Son of the sage Agastya and Lopamudra.

gods.name: Shakti
gods.description: Eldest son of the sage Vasistha and himself a rishi; father of Parashara. Not to be confused with the goddess-concept Shakti.

gods.name: Shilada
gods.description: Sage who, through long austerity, gained Nandi as his son.

gods.name: Varuni
gods.description: Goddess of wine, arisen from the churning of the ocean; consort of Varuna.

gods.name: Devasena
gods.description: Consort of Kartikeya, given to him by Indra; her name means 'army of the gods.'

gods.name: Valli
gods.description: Tamil maiden who became a consort of Kartikeya (Murugan).

gods.name: Prativindhya
gods.description: Son of Yudhishthira and Draupadi, one of the five Upapandavas; slain in the night raid on the sleeping Pandava camp.

gods.name: Sutasoma
gods.description: Son of Bhima and Draupadi, one of the five Upapandavas; distinct from Sarvaga, Bhima's son by Balandhara.

gods.name: Suhotra
gods.description: Son of Sahadeva by his wife Vijaya; not to be confused with other figures of the common dynastic name Suhotra.

gods.name: Yaudheya
gods.description: Son of Yudhishthira by his wife Devika; the individual prince, not the historical Yaudheya people.

gods.name: Karenumati
gods.description: Wife of Nakula and mother of Niramitra.

gods.name: Niramitra
gods.description: Son of Nakula and Karenumati.

gods.name: Devika
gods.description: Wife of Yudhishthira and mother of Yaudheya.

gods.name: Vijaya
gods.description: Wife of Sahadeva and mother of Suhotra; distinct from unrelated uses of the name Vijaya, an epithet and the name of Arjuna's bow.

gods.name: Shrutakarma
gods.description: Son of Arjuna and Draupadi, one of the five Upapandavas; called Shrutakirti in some recensions.

gods.name: Shatanika
gods.description: Son of Nakula and Draupadi, one of the five Upapandavas; distinct from the later Kuru king Shatanika.

gods.name: Shrutasena
gods.description: Son of Sahadeva and Draupadi, one of the five Upapandavas; his name is sometimes exchanged with those of his cousins across variant recensions.

gods.name: Amsa
gods.description: One of the Adityas, the solar sons of Aditi and Kashyapa.

gods.name: Aryaman
gods.description: Aditya presiding over customs, hospitality, and marriage; a solar son of Aditi.

gods.name: Bhaga
gods.description: Aditya of wealth, fortune, and the shares of offerings; a solar son of Aditi.

gods.name: Asti
gods.description: A queen of Kamsa and daughter of Jarasandha; her widowhood spurred Jarasandha's assaults on Mathura.

gods.name: Prapti
gods.description: A queen of Kamsa and daughter of Jarasandha; with her sister Asti, her widowhood drove Jarasandha's wars on Mathura.

gods.name: Bhadra
gods.description: Yakshi consort of Kubera, lord of wealth.

gods.name: Kayadhu
gods.description: Asura queen, wife of Hiranyakashipu and mother of the devotee Prahlada.

gods.name: Kesari
gods.description: Vanara chief, husband of Anjana and earthly father of Hanuman.

gods.name: Kunjara
gods.description: Vanara chief, father of Anjana.

gods.name: Khyati
gods.description: Wife of the sage Bhrigu.

gods.name: Menaka
gods.description: Celestial apsara sent to distract the sage Vishvamitra; mother of Shakuntala.

gods.name: Shakuntala
gods.description: Daughter of Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka; her romance with King Dushyanta and their son Bharata are told in Kalidasa's play.

gods.name: Sambhuti
gods.description: Wife of the sage Marichi.

gods.name: Unnati
gods.description: Consort of Garuda, the divine eagle.

gods.name: Simhika
gods.description: Asuri wife of Viprachitti and mother of Svarbhanu, whose severed head and body became Rahu and Ketu.

gods.name: Viprachitti
gods.description: Danava ruler, husband of Simhika and father of Svarbhanu.

gods.name: Devayani
gods.description: Daughter of the asura-guru Shukra; wife of King Yayati in the Mahabharata.

gods.name: Ikshvaku
gods.description: Son of Vaivasvata Manu and founder of the Solar dynasty (the Ikshvaku line) into which Rama was later born.

gods.name: Vrishabhanu
gods.description: Gopa chief of Barsana; father of Radha in the Krishna-bhakti tradition.

gods.name: Svarbhanu
gods.description: Asura who took a draught of amrita during the churning of the ocean and was beheaded by Vishnu; his severed head became Rahu and his body became Ketu, the two eclipse-associated shadow-planets.

gods.name: Mitra
gods.description: Vedic Aditya of covenant, friendship, and the daylit order; with Varuna he upholds cosmic law and, in the pot-birth myth, fathered Agastya and Vasistha.

gods.name: Indrajit (Meghanada)
gods.description: Son of Ravana and Mandodari; born Meghanada, he took the title Indrajit ('conqueror of Indra') after defeating the king of the gods, and fell to Lakshmana in the Ramayana war.

gods.name: Tara (wife of Brihaspati)
gods.description: Wife of Brihaspati, abducted by Chandra; mother of Budha by Chandra. Distinct from Tara, the vanara queen of the Ramayana.

gods.name: Ila
gods.description: Progenitor of the Lunar dynasty, consort of Budha and mother of Pururavas. Traditions concerning Ila and Sudyumna describe transformations between female and male forms; the archive uses female here for the relationship in which Ila bears Pururavas.

gods.name: Pururavas
gods.description: Early king of the Lunar dynasty, son of Budha and Ila; celebrated in the tradition of Pururavas and Urvashi.

gods.name: Rambha (asura)
gods.description: Male asura described as the father of Mahishasura; distinct from Rambha, the female apsara of the same name.

gods.name: Daityas
gods.description: Collective race of asuras descended from Diti and Kashyapa; individual Daityas such as Hiranyakashipu are catalogued separately.

gods.name: Danavas
gods.description: Collective race of asuras born of Kashyapa and the Hindu mother Danu, who is not separately catalogued here; often opposed to the devas.

gods.name: Maruts
gods.description: Band of storm and wind deities who accompany Indra; treated here as children of Rudra, while other traditions connect them with Diti.

gods.name: Saptarishis
gods.description: The seven great sages associated with Brahma; their membership varies by cosmic age and source, and several sages of the Saptarishi traditions are catalogued individually.

gods.name: Twenty-seven Nakshatras
gods.description: The twenty-seven lunar mansions, daughters of Daksha and collective wives of Chandra; his special affection for Rohini is associated with Daksha's curse and the moon's waxing and waning.

gods.name: Adharma
gods.description: Personification of unrighteousness and the mythic counterpart of Dharma; consort of Nirriti in the Puranic descent of vices.

gods.name: Prakriti
gods.description: Primordial nature or materiality in Samkhya philosophy, paired conceptually with Purusha, pure consciousness. They are complementary principles rather than a married couple; later Shakta traditions may personify Prakriti as the Great Goddess.

gods.name: Riddhi
gods.description: Personification of prosperity; named with Siddhi as a consort of Ganesha in North-Indian traditions, while other traditions regard Ganesha as celibate.

gods.name: Siddhi
gods.description: Personification of spiritual attainment and success; named with Riddhi as a consort of Ganesha in North-Indian traditions.

gods.name: Nabhiraja
gods.description: King in Jain tradition, husband of Marudevi and father of Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara.

gods.name: Marudevi
gods.description: Queen in Jain tradition, wife of Nabhiraja and mother of Rishabhanatha.

gods.name: Sumangala
gods.description: Consort of Rishabhanatha and mother of Bharata Chakravartin in Jain tradition.

gods.name: Sunanda
gods.description: Consort of Rishabhanatha and mother of Bahubali in Jain tradition.

gods.name: Bharata (Chakravartin)
gods.description: Eldest son of Rishabhanatha and Sumangala and the first Chakravartin of the present Jain time cycle; distinct from the other mythological figures named Bharata.

gods.name: Bahubali
gods.description: Son of Rishabhanatha and Sunanda, renowned for renouncing worldly power and attaining spiritual liberation; venerated in the monumental Gommateshwara tradition.

gods.name: Ajitanatha
gods.description: Second Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, situated in the distant past of Jain sacred history.

gods.name: Chandraprabha
gods.description: Eighth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, traditionally represented by the crescent-moon emblem.

gods.name: Vasupujya
gods.description: Twelfth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, traditionally counted among those who renounced without marrying.

gods.name: Shantinatha
gods.description: Sixteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, traditionally also remembered as a Chakravartin and associated with peace.

gods.name: Mallinatha
gods.description: Nineteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle. Shvetambara tradition identifies Malli as female and the only woman among the twenty-four Tirthankaras, while Digambara tradition identifies Mallinatha as male.

gods.name: Munisuvrata
gods.description: Twentieth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Naminatha
gods.description: Twenty-first Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Neminatha
gods.description: Twenty-second Tirthankara, also called Aristanemi. Jain tradition connects him with Krishna's extended family and tells that he renounced worldly life after witnessing animals gathered for slaughter before his wedding.

gods.name: Parshvanatha
gods.description: Twenty-third Tirthankara, traditionally represented by the serpent emblem. He is often regarded as probably historical, with scholarly estimates commonly placing him sometime between approximately the eighth and sixth centuries BCE.

gods.name: Mahavira
gods.description: Twenty-fourth and final Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, born Vardhamana. A central historical teacher and organizer of the Jain community, he taught a path of disciplined nonviolence, restraint, and liberation. He lived near the period conventionally associated with the Buddha.

gods.name: Siddhartha (father of Mahavira)
gods.description: Ruler associated with Kundagrama, husband of Trishala and father of Mahavira; distinct from Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha.

gods.name: Trishala
gods.description: Mother of Mahavira and consort of Siddhartha in Jain tradition.

gods.name: Sambhavanatha
gods.description: Third Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Abhinandananatha
gods.description: Fourth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Sumatinatha
gods.description: Fifth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Padmaprabha
gods.description: Sixth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, traditionally associated with a lotus emblem.

gods.name: Suparshvanatha
gods.description: Seventh Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Suvidhinatha (Pushpadanta)
gods.description: Ninth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle, also known as Pushpadanta.

gods.name: Shitalanatha
gods.description: Tenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Shreyansanatha
gods.description: Eleventh Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Vimalanatha
gods.description: Thirteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Anantanatha
gods.description: Fourteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Dharmanatha
gods.description: Fifteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Kunthunatha
gods.description: Seventeenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Aranatha
gods.description: Eighteenth Tirthankara of the present Jain time cycle.

gods.name: Amaethon
gods.description: Welsh god of agriculture, a son of the goddess Dôn in the Mabinogi tradition.

gods.name: Gofannon
gods.description: Welsh divine smith, a son of Dôn; cognate with the Irish smith-god Goibniu.

gods.name: Gilfaethwy
gods.description: Son of Dôn and brother of Gwydion in the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi.

gods.name: Blodeuwedd
gods.description: Woman conjured from flowers by Math and Gwydion to be Lleu's wife; for her betrayal she was turned into an owl.

gods.name: Penarddun
gods.description: Wife of Llŷr and mother of Brân, Branwen, and Manawydan; her wider parentage differs across Welsh sources.

gods.name: Tuoni
gods.description: Ruler of Tuonela, the Finnish land of the dead, with his consort Tuonetar.

gods.name: Kyllikki
gods.description: Maiden of Saari abducted and wed by Lemminkäinen in the Kalevala.

gods.name: Nyyrikki
gods.description: Forest deity of the hunt, son of Tapio and Mielikki.

gods.name: Tuulikki
gods.description: Forest goddess who tends wild creatures, daughter of Tapio and Mielikki.

gods.name: Anu (Hurrian tradition)
gods.description: Sky god who held the kingship of heaven at the start of the Hurrian-Hittite succession myth before being overthrown by Kumarbi; this precedence is a sequence of divine rule, not a settled genealogy.

gods.name: Tashmishu
gods.description: Divine attendant and brother-in-arms of the Storm God Teshub, brought forth in the Kumarbi cycle.

gods.name: Ullikummi
gods.description: Monstrous being of diorite stone that Kumarbi caused to grow to challenge Teshub; not born in the ordinary human sense.

gods.name: Sun Goddess of Arinna
gods.description: Chief goddess of the Hittite state cult and protector of the king and land, named for her principal cult city of Arinna (the city itself being distinct from the deity). Conventionally called Arinniti, with the Hattian antecedent Wurušemu; paired with the Storm God and later identified in prose with the Hurrian Hebat.

gods.name: Age
gods.description: Vodun of the hunt and wild animals, a child of the creator pair Mawu-Lisa.

gods.name: Agbe
gods.description: Vodun of the sea, a child of Mawu-Lisa; genealogies of the sea-vodun vary across Fon tradition.

gods.name: Ayizan
gods.description: Vodun of the earth and the marketplace, consort of Loko.

gods.name: Dijun
gods.description: High god of the eastern heavens, husband of the sun-mother Xihe; his traditions vary and are not a single fixed genealogy.

gods.name: Li Jing
gods.description: The Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King, father of Nezha.

gods.name: Lady Yin
gods.description: Wife of Li Jing and mother of Nezha.

gods.name: Niulang (the Cowherd)
gods.description: The mortal cowherd of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl tale, husband of Zhinu.

gods.name: Tudi Po
gods.description: Local earth-goddess, wife of the earth-god Tudi Gong.

gods.name: Haumia-tiketike
gods.description: In Māori tradition, atua of uncultivated food such as fern-root; a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku.

gods.name: Tāwhirimātea
gods.description: In Māori tradition, atua of storms and winds; the child of Rangi and Papa who opposed the separation of his parents.

gods.name: Hine-ahuone
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the first woman, formed from earth by Tāne, who took her as consort.

gods.name: Makeatutara
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the father of Māui.

gods.name: Taranga
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the mother of Māui, who wrapped her prematurely born son in her hair-knot and cast him to the sea.

gods.name: Vohu Manah
gods.description: Amesha Spenta of the Good Mind, an emanation of Ahura Mazda embodying righteous thought and wisdom; one of the Bounteous Immortals rather than a biological offspring.

gods.name: Khshathra Vairya
gods.description: Amesha Spenta of Desirable Dominion, an emanation of Ahura Mazda embodying divine sovereignty and, in later tradition, guardian of metals; one of the Bounteous Immortals, not a biological offspring.

gods.name: Haurvatat
gods.description: Amesha Spenta of Wholeness and health, an emanation of Ahura Mazda associated with the waters; one of the Bounteous Immortals, paired conceptually with Ameretat, not a biological offspring.

gods.name: Ameretat
gods.description: Amesha Spenta of Immortality, an emanation of Ahura Mazda associated with plants; one of the Bounteous Immortals, paired conceptually with Haurvatat, not a biological offspring.

gods.name: Pourushaspa
gods.description: In Zoroastrian tradition, the father of the prophet Zarathustra and husband of Dughdova.

gods.name: Dughdova
gods.description: In Zoroastrian tradition, the mother of the prophet Zarathustra and wife of Pourushaspa.

gods.name: Cheonji-wang
gods.description: Heavenly king of the Jeju creation narrative who descends and, by his earthly wife (Chongmyeong-agissi in the bon-puri), fathers the twin brothers Daebyeol-wang and Sobyeol-wang.

gods.name: Daebyeol-wang
gods.description: Elder twin son of Cheonji-wang and his earthly wife (Chongmyeong-agissi); in the Jeju myth he becomes ruler of the realm of the dead.

gods.name: Sobyeol-wang
gods.description: Younger twin son of Cheonji-wang and his earthly wife (Chongmyeong-agissi); in the Jeju myth he wins governance of the world of the living.

gods.name: Jacheongbi
gods.description: Self-made goddess of agriculture and grain in Jeju shamanic tradition, celebrated for winning her own divine station.

gods.name: Shapash
gods.description: Ugaritic sun goddess who traverses the sky and the underworld and acts as a divine arbiter in the Baal Cycle.

gods.name: Yarikh
gods.description: Ugaritic moon god, celebrated in the marriage hymn as the husband of the moon-goddess Nikkal.

gods.name: Nikkal
gods.description: Ugaritic goddess of orchards and fruit, bride of the moon god Yarikh in the Hurrian-derived marriage hymn.

gods.name: Resheph
gods.description: West Semitic god of plague, war, and pestilence, invoked both to bring and to avert disease.

gods.name: Attar
gods.description: West Semitic astral deity associated with the morning star and with irrigation; a masculine figure distinct from the goddesses Astarte and Ishtar.

gods.name: Atunis
gods.description: Etruscan youth beloved of the goddess Turan, cognate with the Greek Adonis but received as a distinct Etruscan figure.

gods.name: Phersipnai
gods.description: Etruscan queen of the underworld, consort of Aita, cognate with the Greek Persephone but a distinct Etruscan figure.

gods.name: Nethuns
gods.description: Etruscan god of wells, springs, and the sea; his name and functions influenced but are distinct from the Roman Neptune.

gods.name: Fufluns
gods.description: Etruscan god of wine, vegetation, and ecstatic celebration, comparable to but distinct from Greek Dionysus and Roman Liber.

gods.name: Turms
gods.description: Etruscan messenger god and guide of souls, comparable to but distinct from Greek Hermes and Roman Mercury.

gods.name: Svarozhits
gods.description: Slavic deity of the sacred fire whose name means 'son of Svarog'; worshipped at Rethra among the Polabian Slavs.

gods.name: Triglav
gods.description: Three-headed Slavic deity venerated among the Pomeranian Slavs, his three heads taken to survey heaven, earth, and the underworld.

gods.name: Hun-Hunahpu
gods.description: One-Hunahpu of the Popol Vuh, a ballplayer of the earlier generation slain in Xibalba; his severed head begat the Hero Twins when it caused the underworld maiden Xquic to conceive. Later tradition links him with the Maize God.

gods.name: Xquic
gods.description: Blood Moon, a maiden of the underworld Xibalba who conceived the Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque when the severed head of Hun-Hunahpu spat into her hand, then fled to the surface world.

gods.name: Xmucane
gods.description: Divine grandmother and diviner of the Popol Vuh, one of the aged creator pair who ground maize to form humankind and reared the Hero Twins; her ancestral link to the twins is left in prose.

gods.name: Vucub-Caquix
gods.description: Seven Macaw, the vainglorious bird-demon of the Popol Vuh who falsely proclaimed himself sun and moon before he was humbled and destroyed by the Hero Twins.

gods.name: Amunet
gods.description: Female counterpart of Amun in the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, embodying the hidden, invisible power of the primordial air; this Ogdoad pairing predates and is distinct from the later Theban theology of Amun as king of the gods.

gods.name: Anput
gods.description: Funerary goddess of the seventeenth Upper Egyptian nome, understood as the feminine counterpart and consort of Anubis rather than as part of a single universal Egyptian family.

gods.name: Kebechet
gods.description: Goddess of the purifying and embalming liquids used in mummification, generally described as a daughter of Anubis; her mother is given as Anput in the traditions that name one.

gods.name: Ihy
gods.description: Child-god of music and jubilation who shakes the sistrum, counted as a son of Hathor; the Dendera theology names his father as Horus of Edfu, though the exact Horus varies by tradition.

gods.name: Maahes
gods.description: Lion-headed god of war and protection, called a son of Bastet in Lower Egypt and of the lioness Sekhmet in Upper Egypt; his father is variously given as Ptah or Ra in prose sources.

gods.name: Nepri
gods.description: God of grain and the harvest, a son of the harvest-goddess Renenutet; his father is given in some accounts as Geb, her consort.

gods.name: Antu
gods.description: Akkadian sky-goddess and consort of Anu; a distinct Semitic development kept separate from the Sumerian earth-mother Ki, with whom Anu is paired in the older tradition.

gods.name: Ningishzida
gods.description: Sumerian god of the underworld, vegetation, and serpents, a son of Ninazu and consort of Geshtinanna; patron of the ruler Gudea of Lagash.

gods.name: Tashmetu
gods.description: Akkadian goddess associated with hearing and reconciliation, the consort of the scribal god Nabu.

gods.name: Duttur
gods.description: Sumerian ewe-goddess named in the Dumuzi laments as the mother of Dumuzi and his sister Geshtinanna.

gods.name: Shulpae
gods.description: Sumerian god of feasting and the wild animals, identified with the planet Jupiter; named as a consort of the mother-goddess Ninhursag in the tradition that pairs them.

gods.name: Ame-no-Oshihomimi
gods.description: One of the five male kami produced during the oath (ukehi) between Amaterasu and Susanoo; because he was born from the beads belonging to Amaterasu, tradition counts him as her child, though attribution shifts with which deity owns or uses the generating objects across accounts. Father of Ninigi and forebear of the imperial line.

gods.name: Hoori
gods.description: Yamasachihiko, the luck of the mountains; son of Ninigi and Konohanasakuya, husband of the sea-princess Toyotama, and father of Ugayafukiaezu. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree on his descent line with minor variation in the fishhook narrative.

gods.name: Hoderi
gods.description: Umisachihiko, the luck of the sea; a son of Ninigi and Konohanasakuya and elder brother of Hoori, regarded as ancestor of the Hayato people. The Nihon Shoki orders the fire-born brothers differently from the Kojiki.

gods.name: Hosuseri
gods.description: One of the three sons borne by Konohanasakuya in the burning hut to prove their divine paternity; his prominence and birth-order vary between the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

gods.name: Ugayafukiaezu
gods.description: Son of Hoori and Toyotama, born on the shore in a birthing-hut thatched with cormorant feathers; father of the first emperor Jimmu, who is not catalogued in this batch.

gods.name: Osanyin
gods.description: Orisha of herbal medicine and the secret power of leaves in Yoruba religion; his knowledge is invoked before any healing work. Distinct developments appear in Fon, Edo, and diaspora systems such as Santeria/Lukumi and Candomble.

gods.name: Orisha Oko
gods.description: Yoruba orisha of agriculture, farmland, and its fertility, honoured at the new-yam harvest; a specifically Yoruba figure not to be conflated with Fon Vodun or diaspora agricultural cults.

gods.name: Erinle
gods.description: Yoruba riverine orisha of hunting and healing, also known by the name Inle; associated with the Erinle river. Represented here as a single record despite the Inle name variant used in diaspora traditions.

gods.name: Aje
gods.description: Aje (Aje Saluga), the Yoruba orisha who personifies wealth, profit, and the increase of the marketplace; a distinct deity, not the general Yoruba concept of ase (divine authority) nor wealth in the abstract.

gods.name: Medeina
gods.description: Lithuanian goddess of forests, hunting, and wild animals, named among the chief Lithuanian deities in the 1249 treaty of the Teutonic Order; a distinctly Lithuanian figure, not shared uniformly across Baltic peoples.

gods.name: Potrimpo
gods.description: Old Prussian god of grain, running water, and good fortune. He is named in Prussian sources as one of a divine triad, though the fuller triadic scheme and its iconography derive largely from the later, partly unreliable chronicle of Simon Grunau; his identity as a named Prussian deity is nonetheless well established.

gods.name: Pikuolis
gods.description: Old Prussian god of death and the underworld (also Patollo or Peckols), paired with Potrimpo and Perkunas in the Prussian triad. As with Potrimpo, the systematic triad is a later reconstruction, but the death-deity himself is attested across Prussian sources; a specifically Old Prussian figure.

gods.name: Jumis
gods.description: Latvian field-spirit of the harvest and fertility, personified in the double ear of grain sought at reaping to secure the next year's abundance; a specifically Latvian folk deity.

gods.name: Xiuhtecuhtli
gods.description: Aztec god of fire, the hearth, turquoise, and the turning of time and the calendar; he is closely associated with, and in many sources identified as, the aged fire god Huehueteotl, the two treated conservatively here as overlapping aspects rather than forced into a family link.

gods.name: Cihuacoatl
gods.description: Aztec earth and mother goddess connected with childbirth and with women who died in labour. The same name was also borne as the title of the senior civil official of Tenochtitlan; this record is the deity, distinct from that office.

gods.name: Itzpapalotl
gods.description: The Obsidian Butterfly, a fearsome Aztec star- and warrior-goddess of the Tamoanchan paradise; sometimes counted among but distinct from the broader collective of the Tzitzimime star-demons.

gods.name: Tlaltecuhtli
gods.description: Primordial earth-being of Nahua cosmology, torn apart by Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca to form the earth and sky. The name carries the masculine lord-title '-tecuhtli', yet the being is frequently depicted with female characteristics, and its gender varies across scholarly and iconographic descriptions.

gods.name: Xochipilli
gods.description: Aztec 'Flower Prince', god of flowers, music, dance, games, and pleasure; a male counterpart in domain to Xochiquetzal, associated with her in the sources without an asserted family or identity link here.

gods.name: Vertumnus
gods.description: Roman god of the seasons, ripening, and change, and husband of the orchard-goddess Pomona. He carries an older Etruscan background (Voltumna) but is received here as a Roman deity, not reassigned to the Etruscan pantheon.

gods.name: Juturna
gods.description: Roman goddess of springs, wells, and fountains, honoured at a pool in the Forum; in the tradition followed here she is a consort of Janus and mother of Fons.

gods.name: Fons
gods.description: Roman god of wells and springs, whose festival the Fontinalia fell in October; counted in one genealogical tradition as the son of Janus and Juturna.

gods.name: Salacia
gods.description: Roman goddess of salt water and the deep sea, the consort of Neptune. A genuinely Roman cult figure rather than merely a Latin name for the Greek Amphitrite.

gods.name: Nerio
gods.description: Archaic Roman personification of the valour and strength of Mars. The archive structures Mars's cult partners as consorts, and she is placed here accordingly; ancient and later accounts variously describe her as that martial force or explicitly as the wife of Mars.

gods.name: Tiberinus
gods.description: Personified god of the river Tiber, invoked in Roman state cult for the river central to the city. One genealogical tradition, followed here, makes him a son of Janus; this is a single account rather than an uncontested Roman genealogy.

gods.name: Ériu
gods.description: Sovereignty goddess of the Tuatha Dé Danann and eponym of Ireland (Éire), a daughter of Ernmas; her genealogy and consort traditions vary across sources, and the structured links here reflect one such tradition (consort Elatha, mother of Bres).

gods.name: Banba
gods.description: One of the three sovereignty goddesses who gave their names to Ireland, a daughter of Ernmas; her husband and further genealogy vary by source and are left to prose.

gods.name: Fódla
gods.description: One of the three sovereignty goddesses of Ireland alongside Ériu and Banba, a daughter of Ernmas; further relationships vary and are not structured here.

gods.name: Credne
gods.description: Bronze- and metal-worker of the Tuatha Dé Danann, one of the three craft-gods (trí dé dána) with the smith Goibniu and the wright Luchta.

gods.name: Luchta
gods.description: Wright and carpenter of the Tuatha Dé Danann, one of the three craft-gods with Goibniu and Credne, who together made the weapons for the second battle of Mag Tuired.

gods.name: Cian
gods.description: Father of the god Lugh in Irish tradition; Lugh's mother was Ethniu, daughter of the Fomorian Balor, named here in prose rather than as a separate record.

gods.name: Ch’aska
gods.description: Andean goddess associated with the planet Venus and the light of dawn and dusk, a herald and attendant of the sun Inti.

gods.name: Urcuchillay
gods.description: Andean protector deity of llamas and herds, identified with a dark-cloud constellation (the Llama) in the night sky and venerated by pastoralists.

gods.name: Cuniraya
gods.description: Coastal creator and trickster deity of the Huarochirí Manuscript who wandered in disguise animating the land. Though the source pairs his name with Viracocha, he is treated here as a distinct local creator-form rather than simply identified with the highland Viracocha.

gods.name: Cavillaca
gods.description: Divine maiden of the Huarochirí Manuscript who conceived a child after unknowingly eating a fruit into which Cuniraya had transformed his seed; refusing him, she fled to the sea and was turned to stone. This is not modelled as a marriage or ordinary union.

gods.name: Suwāʿ
gods.description: Pre-Islamic Arabian deity named in the Qur'an (71:23) among the idols of the people of Noah. Later Islamic historical and exegetical tradition, such as Ibn al-Kalbi's Book of Idols, describes tribal worship and a female form; these details belong to that later tradition rather than to the Qur'anic verse itself.

gods.name: Yaghūth
gods.description: Pre-Islamic Arabian deity named in the Qur'an (71:23) among the idols of Noah's people. Later Islamic tradition associates the name with particular tribes and, in some accounts, a lion form; the verse itself names only the deity.

gods.name: Yaʿūq
gods.description: Pre-Islamic Arabian deity named in the Qur'an (71:23). Later exegetical and historical tradition links the name to specific tribes and, in some accounts, a horse form, which are not stated directly in the verse.

gods.name: Nasr
gods.description: Pre-Islamic Arabian deity named in the Qur'an (71:23). Later Islamic tradition associates the name with tribal worship and, in some accounts, a vulture or eagle form; the Qur'anic verse names only the deity.

gods.name: Almaqah
gods.description: Chief national deity of the ancient South Arabian kingdom of Saba, worshipped prominently at the Awwam sanctuary (Mahram Bilqis) near Marib and attested also in the Ethio-Sabaean sphere. His lunar versus solar character is a disputed scholarly classification and he is not linked structurally to another astral deity here.

gods.name: Tsovinar
gods.description: Armenian goddess associated with the sea, rain, and storm; a fiery water-being in tradition. Later epic genealogies attached to her name are left to prose rather than structured fields.

gods.name: Barsamin
gods.description: Armenian god of the sky and weather whose name and cult derive from the West Semitic Baʿal Šamem (Baʿal Shamin, 'lord of the heavens'); he is kept here as a distinct Armenian record without a merged or structured Semitic parallel.

gods.name: Hayk
gods.description: Legendary ancestral patriarch and culture hero of the Armenians, the master archer who in tradition slew the tyrant Bel and led his people to their homeland; no royal genealogy is opened here.

gods.name: Ara the Beautiful
gods.description: Legendary Armenian king renowned for his beauty. In the preserved legend the Assyrian queen Shamiram (Semiramis) desired him, he fell in battle against her, and she sought to have him restored to life. Later scholars have interpreted the figure in terms of fertility or a dying-and-returning divinity; that reading is noted only as interpretation.

gods.name: Thánh Gióng
gods.description: Phù Đổng Thiên Vương, the boy of Vietnamese legend who grew overnight into a giant warrior and, riding an iron horse, drove off invaders before ascending to heaven; counted among the Four Immortals of Vietnamese tradition.

gods.name: Chử Đồng Tử
gods.description: A poor marshland fisherman of Vietnamese legend who, through virtue and a fated marriage, attained immortality; one of the Four Immortals. His wife Tiên Dung is mentioned here in prose only.

gods.name: Liễu Hạnh
gods.description: Princess Liễu Hạnh, a principal deity of the Vietnamese Đạo Mẫu (Mother Goddess) tradition and one of the Four Immortals; her role is specifically that of the venerated Mother Goddess rather than a generic creator or universal mother-goddess.

gods.name: Ité
gods.description: In the Oglala Lakota narrative recorded by James R. Walker, the wife of the Wind Tate and mother of the wind-brothers; for her vanity she was doubled into the beautiful-and-terrible Aŋúŋg Ité (Double-Face Woman). This is the Oglala corpus and not a single account shared identically by every Lakota community.

gods.name: Yata
gods.description: Eldest son of Tate and Ité and the North Wind in the Oglala Lakota corpus recorded by Walker; disgraced, he was set to the cold north.

gods.name: Eya
gods.description: Son of Tate and Ité and the West Wind in the Oglala Lakota corpus; granted the first place among the directions, associated with the coming of storms.

gods.name: Yanpa
gods.description: Son of Tate and Ité and the East Wind in the Oglala Lakota corpus, associated with the dawn.

gods.name: Okaga
gods.description: Son of Tate and Ité and the South Wind in the Oglala Lakota corpus, associated with warmth and growth; the falling-star goddess Wohpe came to dwell with him.

gods.name: Yumni
gods.description: The Whirlwind, fifth and youngest son of Tate and Ité in the Oglala Lakota corpus recorded by Walker; a small, restless power associated with games, chance, and love.

gods.name: Sáráhkká
gods.description: Most venerated of the Áhkká, daughters of Máttaráhkká in Sámi tradition; goddess of childbirth, menstruation, and women, dwelling beneath the hearth. Sámi belief varied by region and is not a single uniform pantheon.

gods.name: Juksáhkká
gods.description: The 'bow-woman' among the Áhkká, a daughter of Máttaráhkká who guards children and was said to influence a child's sex; regional traditions differ.

gods.name: Uksáhkká
gods.description: The 'door-woman' among the Áhkká, a daughter of Máttaráhkká who watches the doorway and protects the newborn as it enters the world; regional traditions differ.

gods.name: Rávdna
gods.description: Sámi goddess associated with the rowan tree and its berries, honoured as the consort of the thunder-god Horagalles; the pairing and her rowan symbolism show regional variation and possible Scandinavian influence.

gods.name: Beaivi-nieida
gods.description: The daughter of the Sámi sun-mother Beaivi, a figure of light and the returning sun; represented in tradition as Beaivi's daughter rather than as an epithet or alternate form of the sun herself.

gods.name: Wakka-us-Kamuy
gods.description: Ainu kamuy of fresh water, springs, and wells. In Ainu understanding a kamuy is a spirit-being present in a thing or force and does not map exactly onto the Western category 'god'.

gods.name: Kanna-Kamuy
gods.description: Ainu kamuy of thunder and lightning, envisaged in serpent- or dragon-like form. As with all kamuy, the term denotes a spirit-being rather than a 'god' in the Western sense.

gods.name: Hash-inau-uk-Kamuy
gods.description: Ainu kamuy of the hunt and the forest, invoked for success in taking game. A kamuy is a spirit-being of a place or activity, not straightforwardly a 'god'.

gods.name: Shiramba-Kamuy
gods.description: Ainu kamuy of vegetation, trees, and growing wood. The kamuy category describes a spirit-being immanent in the plant world rather than a Western deity.

gods.name: Pauchi-Kamuy
gods.description: Ainu kamuy associated with madness and mental affliction, a harmful spirit-being named in Ainu tradition; a kamuy in the Ainu sense rather than a 'god' in the Western sense.

gods.name: Birrahgnooloo
gods.description: In the southeastern Australian traditions of the Kamilaroi and Wiradjuri, the wife of the sky-father Baiame and a goddess of fertility and floodwaters; this is a regional tradition, not a continent-wide Aboriginal mythology.

gods.name: Daramulum
gods.description: In southeastern Australian (Kamilaroi and Wiradjuri) tradition, a sky-being and son of Baiame and Birrahgnooloo, associated with male initiation and the sound of the bullroarer; a regional figure, not universal across Aboriginal Australia.

gods.name: Barrginj
gods.description: In the western Arnhem Land tradition of the Kunwinjku, the wife of Namarrgon the 'Lightning Man'; a regional Arnhem Land figure distinct from the southeastern sky-father traditions.

gods.name: Arasy
gods.description: In popular Paraguayan Guaraní tradition, the 'mother of the heavens' paired with the thunder-god Tupã in the creation of the first people; this completes the Tupã–Arasy pairing already carried by the Tupã record.

gods.name: Jakaira
gods.description: In the Mbyá-Guaraní cycle recorded by León Cadogan, one of the divine 'fathers' whom Ñamandú brought forth through sacred speech; lord of the life-giving mist and the origin of good words. His link to Ñamandú is one of divine origination in Mbyá sacred language rather than ordinary biological descent.

gods.name: Karai
gods.description: In the Mbyá-Guaraní cycle recorded by León Cadogan, one of the divine 'fathers' brought forth by Ñamandú; lord of the sacred flame and its sound. As with Jakaira, his relation to Ñamandú is divine origination through sacred speech, not ordinary parentage.

gods.name: Máni
gods.description: The personified Moon of Norse cosmology, son of Mundilfari and brother of the Sun; he guides the moon's course and is pursued by a wolf. Accounts vary in detail across the Eddic sources.

gods.name: Sól
gods.description: The personified Sun of Norse cosmology, daughter of Mundilfari and sister of Máni, who drives the sun's chariot pursued by a wolf. She is also called Sunna; that alternate name is noted here without a separate record.

gods.name: Mundilfari
gods.description: Father of Sól and Máni in Norse tradition, who named his radiant children after the sun and moon; the gods, angered by his presumption, set the children in the sky to guide those lights.

gods.name: Eurynome
gods.description: In Hesiod's Theogony, the Oceanid daughter of Oceanus and Tethys who bore the three Graces (Charites) to Zeus; her parentage and Zeus's fatherhood are given in prose. Other traditions — notably the Orphic/Pelasgian cosmogony in which a creator-goddess Eurynome danced the world into being — use the same name for a different figure.

gods.name: Perses (Titan)
gods.description: A second-generation Titan, son of Crius and Eurybia, husband of the Titaness Asteria and father of Hecate (all given in prose here). He is distinct from the hero Perseus and from Perses the son of Helios. The association with 'destruction' rests largely on his name's etymology and is not treated as an established ancient cult domain.

gods.name: Campe
gods.description: In later mythographic tradition, the monstrous she-being set by Cronus to guard the Cyclopes and Hundred-Handers in Tartarus, slain by Zeus so he could free them. Her role appears in mythographers rather than as part of one uniform early Greek canon.

gods.name: Python
gods.description: The great serpent of Delphi, offspring of the earth, slain by Apollo who then claimed the oracle (Gaia and Apollo associations given in prose). Ancient sources vary, some describing the Delphic dragon as female; the male Python is the more common later form.

gods.name: Proteus
gods.description: The 'Old Man of the Sea' of Homeric tradition, a shape-changing sea-god and herdsman of seals who prophesies to those who can hold him fast. He is distinct from Egyptian king traditions and later literary figures bearing the same name.

gods.name: Ayida-Wedo
gods.description: The rainbow-serpent lwa of Haitian Vodou, paired with Damballa as a serpent couple of fertility and cosmic continuity; the exact relationship model varies across Vodou houses and lineages.

gods.name: La Sirène
gods.description: The mermaid lwa of the sea, wealth, and music in Haitian Vodou, associated with Agwe as a lord and lady of the waters; her associations differ by house and rite.

gods.name: Ti-Jean Petro
gods.description: A lwa of the fiery Petro rite in Haitian Vodou, linked in tradition with Marinette; the specific relationships and characterizations vary among Vodou lineages.

gods.name: Azaka (Kouzen)
gods.description: Kouzen Zaka (Azaka Mede), the peasant-farmer lwa of Haitian Vodou, patron of agriculture, the countryside, and rural labour; this record represents that figure rather than collapsing several agricultural lwa.

gods.name: Papa Loko
gods.description: The lwa of plants, herbal healing, and the Vodou priesthood in Haiti, guardian of sacred trees and patron of the houngan and mambo. He shares a name-root with the Fon deity Loko but is treated here as a distinct Haitian Vodou figure, with no asserted literal identity or structured cross-pantheon link.

gods.name: Sisiutl
gods.description: In Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, the great double-headed serpent, a powerful and ambivalent supernatural being: dangerous to the unworthy yet a source of protection, strength, and power to those who face it rightly. Related double-headed serpent beings appear among other Northwest Coast peoples and are not collapsed into this one figure.

gods.name: Bakbakwalanooksiwae
gods.description: The 'Cannibal-at-the-North-End-of-the-World' of Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, the towering supernatural being at the heart of the Hamatsa ceremonial complex, whose encounter and taming are re-enacted in initiation. Only the publicly established outline is given here, without restricted ceremonial detail.

gods.name: Qamaits
gods.description: In Nuxalk (Bella Coola) tradition, a powerful sky-dwelling goddess associated with warfare and with acts of creation and world-ordering; a specifically Nuxalk figure, not generalized to all Northwest Coast peoples.

gods.name: Black God (Haashchééshzhiní)
gods.description: A Diné (Navajo) Holy Person, the fire-bringer credited in ceremonial tradition with placing the stars and constellations in the night sky; his associations belong to ceremonial narrative rather than to a Western-style pantheon.

gods.name: Calling God (Haashchééʼooghaan)
gods.description: A Diné Holy Person often paired with Talking God, from whom he is distinct; the 'Calling God' or House God, associated in ceremonial tradition with dwellings, crops, and the calling that opens ceremony.

gods.name: Water Sprinkler (Tó Neinilí)
gods.description: A Diné Holy Person, the rain-bringing 'Water Sprinkler', who in the same ceremonial tradition also takes the role of the sacred clown; both aspects belong to this single named figure.

gods.name: Opiyelguobirán
gods.description: A Taíno cemí of dog-like form associated with the guarding of the dead, recorded in the early account attributed to Ramón Pané, in which the being repeatedly slips away toward the swamp at night; details beyond that early, limited colonial source are treated cautiously.

gods.name: Baibrama
gods.description: A Taíno cemí associated with cassava (yuca) and its cultivation, invoked in Pané's account for the growth of the crop and for healing the sickness caused by its raw poison; represented as one such cemí rather than a single universal supreme agricultural deity.

gods.name: Deminán Caracaracol
gods.description: In the Taíno origin narrative recorded by Ramón Pané, one of four brothers and a culture hero whose deeds — including the origin of the sea and of the first woman-figures — shape the world. He is one of the four brothers, not a stand-in for all of them; no structured kin links are asserted in this batch.

gods.name: Antü
gods.description: In Mapuche cosmology, the sun and a principal celestial being of the sky, paired with the moon Küyen; accounts of the Mapuche divine order vary across communities and periods.

gods.name: Küyen
gods.description: In Mapuche cosmology, the moon and a principal celestial being of the night, paired with the sun Antü; representations differ across Mapuche traditions and sources.

gods.name: Kuntu Zangmo
gods.description: In Yungdrung Bon (and paralleled in Nyingma), the primordial female principle paired with Kuntu Zangpo; the two represent wisdom and method as inseparable primordial aspects rather than an ordinary married couple. The relationship is a yab-yum unity of the enlightened base.

gods.name: Tsewang Rigdzin
gods.description: In Bon tradition a son of the sage Drenpa Namkha, a master associated with the attainment of long life (a vidyadhara of longevity); his mother is not the focus of the lineage account and is left to prose.

gods.name: Shenlha Ökar
gods.description: In Yungdrung Bon, one of the Four Transcendent Lords (bder gshegs gtso bzhi), the luminous deity of compassion and light. The grouping is a set of transcendent principles, not an ordinary family or creator hierarchy.

gods.name: Satrig Ersang
gods.description: In Yungdrung Bon, one of the Four Transcendent Lords, the great mother and goddess of wisdom (also known as Sherab Chamma); a transcendent principle within the Bon fourfold, alongside Tonpa Shenrab, Shenlha Ökar, and Sangpo Bumtri.

gods.name: Sangpo Bumtri
gods.description: In Yungdrung Bon, one of the Four Transcendent Lords, associated with the manifestation and ordering of the world; a transcendent principle of the Bon fourfold rather than a biological creator-god.

gods.name: Third Messenger
gods.description: In Manichaean cosmology, an emanated luminous being (the tertius legatus) sent to set in motion the machinery by which imprisoned Light is drawn back toward the Kingdom of Light; a stable named being, not a biological offspring.

gods.name: Maiden of Light
gods.description: In Manichaean cosmology, the luminous Virgin of Light who appears to the powers of Darkness so that the Light they have swallowed may be released; an emanated being defined by role rather than by family descent.

gods.name: Diyan Masalanta
gods.description: A goddess of love, conception, and childbirth honoured in the Tagalog region, remembered in early Spanish-period accounts as a deity invoked by lovers. As with much precolonial Philippine religion, the surviving evidence is fragmentary and filtered through colonial sources.

gods.name: Anitun Tabu
gods.description: A capricious goddess of wind and rain of Central Luzon, best attested among the Sambal (Zambales) rather than as a strictly Tagalog figure, invoked and appeased for storms. The precise attributes survive mainly through early ethnographic reports and are treated cautiously.

gods.name: Heno (Hino)
gods.description: The Thunderer of Haudenosaunee (notably Seneca) tradition, wielder of lightning and bringer of rains who wars on monsters, as recorded in nineteenth-century sources such as Erminnie A. Smith's Myths of the Iroquois (1883).

gods.name: Eithinoha
gods.description: In the Haudenosaunee tradition recorded by Erminnie A. Smith (1883), 'the earth, our mother', the source of vegetation and mother of the grain-maiden Onatha.

gods.name: Onatha
gods.description: In the same Haudenosaunee tradition (Smith, 1883), the maiden of the grain and daughter of Eithinoha, whose seasonal loss and recovery mirror the growth of the crops; a distinct named figure rather than the collective Three Sisters.

gods.name: Torngarsuk
gods.description: In Greenlandic (Kalaallit) tradition, a great and ambivalent spirit invoked by the angakkoq (shaman) as chief of the helping-spirits and, in several accounts, a master of the sea-animals; his exact nature and rank vary considerably between sources and regions.

gods.name: Qailertetang
gods.description: Among the Central Inuit of Baffin Island, a weather-spirit and guardian of animals connected with the autumn sea-goddess ceremonies, as recorded by Franz Boas in The Central Eskimo (1888); a regional figure, not a universal Inuit deity.

gods.name: Abraxas
gods.description: In the Basilidean system, transmitted mainly through hostile heresiologists, the great ruler over 365 heavens (the letters of his name summing to 365). In certain Sethian Nag Hammadi texts an entity Abrasax instead appears among the powers of light rather than as an evil archon; the sources do not agree and are treated separately.

gods.name: Sabaoth (Gnostic ruler)
gods.description: In Sethian cosmologies such as the Hypostasis of the Archons and On the Origin of the World, a ruler and son of the Demiurge Yaldabaoth who turns against his father, is exalted for it, and is set over the seventh heaven. This record is that Gnostic ruler specifically, not the biblical divine title 'Lord of Hosts'.

gods.name: Norea
gods.description: In Sethian texts such as the Hypostasis of the Archons and the Thought of Norea, a revelatory heroine associated with the line of Seth who resists the archons and is aided by a luminous power; a human-associated salvific figure rather than a creator goddess or aeon.

gods.name: Sopdet (Sothis)
gods.description: Deification of the star Sirius, whose heliacal rising heralded the Nile inundation. With Sah (Orion) she forms an astral couple, and their son is the falcon-god Sopdu. This astral family is distinct from the later syncretism that linked Sah with Osiris and Sopdet with Isis.

gods.name: Sah (Orion)
gods.description: Deification of the constellation Orion, 'father of the gods' among the stars; with Sopdet (Sirius) his consort, father of Sopdu. In later theology Sah was assimilated to Osiris, but here he is the older astral figure of the Pyramid Texts.

gods.name: Menhit
gods.description: Lioness war-goddess of Upper Egypt, worshipped at Esna where local theology made her, with the ram-god Khnum, a parent of the child-god Heka. Other regional traditions give Heka different mothers; she is also at times syncretised with Neith.

gods.name: Tjenenet
gods.description: A Theban goddess of childbirth and brewing associated with the war-god Montu at Armant. She is one of several consorts linked to Montu in Theban tradition, alongside Iunit and Raet-Tawy, and is not presented as his universal or sole consort.

gods.name: Aya
gods.description: Akkadian goddess of the dawn and consort of the sun-god Shamash (Sumerian Utu); the Sumerian form of this dawn-bride is Sherida, understood here as the same identity rather than a separate record.

gods.name: Bau
gods.description: A healing and mother goddess of the Lagash region, chiefly the consort of Ningirsu — whom this archive treats within the single Ninurta record — hence her placement as a consort of Ninurta. In later tradition Bau was increasingly identified with the healing goddess Gula, though the two have distinct origins.

gods.name: Gugalanna
gods.description: In the myth of Inanna's Descent, the husband of the underworld queen Ereshkigal whose funeral Inanna claims to attend. Scholars have debated an identification with the 'Bull of Heaven' slain in the Gilgamesh tradition, and with Ennugi; those equations are uncertain and no bull-genealogy is asserted here.

gods.name: Ningirida
gods.description: Goddess of the netherworld family, consort of Ninazu and mother of Ningishzida; distinct from the similarly named reed-goddess Ningikuga.

gods.name: Kotoshironushi
gods.description: A son of Okuninushi and a kami of oracles and the sea; in the Kuni-yuzuri narrative he counsels the ceding of the land to the heavenly deities. Accounts differ between the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki over the details of that episode.

gods.name: Takemikazuchi
gods.description: A thunder- and sword-god born from the blood of the slain fire-kami, sent to pacify the Central Land; the tutelary deity of Kashima Shrine. He acts alongside — but is not identical to — Futsunushi in the land-subjugation narratives, with the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki weighting their roles differently.

gods.name: Futsunushi
gods.description: A sword-god and tutelary deity of Katori Shrine, prominent in the Nihon Shoki account of the pacification of the land, where he is paired with Takemikazuchi; the two are distinct kami rather than alternate names.

gods.name: Toyouke
gods.description: Toyouke-Ōmikami, goddess of food, agriculture, and grain, enshrined at the Outer Shrine (Gekū) of Ise to provide sustenance for Amaterasu. She is distinct from the food-deities Ukemochi and Ōgetsuhime and from later syncretic identifications.

gods.name: Airmed
gods.description: A healing goddess of the Tuatha Dé Danann, daughter of the physician Dian Cécht; after her brother Miach's death she sorted the healing herbs that grew from his grave until her grieving father scattered them.

gods.name: Miach
gods.description: A healer of the Tuatha Dé Danann, son of Dian Cécht, who restored the severed arm of Nuada with living flesh, surpassing his father's silver replacement; Dian Cécht killed him in jealousy.

gods.name: Ethniu
gods.description: Daughter of the Fomorian Balor and mother of the god Lugh (by Cian of the Tuatha Dé), through whom the prophecy that Balor would be slain by his grandson was fulfilled. Her name also appears as Ethliu or Eithne; the Balor and Cian ties are given in prose.

gods.name: Midir
gods.description: A lord of the Tuatha Dé Danann associated with the otherworld sídhe of Brí Léith, named as a son of the Dagda; a proud and wealthy figure of the wooing-tales.

gods.name: Kalma
gods.description: A goddess of death and the stench of decay in Finnish folk tradition, a daughter of Tuoni and Tuonetar who dwell in the underworld Tuonela; one of the death-realm's personifications rather than a Kalevala protagonist.

gods.name: Kivutar
gods.description: A goddess of pain and suffering in Finnish folk poetry, a daughter of Tuoni and Tuonetar, invoked in healing charms to gather and carry away pain.

gods.name: Vammatar
gods.description: A goddess of disease, injury, and misfortune in Finnish folk tradition, a daughter of Tuoni and Tuonetar of Tuonela; a personification of affliction in the charm-poetry.

gods.name: Hvovi
gods.description: In Avestan tradition the wife of the prophet Zarathustra, of the Hvōgva family; a legendary human rather than a divinity. Later Zoroastrian traditions differ over Zarathustra's marriages and children.

gods.name: Vivanghvant
gods.description: In the Avesta, the first mortal to press the sacred Haoma, and for that devotion rewarded with the son Yima; a legendary human progenitor, not a god.

gods.name: Tishtrya
gods.description: The yazata of the star Sirius, bringer of the rains, who does battle with the drought-demon Apaosha to release the waters; a divine being of the Avestan hymns.

gods.name: Rashnu
gods.description: The yazata of justice who, with Mithra and Sraosha, weighs the souls of the dead at the Chinvat Bridge; a divinity of righteous judgment.

gods.name: Atar
gods.description: The divinity of fire in Zoroastrianism, the sacred flame of the rituals and son of Ahura Mazda in Avestan idiom; the fire-yazata is distinguished from ordinary physical fire, which is its visible token rather than a separate being.

gods.name: Haoma
gods.description: The divine being Haoma, yazata of the sacred plant and of healing and vital force. The tradition distinguishes the god Haoma from the ritual plant and from the pressed sacred drink that bears the same name.

gods.name: Juventas
gods.description: Roman personification and cult goddess of youth and of young men taking the toga of manhood, with a shrine on the Capitoline. Later mythography made her a daughter of Juno (and Jupiter) and equated her with the Greek Hebe; those genealogical and Greek associations are secondary to her Roman cult.

gods.name: Canens
gods.description: A Latin nymph and personification of song in Ovid's Metamorphoses, wife of Picus; after Circe transformed him she wasted away into nothing but voice. A literary figure rather than an independently attested major cult goddess.

gods.name: Marica
gods.description: A nymph of the coastal marshes near Minturnae in Latium, honoured in a sacred grove; in the Latian tradition followed here she is the mother, by Faunus, of King Latinus.

gods.name: Hora
gods.description: In Roman tradition the deified form of Hersilia, wife of Romulus, taken up to the heavens and given the name Hora as the consort of the deified Romulus under his divine name Quirinus.

gods.name: Flora
gods.description: Roman goddess of flowers, blossoming plants, and spring, honoured at the exuberant Floralia games; an old Italic cult figure with her own flamen, not merely a Latin rendering of a Greek flower-goddess.

gods.name: Leigong
gods.description: The Duke of Thunder in Chinese folk and Daoist religion, a beaked, winged deity who executes heaven's punishments by striking the guilty with thunder. In a later popular story he is paired in marriage with the lightning goddess Dianmu, but that tale does not define his older role.

gods.name: Dianmu
gods.description: The Mother of Lightning in Chinese folk religion, who flashes her mirrors to light the way before Leigong's thunder so the innocent are spared. A later explanatory tale makes her his wife, but her identity as the lightning goddess is primary.

gods.name: Caishen
gods.description: Cáishén, the 'God of Wealth' of Chinese popular religion — not a single biography but a divine office invoked for prosperity, identified across traditions with several figures such as the martial Zhao Gongming and the civil wealth-gods (Bi Gan, Fan Li). This record represents that composite title rather than one person.

gods.name: Zhurong
gods.description: A fire deity of early Chinese mythology; the name also denotes an office of fire and appears in some texts as a divine official or culture hero. He is remembered for his cosmic battle with the water-god Gonggong, related here as narrative rather than genealogy.

gods.name: Gonggong
gods.description: A monstrous water-deity of early Chinese myth associated with floods and cosmic disorder, who in the tradition struck Mount Buzhou and tilted the heavens; his conflict with Zhurong and the damage to the world-pillar are kept as narrative, not family relationships.

gods.name: Xpiyacoc
gods.description: In the K'iche' Popol Vuh, the aged diviner and matchmaker who with his wife Xmucane forms the elder grandparent pair consulted at creation; their ancestral and creative roles are described in prose rather than structured as ordinary genealogy.

gods.name: Hun-Came
gods.description: In the K'iche' Popol Vuh, 'One Death', one of the two supreme lords who rule the underworld Xibalba and preside over its councils and deadly trials, alongside Vucub-Came.

gods.name: Vucub-Came
gods.description: In the K'iche' Popol Vuh, 'Seven Death', the second of the two supreme lords of Xibalba who, with Hun-Came, sets the ordeals that the Hero Twins ultimately overturn.

gods.name: Zipacna
gods.description: In the K'iche' Popol Vuh, a boastful mountain-making demon who claimed to raise the mountains overnight; a son of Vucub-Caquix (noted in prose), he slew the Four Hundred Boys before the Hero Twins destroyed him.

gods.name: Cabracan
gods.description: In the K'iche' Popol Vuh, the earthquake-demon who threw down mountains, a son of Vucub-Caquix (noted in prose); the Hero Twins subdued him by feeding him a poisoned bird and burying him.

gods.name: Efnysien
gods.description: In the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, a half-brother of Brân and Branwen (son of Penarddun) whose spiteful mutilation of Matholwch's horses helps ignite the war with Ireland, and who finally destroys the magic cauldron at the cost of his life. A tragic saga figure, not a god of discord.

gods.name: Nisien
gods.description: In the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, the gentle half-brother of Efnysien (son of Penarddun), remembered as one who would make peace where his brother made strife; a narrative foil rather than a deity of peace.

gods.name: Gwern
gods.description: In the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, the infant son of Branwen and the Irish king Matholwch (given in prose), briefly made king of Ireland before Efnysien cast him into the fire, precipitating the final slaughter.

gods.name: Cigfa
gods.description: In the Third Branch of the Mabinogi, the wife of Pryderi, who endures the enchantment that empties Dyfed alongside Manawydan and Rhiannon; a legendary human of the tales.

gods.name: Rugievit
gods.description: A god of the Rani of Rügen, recorded at the temple of Charenza (Karenz) by Saxo Grammaticus, whose great idol had seven faces and seven swords at his belt; the account associates him with war.

gods.name: Porevit
gods.description: A god of the Rani of Rügen worshipped at Charenza alongside Rugievit and Porenut, described by Saxo Grammaticus as having a five-headed idol; his specific functions are not securely recorded and no invented role is asserted here.

gods.name: Porenut
gods.description: A god of the Rani of Rügen worshipped at Charenza, whose idol Saxo Grammaticus describes with four faces and a fifth upon its breast; his precise functions are unknown, and he is not equated with Svantovit or the other Rani gods.

gods.name: Rūaumoko
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the atua of earthquakes and volcanoes, the youngest child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku (given in prose) who remains within his mother the earth and whose movements are felt as tremors; a specifically Māori figure.

gods.name: Whiro
gods.description: In Māori tradition, an atua of darkness and illness and an adversary of Tāne, associated with the underworld and with malign forces; a Māori figure distinct from the Tahitian hero Hiro and other cognate island beings.

gods.name: Tinirau
gods.description: In Māori tradition, a guardian of fish and sea creatures connected with the ocean cycles and the tales of Hina and the whale Tutunui; represented here in the Māori tradition rather than merged with all cognate Polynesian forms.

gods.name: Mālik
gods.description: Angel set over Hell (Jahannam). Named in Qur'an 43:77, where the damned call to him to have their Lord finish them and he answers that they will remain. Tradition gives him charge of the Fire as its keeper — an office, not authorship of its torment.

gods.name: Riḍwān
gods.description: Angel said to guard the gates of Paradise (Jannah), and the counterpart of Mālik. He is not named in the Qur'an, where riḍwān is God's 'good pleasure' rather than a person; the name belongs to later Islamic tradition and popular piety — as does the name Azrael for the angel of death.

gods.name: Hārūt
gods.description: One of the two angels at Babylon in Qur'an 2:102, which says they taught men what became sorcery while warning, 'We are only a trial (fitna); do not disbelieve.' Later exegesis divides sharply — some read the pair as angels tested and fallen, others as warners whose knowledge was misused. The Qur'anic wording itself does not call them evil.

gods.name: Mārūt
gods.description: The second angel of Babylon named in Qur'an 2:102, always paired with Hārūt and never appearing alone. Their status is disputed across the commentary tradition; the Qur'an presents them as a trial (fitna) rather than as fallen or malevolent angels.

gods.name: Adam
gods.description: The first man of Genesis, formed from the earth (adamah) and set in Eden. Later Jewish folklore — chiefly the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira — gave him a first wife before Eve, Lilith, who left him for demanding she lie beneath him. That tradition is late and legendary rather than biblical, and is kept here in prose rather than built into the family tree.

gods.name: Ziz
gods.description: Giant bird of rabbinic aggadah, its name taken from a reading of the 'ziz sadai' of Psalm 50:11. In Bava Batra 73b and later midrash he stands beside Behemoth and Leviathan, and the three are served at the banquet of the righteous at the end of days. The tidy land-sea-air scheme is a later systematization; the sources themselves vary.

gods.name: Raziel
gods.description: Angel of divine secrets. Not a biblical figure: the name belongs to Jewish mystical and magical literature, above all the medieval Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh, said to be the book of mysteries given to Adam after his expulsion. Later occult writers enlarged the role far beyond its Jewish sources.

gods.name: Sandalphon
gods.description: Towering angel of the rabbinic and Hekhalot traditions; in Hagigah 13b he overtops his fellows by a journey of five hundred years, and later texts have him weave Israel's prayers into crowns. Medieval tradition links him to the ascended Elijah and sets him beside Metatron — associations of legend, not genealogy.

gods.name: Adam Kadmon
gods.description: 'Primordial Man' — in Lurianic Kabbalah the first configuration to arise in the void left by the tsimtsum, the form through which the lights of emanation are ordered. Not the Adam of Genesis and not a human being: a schematic first shape of the divine, described in the image of a body only because the sefirot are mapped onto it.

gods.name: Arich Anpin
gods.description: 'The Long Face' — the partzuf, or divine configuration, of unbounded mercy and patience, developed in the Idrot of the Zohar and in Lurianic Kabbalah out of the sefirah Keter. A configuration rather than a person; the masculine form is grammatical and symbolic, as with the father-principle of Chokhmah.

gods.name: Zeir Anpin
gods.description: 'The Short Face' — the partzuf gathering the six sefirot around Tiferet: the divine turned toward the world, impatient and capable of judgment, over against the boundless forbearance of Arich Anpin. Its union with the partzuf Nukva is a central concern of Lurianic prayer. A configuration, not a mythological person.

gods.name: Aso
gods.description: Wife of Kwaku Anansi in the Akan anansesem, the spider-tales, and often the sharper of the two — in a number of stories the scheme Anansi carries off and takes credit for is hers. The corpus is oral and its tellers differ; her role varies from tale to tale.

gods.name: Bosomtwe
gods.description: The abosom of Lake Bosomtwe, the crater lake south-east of Kumasi and the holiest water of the Asante. The name carries both the lake and its god. Asante tradition held that the souls of the dead came to the lake to take their leave of him, and fishing there was hedged about with prohibitions. Reckoned, with Tano and Bia, among the abosom — the children of Nyame.

gods.name: Amokye
gods.description: The old woman who receives the dead at the river bordering Asamando, the Asante land of the dead, hauling them from the water and taking their beads as they pass — recorded in Asante ethnography, notably Rattray's. A gatekeeper at the crossing rather than a ruler of the dead; death itself is Owuo.

gods.name: Seh₂ul
gods.description: Reconstructed Proto-Indo-European sun — *Seh₂ul, also given as *Sóh₂wĺ — a reconstruction, not an attested deity. The word is secure and its reflexes are everywhere (Sūrya, Hēlios, Sōl, Saulė, Sunna, Sól); how far a personal sun-god, as against the sun itself, can be reconstructed is less certain, and the daughter traditions do not even agree on the sun's gender — feminine in Germanic and Baltic, masculine in Vedic and Greek.

gods.name: Yemós
gods.description: Reconstructed Proto-Indo-European primordial twin — *Yemós, 'twin' — the first mortal, dismembered so that the ordered world could be made from his body. A reconstruction rather than an attested god, and a contested one: Yama, Yima, Ymir and Remus are the usual comparanda, and in one influential account he is killed by his brother, the first sacrificer. Whether he is best read as the first man, the first victim, or the first of the dead is not agreed.

gods.name: Bodb Derg
gods.description: Son of the Dagda, chosen king of the Tuatha Dé Danann after their retreat into the síde. In the Mythological Cycle he presides over the Otherworld mounds and is the foster-father in the tale of the Children of Lir.

gods.name: Fand
gods.description: Otherworld woman, wife of Manannán mac Lir. In the Ulster Cycle tale Serglige Con Culainn she draws Cú Chulainn to her, and Manannán at last shakes his cloak between them so that they may never meet again. Her name is glossed 'tear' or 'pearl of beauty'.

gods.name: Nechtan
gods.description: Guardian of the hidden well of wisdom, whose waters only he and his cupbearers might approach. When his wife Boann circled it in defiance the well rose against her and became the river Boyne. Sometimes identified with Nuada; the sources vary.

gods.name: Balor
gods.description: King of the Fomorians in Cath Maige Tuired, whose single eye laid waste to whatever it looked upon and needed four men to lift its lid. Warned that his own grandson would kill him, he shut his daughter Ethniu away — and was killed at Mag Tuired by her son Lugh, who put the eye out with a sling-stone.

gods.name: Donn
gods.description: 'The Dark One'. In Lebor Gabála he is a son of Míl and the first of the Gaels to die in the taking of Ireland, buried on the rock called Tech Duinn — the House of Donn — off the south-west coast, where medieval texts say the dead gather before departing. Later folklore makes him a storm- and death-figure. Whether he was first a death-god later written down as a mortal ancestor, or an ancestor who acquired the office, is disputed; 'lord of the dead' is a modern summary, not an attested title.

gods.name: Ḫaya
gods.description: God of the scribal craft and of the storehouse, husband of the grain- and writing-goddess Nisaba. The god-lists (An = Anum and related traditions) make him the father of Ninlil; this is not the only account — the tale of Enlil and Ninlil gives her mother as Nunbaršegunu and names no father. The genealogy here follows the god-list tradition and is not universal.

gods.name: Šara
gods.description: City-god of Umma, a warrior god called the son of Inanna in Sumerian tradition. In Inanna's Descent he abases himself before her and is spared from being given to the galla in her place.

gods.name: Kittum
gods.description: Truth personified, a daughter of the sun-god Utu/Šamaš, who judges by daylight. She stands with Mišaru (justice) as an attendant of his court — an abstraction given a person, in the manner of Mesopotamian divine bureaucracy.

gods.name: Mišaru
gods.description: Justice personified, son of Utu/Šamaš and counterpart of Kittum (truth). Associated with the royal mīšarum edicts that cancelled debts and 'set things right' at the start of a reign.

gods.name: Ningikuga
gods.description: 'Lady of the pure reed' — a goddess of the reed-marshes. In the Sumerian god-list tradition she is a daughter of An, and by Enki the mother of Ningal. The name is used of more than one figure in the sources, and the Enki marriage is given in prose here rather than in the structured family.

gods.name: Omoikane
gods.description: The kami of deliberation, whose name suggests the gathering of many thoughts into one. In the Kojiki the gods call on him when Amaterasu shuts herself in the rock-cave, and it is his plan — the mirror, the jewels and the cock-crow — that draws her out.

gods.name: Sarutahiko
gods.description: Earthly kami who stands at the eight crossroads of heaven, huge and long-nosed, and guides Ninigi's descent to the islands. Ame-no-Uzume alone dares to face him and is afterwards given to him; shrine tradition later ties him to the Sarume line and to roadside guardian cults.

gods.name: Takeminakata
gods.description: Son of Ōkuninushi who refuses to yield the land and wrestles Takemikazuchi, in what the Kojiki tells as the first trial of strength. Beaten, he flees to Suwa and stays there — the deity of the Suwa shrines. The Nihon Shoki does not carry the episode; the Suwa cult has its own traditions.

gods.name: Suseri-hime
gods.description: Daughter of Susanoo and principal wife of Ōkuninushi, whom she helps through her father's ordeals in the underworld before the two escape together with his sword, bow and koto. Fierce and jealous in the Kojiki's account of his other marriages.

gods.name: Hymir
gods.description: Jötunn of the cold sea, owner of the mile-wide cauldron the gods need for their ale.
