In Hymiskviða he rows out with Thor, who hooks Jörmungandr over the gunwale, and it is there that Hymir is called Týr's father — a genealogy that flatly contradicts Snorri, who makes Týr a son of Odin.

gods.name: Sköll
gods.description: The wolf who runs behind Sól and will at the last swallow her. Grímnismál names him; the Prose Edda reckons him among the brood of Fenrir in Járnviðr. Some sources name the sun's pursuer Fenrir himself — the wolves and their tasks are not told the same way twice.

gods.name: Hati
gods.description: The wolf who runs ahead of the sun and hunts the moon, called Hati Hróðvitnisson in Grímnismál. He will catch Máni before the end. Counted with Sköll among the wolves born of Fenrir's line in the Prose Edda.

gods.name: Hœnir
gods.description: One of the three gods who walk the shore in Völuspá and make the first man and woman from two trees — Odin gives breath, Hœnir gives óðr (mind or spirit), Lóðurr gives blood and colour. Later given to the Vanir as a hostage, where Snorri makes him handsome but unable to decide anything without Mímir at his elbow. He survives Ragnarök.

gods.name: Meret
gods.description: Native Egyptian goddess of song and rejoicing, who greets the coming of the Nile flood with clapping and music. Usually doubled as Meret of Upper and Meret of Lower Egypt, and attached to Hapi as the welcome given to the inundation.

gods.name: Qetesh
gods.description: Goddess known almost entirely from Egyptian New Kingdom stelae, shown nude on a lion with lotus and serpents, and set beside Min and the Levantine Resheph. Her name is Semitic — qdš, 'the holy one' — and it is disputed whether she was an imported Levantine goddess, an Egyptian goddess given a Semitic epithet, or a title that settled into a person. She is not attested under this name in Levantine sources, and should not be silently merged with Astarte, Anat or Asherah, with whom Egyptian compound forms sometimes group her.

gods.name: Tatenen
gods.description: The risen land itself — the primeval mound emerging from the waters, worshipped at Memphis and drawn into Ptah as Ptah-Tatenen. Bearded, ram-horned, and called the father of the gods; the mines and quarries of the earth are his.

gods.name: Nehebkau
gods.description: Serpent god whose name means roughly 'he who harnesses the kas'. In the Pyramid Texts he is a danger to be warded off; later he becomes a benign guardian who binds the ka to the body and serves the dead their food in the next world.

gods.name: Hygieia
gods.description: Goddess of health, and the one to keep it rather than to restore it — where Asclepius cures, Hygieia prevents. Daughter of Asclepius in the usual account, she had her own cult at Epidaurus and Athens, and the physician's oath is sworn by both.

gods.name: Geryon
gods.description: Three-bodied giant of the far western island of Erytheia, son of Chrysaor, who kept a red herd guarded by the herdsman Eurytion and the two-headed dog Orthrus. Heracles killed all three and drove the cattle home — the tenth labour.

gods.name: Ananke
gods.description: Necessity — the compulsion that binds gods as well as men. In the Orphic cosmogonies she is a primordial power, coiled with Chronos about the world-egg; in Plato's Republic the spindle of the cosmos turns on her knees while her daughters the Fates sing. She has almost no cult and no myths of her own: she is a principle given a face.

gods.name: Niamh
gods.description: Niamh Chinn Óir, 'Niamh of the Golden Hair', who rides out of the sea on a white horse and carries Oisín away to Tír na nÓg, where three hundred years pass as three. The tale is told chiefly in the late Fenian lay of Micheál Coimín (18th century). Her father is variously given as Manannán or simply as the king of the Land of Youth, and other women named Niamh in Irish tradition are distinct figures; the parentage is left out of the structured family here.

gods.name: Caer Ibormeith
gods.description: Otherworld woman of the Aislinge Óenguso, who appears to Aengus in dreams until he sickens for want of her. She lives a year as a woman and a year as a swan; Aengus finds her among a hundred and fifty swans at Loch Bél Dracon, takes swan-shape himself, and the two fly away together.

gods.name: Étaín
gods.description: Heroine of Tochmarc Étaíne, the Mythological Cycle's tale of her wooing. Midir takes her to wife; his first wife Fuamnach drives her out by magic, and after long wandering she is reborn and married to the king of Ireland, from whom Midir wins her back at chess. Her transformations are narrative, not genealogy, and are kept out of the structured family.

gods.name: Fuamnach
gods.description: First wife of Midir in Tochmarc Étaíne, learned in magic and reared among the druids. Out of jealousy she turns Étaín into a pool, then a worm, then a purple fly, and raises a wind to blow her about Ireland for seven years. Her enchantments belong to the narrative and are not modelled as family ties.

gods.name: Lulal
gods.description: God of Bad-tibira. In the Sumerian Descent of Inanna he is one of the two gods — with Šara of Umma — who sit in dust and mourning for her and are therefore spared when the galla demand a substitute. That text calls him her son; the filiation belongs to this Sumerian tradition and is not asserted everywhere.

gods.name: Nindara
gods.description: God of Ki-esa, husband of Nanshe in the local theology of the Lagash state, where the pair are named together in the Gudea inscriptions and temple hymns. He is little more than a name outside that regional tradition.

gods.name: Nin-MAR.KI
gods.description: Goddess of Guabba on the Lagash coast, called the daughter of Nanshe in the Lagash tradition that the Gudea texts and the temple hymns record. Her name is written with the place-sign and is conventionally left untranslated; the filiation is regional, not pan-Mesopotamian.

gods.name: Hanbi
gods.description: Named almost solely in the formula the Pazuzu amulets carry: 'I am Pazuzu, son of Hanbi, king of the evil lilû-demons.' Beyond that title and the fatherhood it states, next to nothing is known of him — no myth, no cult, no independent narrative.

gods.name: Ōyamatsumi
gods.description: The great kami of the mountains, born in the Kojiki when Izanagi cuts down the fire-god. He offers both his daughters to Ninigi; when Ninigi keeps the blossom-princess and sends the rock-princess home, it is Ōyamatsumi who declares that the lives of Ninigi's descendants will therefore be brief as blossom rather than enduring as stone. Distinct from the sea-kami Ōwatatsumi.

gods.name: Ōwatatsumi
gods.description: The great kami of the sea, in whose palace beneath the waves Hoori goes to seek his brother's lost fish-hook and marries the sea-king's daughter Toyotama-hime. The Kojiki keeps him separate from the mountain-kami Ōyamatsumi; the later dragon-king Ryūjin of popular tradition is often identified with him, but that identification is not made here.

gods.name: Kushinadahime
gods.description: The last of eight daughters, and the one Susanoo saves from the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi by hiding her — in the Kojiki, as a comb set in his hair — while he makes the serpent drunk and cuts it apart. He then builds his hall at Suga and takes her to wife.

gods.name: Yakami-hime
gods.description: The princess of Inaba, whom the eighty brother-deities go to court and who chooses instead their despised younger brother Ōkuninushi — the beginning of his rise, and of his brothers' attempts to kill him. In the Kojiki she later leaves her child behind and returns home for fear of Suseri-hime.

gods.name: Iwanaga-hime
gods.description: 'Rock-Long Princess', the elder daughter of Ōyamatsumi, offered to Ninigi together with her sister Konohanasakuya-hime. Ninigi sends her back because she is not fair, and so — her father says — the lives of his line are blossom-brief instead of rock-enduring. She is the explanation the Kojiki gives for human mortality.

gods.name: Svaðilfari
gods.description: The stallion of the builder who offers to wall Asgard, and who hauls stone by night with more than a horse's strength. Loki, in the shape of a mare, lures him away so the work fails, and from that meeting is born the eight-legged Sleipnir. A mythic animal, filed under the archive's existing convention for such creatures rather than as a deity.

gods.name: Sinmara
gods.description: A figure named only in the eddic poem Fjölsvinnsmál, where she is the pale one who keeps the weapon Lævateinn locked in a chest. Almost nothing else is said of her. She is often taken as Surtr's consort, but the poem does not say so: that pairing is an inference of later readers, and it is left out of the structured family here.

gods.name: Fulla
gods.description: Goddess who carries Frigg's ashen box, looks after her shoes, and knows her secrets. Snorri lists her among the Ásynjur, unmarried, with her hair loose and a gold band about her head. The Old High German Volla of the Second Merseburg Charm — sister of Frija — is the same name in a continental form and almost certainly the same figure; she is recorded here once, not twice. Her service to Frigg is an office, not kinship, so the family fields are left empty.

gods.name: Serqet
gods.description: Scorpion-goddess, shown with the creature poised on her head, who binds venom and looses it. She guards Qebehsenuef and his canopic jar, watches over the dead with Isis, Nephthys and Neith, and stands behind the magicians who cure stings and bites. Also transliterated Serket, Selket or Selkis — spellings of one goddess, not several.

gods.name: Shai
gods.description: Fate — the span and lot allotted to a person, personified as a god who is born with them and stands by at the weighing of the heart. He is a concept given a face rather than a deity with myths of his own, and though he is often shown beside Renenutet, that pairing is iconographic and is not made a marriage here.

gods.name: Meskhenet
gods.description: Goddess of birth, present at every delivery and identified with the brick on which Egyptian women crouched to bear — she is sometimes drawn as that brick with a human head. In the Westcar Papyrus she attends the births of the first kings of the Fifth Dynasty and fixes their fate, and she appears again at the judgment of the dead, where the birth she oversees is the second one.

gods.name: Panacea
gods.description: 'All-healing', a daughter of Asclepius, who stands for the remedy as her sister Hygieia stands for health kept. She is invoked by name in the Hippocratic oath alongside her father and sister, and belongs to the cult of healing rather than to narrative myth.

gods.name: Morpheus
gods.description: The dream that takes human shape — he can counterfeit any person's gait, face and voice, and is sent to carry the news of a death in a dream. He is essentially a figure of Ovid's Metamorphoses, one of the sons of Somnus (Hypnos) named there; the older Greek tradition speaks of the Oneiroi as a body of dreams and does not give him this role. The later 'god of dreams' of popular usage should not be read back into archaic Greece.

gods.name: Zephyrus
gods.description: The west wind, gentlest of the Anemoi, who brings the spring — though Homer also knows him as a hard, storm-bringing wind. Traditions differ on his partners: Alcaeus makes Eros the child of Iris and Zephyrus, while other accounts give him the harpy Podarge or the nymph Chloris. No one of these is universal, so none is placed in the structured family.

gods.name: Polyphemus
gods.description: The Cyclops of Odyssey 9 — son of Poseidon and the nymph Thoösa — who pens Odysseus and his men in his cave and eats them two at a time, until Odysseus blinds his single eye and escapes beneath the rams. His cry to his father is what sets Poseidon against Odysseus for the rest of the voyage. Distinct from other bearers of the name.

gods.name: Bia
gods.description: Personification of force and violent might, daughter of the Titan Pallas and the Oceanid Styx, and one of the four winged attendants who stand by Zeus with her siblings Nike, Kratos and Zelus. In Aeschylus she comes with Kratos to bind Prometheus, and does not speak. Hesiod's Theogony gives the parentage. She has no cult and no myths of her own. Distinct from the Akan river-god Bia, who is catalogued separately; the '-greek' in the identifier is this archive's disambiguation, not an ancient name.

gods.name: Yuanshi Tianzun
gods.description: The Primeval Lord of Heaven, first and highest of the Three Pure Ones of Taoism. He is said to have existed before the shaping of the cosmos, and out of himself to have brought forth the order of heaven; he teaches, but does not intervene. The second Pure One is Lingbao Tianzun, and the third is Taishang Laojun, the deified Laozi, who is catalogued in this archive as Laozi. The Pure Ones are emanations rather than a family, and no genealogy is recorded here.

gods.name: Lingbao Tianzun
gods.description: The Numinous Treasure Lord, second of the Three Pure Ones, who guards the sacred scriptures and measures out the ages of the world, transmitting the teaching downward from Yuanshi Tianzun. The relation between the Three Pure Ones is one of emanation, not descent; the third is Taishang Laojun, the deified Laozi, catalogued here as Laozi.

gods.name: Houtu
gods.description: The deity of the earth and the soil, to whom the emperor sacrificed at the square altar as he sacrificed to Heaven at the round one. The gender is genuinely unsettled across the tradition: in the early imperial cult Houtu is an earth power whose sex is not marked, and is often taken as male alongside a male Heaven; from the Song period onward the figure is increasingly the goddess Houtu Niangniang, the Empress of Earth, and is worshipped as such today. Neither reading is a misunderstanding of the other, so no gender is asserted here.

gods.name: Chiyou
gods.description: Leader of the Nine Li, who fought Huangdi at Zhuolu with a bronze head and an iron brow, and who is credited in some accounts with the making of the first weapons. He was defeated — but not simply written off as a monster: he was afterwards worshipped as a god of war, offered sacrifice by Han emperors before battle, and is honoured as an ancestor by the Miao. He is recorded here as a war deity rather than as a beast.

gods.name: Banebdjedet
gods.description: The Ram Lord of Mendes in the Delta, a ram-headed god of fertility and generative power. In the Contendings of Horus and Set he is the god asked to judge between the two, and he counsels that the elder should be heard. Later theology made him the union of the souls (ba) of Ra, Osiris, Shu and Geb — an interpretation, not a parentage, and it is left in prose.

gods.name: Heryshaf
gods.description: 'He who is upon his lake' — the ram god of Herakleopolis, worshipped from the First Dynasty and identified by the Greeks with Herakles, which gave the city its Greek name. Later syncretised with Ra and Osiris; those identifications are noted here as theology, not lineage.

gods.name: Shezmu
gods.description: God of the wine- and oil-press, and of the slaughter that the press was made to resemble. The older funerary texts give him a fearful aspect — he crushes the heads of the condemned in his press, and the red must is their blood — while later texts show him more benignly as the maker of unguents and perfumes for the dead. Both faces belong to the same god.

gods.name: Babi
gods.description: The great baboon of the underworld, fierce and virile, who is said in the Pyramid and Coffin Texts to feed on the entrails of the dead. Bloodthirsty and dangerous, he is nonetheless a power the deceased may hope to master, and spells exist to turn his ferocity to the dead man's protection.

gods.name: Sága
gods.description: Goddess who dwells at Sökkvabekkr, the sunken bench, where — as Grímnismál has it — she and Odin drink together gladly every day from golden cups while the cool waves flow over them. Snorri lists her among the Ásynjur, second after Frigg. Some readers have connected her name with saga, a told tale, and some have taken her for Frigg under another name; neither is certain, and no kinship is recorded here.

gods.name: Gná
gods.description: Frigg's messenger, whom she sends on errands into the several worlds, riding the horse Hófvarpnir that runs over air and water. In Gylfaginning the Vanir see her flying and ask what it is that flies there. Her service to Frigg is an office, not kinship, and the family fields are left empty.

gods.name: Laran
gods.description: Etruscan god of war, shown on bronze mirrors as a naked youth with helmet and spear. He is the figure the Romans matched with Mars, though the equation is theirs and not the Etruscans'. Mirrors often set him beside Turan, the goddess of love — a pairing of images whose exact nature is not known, and which is not recorded here as marriage.

gods.name: Sethlans
gods.description: The Etruscan smith god, shown with the craftsman's cap and tongs, and matched by the Romans with Vulcan and by the Greeks with Hephaestus. He appears on mirrors at the birth of Menrva from the head of Tinia, splitting it with his axe.

gods.name: Thesan
gods.description: Goddess of the dawn and of childbirth — the light brought forth each morning and the child brought forth into light being one thought to the Etruscans. She is shown winged, often bearing a youth aloft. Cognate in name with Latin Aurora's Indo-European kin, but her cult is Etruscan.

gods.name: Vanth
gods.description: Winged female figure of the Etruscan underworld, painted on tomb walls with a torch, a key and a scroll, and bare-breasted with straps crossing her chest. She is not a punisher: she attends the dying, and she lights the road. Sometimes shown more than once in a single scene, which has led some to read her as a type rather than one person — but she is named, and is recorded here as one.

gods.name: Charun
gods.description: Etruscan demon of death, blue-fleshed and hook-nosed, with pointed ears and a great hammer, who meets the dead at the threshold of the tomb. He is not the Greek Charon, catalogued separately in this archive: that Charon is a ferryman who rows the dead across a river for a fee. The names are related and the Etruscan figure was probably shaped in part by contact with the Greek one, but Charun neither ferries nor takes payment, and his hammer is his own.

gods.name: Inara
gods.description: Goddess of the wild creatures of the steppe, and the one who brings down the serpent Illuyanka: she sets out a feast, and when the serpent has drunk and gorged past the point of returning to its hole, the mortal Hupasiya binds it and the Storm God kills it. She is the daughter of the Storm God — but this archive holds both Tarhunt and Teshub, and the sources do not let us choose between them, so no parent is recorded.

gods.name: Ḫannaḫanna
gods.description: The Grandmother — mother goddess of the Hittites, whose counsel the gods seek when they are at a loss. When Telipinu vanishes and the land withers, it is she who sends out the bee to find him and sting him awake. Her name doubles the word for grandmother, and she is associated with birth and with the fates.

gods.name: Alalu
gods.description: The first king in heaven in the Hurrian-Hittite Song of Kumarbi. He reigned nine years with Anu as his cupbearer, until Anu overthrew him and drove him down into the dark earth — and Anu was in turn unmanned and overthrown by Kumarbi. The poem calls Kumarbi the offspring of Alalu; whether that is descent or dynastic succession is not clear, so the succession is left in prose and the family fields are empty.

gods.name: Ištanu
gods.description: The sun god of the day and of judgment, who crosses the sky and sees all that is done beneath it, and to whom the king appeals as the lord of right. He is distinct from the Sun Goddess of Arinna, catalogued separately here: she is the chief goddess of the state cult and protector of king and land, while Ištanu is the visible sun and the judge. The Hittites held both.

gods.name: Šauška
gods.description: Hurrian goddess of love, war and healing, taken into the Hittite pantheon and made the patron of Hattusili III; she was sent in her image to Egypt to heal the pharaoh. She is attended by two handmaidens and is winged. She belongs to the same broad tradition as Ishtar and Inanna and is often written with the same sign, but she is a Hurrian goddess with her own cult and is not merged with them in this archive. She is Teshub's sister in the Hurrian myths; that tie is left in prose.

gods.name: Zhong Kui
gods.description: Queller of demons. In the legend he was a scholar who took first place in the imperial examinations and was then stripped of the honour for his ugliness, whereupon he killed himself on the palace steps; the underworld received him and set him over the ghosts. Emperor Xuanzong is said to have dreamt of him devouring a demon and woken cured. His portrait is pasted on gates and doors at the New Year and at the Dragon Boat festival to keep evil out.

gods.name: Meng Po
gods.description: The old woman who waits at the end of the ten courts of hell, on the bridge that leads back to birth, and gives each soul a bowl of broth. Whoever drinks it forgets the life just ended and every life before it, and so goes back into the world remembering nothing.

gods.name: Kuafu
gods.description: The giant of the Classic of Mountains and Seas who set himself to race the sun. He ran it down to the place where it sets, and, dying of thirst, drank the Yellow River and the Wei dry and set out for the great lakes of the north, but fell on the way. His staff, cast down as he died, is said to have become a forest of peach trees. He is read both as a figure of overreaching folly and of unyielding will.

gods.name: Ukemochi
gods.description: The goddess of food in the Nihon Shoki. Sent by Amaterasu to visit her, Tsukuyomi found her producing a feast from her mouth — rice from her looking to the land, fish from her looking to the sea — and, disgusted, killed her; from her body came the ox and horse, millet, rice, wheat and beans, and the silkworm. Amaterasu was so angered that she would no longer look upon Tsukuyomi, and so day and night are apart. The Kojiki tells a closely parallel tale of Ōgetsuhime, killed by Susanoo; the two accounts are kept distinct here and are not merged.

gods.name: Ame-no-Koyane
gods.description: Kami of the ritual word. He chanted the liturgy before the rock-cave to draw Amaterasu out, and came down with Ninigi among the five companions of the descent. The Nakatomi, and after them the Fujiwara, reckoned him their ancestor; he is enshrined at Kasuga.

gods.name: Futodama
gods.description: Kami of the offering. At the rock-cave it was he who held up the sacred branch hung with mirror and jewels, and who stretched the rope behind Amaterasu once she had come out, so that she could not go back in. He descended with Ninigi, and the Inbe, the ritualists who prepared the offerings, held him for their ancestor.

gods.name: Ōyamakui
gods.description: Kami of Mount Hiei, named in the Kojiki as dwelling on the mountain and holding the whistling arrow. Enshrined at Hiyoshi Taisha at the mountain's foot, he became the Sannō, the mountain king, of the Tendai establishment above, and is a patron of brewers. He is a particular mountain's kami and is not the same figure as Ōyamatsumi, the great kami of the mountains, who is catalogued separately.

gods.name: Ahti
gods.description: God of the waters, the sea and the fish in it, to whom fishermen made their prayers before setting out; his wife is Vellamo. In the Kalevala the name is also borne by a man — Ahti Saarelainen, which is one of the names of the hero Lemminkäinen, catalogued separately here. The sea-god and the hero's byname are not the same figure, and the sharing of the name should not be read as identity.

gods.name: Vellamo
gods.description: Mistress of the waters and wife of Ahti. Her maidens drive the fish, and fishermen called on her for a good catch; in the Kalevala Väinämöinen hooks a fish that turns out to be a maiden of Vellamo's household, and loses her back into the sea before he understands what he has caught.

gods.name: Surma
gods.description: Violent and sudden death, given a shape: a monstrous thing with gaping jaws that waits at the gate of Tuonela to take whoever comes. He belongs with the other Finnish personifications of what afflicts the body — Kalma the reek of the grave, Kivutar of pain, Vammatar of injury — and like them is an abstraction with a face rather than a god with a cult.

gods.name: Pekko
gods.description: God of barley and of the ale made from it, called Pellonpekko, 'Pekko of the field'. Mikael Agricola names him in the list of Karelian gods he printed in 1551 — 'Pellon Pecko caused barley and hops to grow' — and his cult survived longest among the Setos, where a wooden image of him was kept and fed at the sowing.

gods.name: Austėja
gods.description: Lithuanian goddess of bees and of the swarming hive, and by extension of families and their increase — the bee and the household being thought of together, so that bees are said to die rather than be counted. She is known chiefly from the list of Lithuanian gods compiled by Jan Łasicki and printed in 1615, a source of the same early-modern kind that underlies several other figures on this shelf, and one whose entries are of uneven reliability.

gods.name: Aglaea
gods.description: 'Splendour' — the youngest of the three Charites, the Graces, and in Hesiod the wife of Hephaestus. She stands for brightness and adornment, and with her sisters attends Aphrodite. She has little story of her own: the Graces are a presence rather than a narrative.

gods.name: Stheno
gods.description: 'The Mighty' — eldest of the three Gorgons and, with Euryale, one of the two who were immortal, so that only their sister Medusa could be killed. She is named in Hesiod and little more is told of her; she has no myth apart from the sisterhood.

gods.name: Echo
gods.description: An Oread of the mountains who could not speak first and could not stay silent when spoken to — a punishment, Ovid says, from Hera, whom she had kept talking while Zeus slipped away. She wasted for love of Narcissus until nothing was left of her but the voice that gives back the last words of others. Greek sources also tell of Pan's pursuit of her; that is a pursuit, not a marriage, and it is left in prose rather than recorded as a consort.

gods.name: Olosa
gods.description: Orisha of the Lagos lagoon and of the fish in it, to whom the fishermen of the waterside made their offerings, and whose messengers are the crocodiles. She is commonly named in relation to Olokun, the orisha of the ocean depths — as wife, or daughter, or simply as the lagoon to his sea — but the accounts differ from teller to teller, so that tie is left in prose and no family is recorded here.

gods.name: Tepēyōllōtl
gods.description: 'Heart of the Mountain' — the jaguar in the cave, whose voice is the echo and whose roar is the earthquake. He is lord of the eighth hour of the night and patron of the day-sign Calli, and is understood as a jaguar aspect of Tezcatlipoca rather than a wholly separate god; he is catalogued on his own here in the same way as Ehecatl, the wind-aspect of Quetzalcoatl.

gods.name: Chantico
gods.description: Goddess of the hearth-fire and of the fire kept in the household box, and patroness of lapidaries. She is said to have broken a fast by eating paprika with roasted fish, and to have been turned into a dog by Tonacatecuhtli for it. Her fire is the domestic one, kept and fed, as against the great fire of Xiuhtecuhtli.

gods.name: Opochtli
gods.description: God of those who live by the water — fishermen and bird-catchers — and, in Sahagún's account, the giver of the net, the fish-spear, the bird-snare and the pole for throwing at waterfowl. He is reckoned among the rain-gods and is dressed like Tlaloc's company.

gods.name: Nanahuatzin
gods.description: The small, scabbed and sore-covered god of Teotihuacan, poorest of the gods, who when the world needed a sun threw himself without hesitation into the bonfire while the rich Tecciztecatl hung back four times. He rose as the fifth sun. He is not merged here with Tonatiuh, the sun of the present age, but kept as the figure who entered the fire — the same distinction the archive already keeps between Tecciztecatl and the moon.

gods.name: Pariacaca
gods.description: Mountain and water deity of the highlands above Lima, born — with his brothers — from five eggs on the peak of Condorcoto, who came as five falcons and then as men, and who overthrew the old fire-god Huallallo Carhuincho with rain and hail. He gave the irrigation water and took the offerings of the villages below. He is known almost entirely from the Huarochirí Manuscript, the early-seventeenth-century Quechua account of the huacas of that province, which is also the source for Cuniraya and Cavillaca on this shelf.

gods.name: Nāmakaokahaʻi
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the goddess of the sea and elder sister of Pele. It is she who drove Pele from island to island down the chain, quenching her fires wherever she tried to dig a home, until Pele came at last to Kīlauea on Hawaiʻi, where the pit was deep enough that the sea could not reach it. Sea against fire is the long quarrel of the two.

gods.name: Kamapuaʻa
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the hog-man — a kupua who takes the form of a pig, a man, a fish, or the kukui tree at will, and who roots up the land and brings the rain that greens it. He is Pele's lover and her enemy by turns: they fight to a standstill and divide the island between them, the dry lava lands to her and the wet windward slopes to him.

gods.name: Poliʻahu
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the snow goddess of Mauna Kea, robed in white, and the chief rival of Pele. In the sledding contest on the slopes she is set upon by Pele, who breaks the mountain open beneath her; Poliʻahu casts her mantle over the summit and freezes the flow. The snow on the high mountain is hers, and the fire is kept below.

gods.name: Huangdi
gods.description: The Yellow Emperor, first of the sovereigns and ancestor of the Chinese. He defeated Chiyou at Zhuolu — having been taught the arts of war, it is said, by the Mysterious Woman of the Nine Heavens — and the creature Bai Ze came to him and named for him every spirit in the world. To his reign are credited the compass-chariot, the calendar, and the medicine of the Inner Canon that bears his name, and to his wife Leizu the rearing of silkworms. He is a founder-figure of the sort that later ages made a god, and both the man and the god are meant here.

gods.name: Shennong
gods.description: The Divine Farmer, who gave men the plough and the market, and who tasted the hundred herbs to learn which healed and which killed — poisoned, by some accounts, seventy times in a day, and at the last by a herb he could not cure. Later tradition identifies him with Yandi, the Flame Emperor, and makes him Huangdi's rival or half-brother; that equation is a later systematisation of what were probably separate figures, and it is not asserted here.

gods.name: Xuanwu (Zhenwu)
gods.description: The Perfected Warrior of the North — a Taoist god, barefoot and black-robed, with loose hair and a sword, standing on a tortoise entwined with a snake. He is said to have been a prince who withdrew to Mount Wudang, cut away his mortal parts, and attained perfection, and he is invoked against demons and disease. The name Xuanwu belongs first to the Dark Warrior of the north, one of the four emblems of the sky — an arrangement of stars figured as a tortoise and snake, not a person. The god took up that emblem and stands upon it; he is not simply the constellation, and it is the god who is catalogued here.

gods.name: Xingtian
gods.description: The headless one of the Classic of Mountains and Seas. He contended with the Supreme God, who cut off his head and buried it in Changyang Mountain; whereupon he took his nipples for eyes and his navel for a mouth, and went on brandishing his axe and shield, and dances so still. He is the figure of a will that will not stop when the body is beaten.

gods.name: Jingwei
gods.description: The small bird with a speckled head and a white beak who carries twigs and pebbles from the western mountains and drops them into the Eastern Sea, meaning to fill it. She was a girl who went out on the water and drowned there, and came back as this bird, and she cries her own name. The transformation, and the tradition that makes her a daughter of Yandi, are told here in prose and are not set down as parentage.

gods.name: Hebo
gods.description: The Earl of the River — the god of the Yellow River, sometimes named Bing Yi, who rides a chariot drawn by dragons and is said to have a white face and the body of a fish. He was a hard god: at Ye, before Ximen Bao put a stop to it, a girl was dressed as a bride each year and set on a mat upon the water to be his wife, and drowned.

gods.name: Ame-no-Tajikarao
gods.description: The strong-armed kami who waited beside the Heavenly Rock Cave. When Amaterasu, drawn by Uzume's dance and the laughter of the gods, put out her head to look, it was he who took her hand and drew her out, and flung the stone door away — the door, they say, falling to earth as a mountain. He came down afterwards with Ninigi.

gods.name: Kuninotokotachi
gods.description: 'The Eternal Land-Standing One'. In the main account of the Nihon Shoki he is the first kami to come into being, formed like a reed-shoot between the parting heaven and earth, and he is the source from which the rest proceed. This is the Nihon Shoki's cosmology and is what the record represents; the Kojiki orders things differently, giving the first place to Amenominakanushi — catalogued separately — and reckoning Kuninotokotachi lower down. The two accounts are not reconciled here.

gods.name: Ame-no-Wakahiko
gods.description: Sent down with a bow and heavenly arrows to pacify the Central Land, he married Shitateruhime, the daughter of Ōkuninushi, and for eight years sent no word, meaning to take the land for himself. When a pheasant was sent to question him he shot it; the arrow went up through the heavens and was flung back down, and it killed him in his bed. At his funeral his friend Ajisukitakahikone, taken for his ghost, kicked the mourning-house down in a rage.

gods.name: Ishikoridome
gods.description: The kami who made the mirror that hung on the branch before the Heavenly Rock Cave, and in which Amaterasu saw a light she took for another sun. The mirror-makers reckoned her their ancestor, and the mirror among the imperial regalia is held to be of her making.

gods.name: Tamanoya
gods.description: The kami who strung the long string of magatama jewels hung on the branch before the Heavenly Rock Cave. The bead- and jewel-makers held him for their ancestor, and the jewels of the imperial regalia are counted his work.

gods.name: Usil
gods.description: The Etruscan sun, shown rising out of the sea with a ray of light held in either hand, and on the Piacenza liver set in the region of the sky's own quarter. The Greeks had Helios and the Romans Sol, and the ancients matched them; the match is theirs, and Usil is catalogued here on his own terms, not as a translation of either.

gods.name: Selvans
gods.description: God of the boundary and of what lies beyond it — the edge of the cultivated field, the limit of the property, the wood past the last stone. He is named on the Piacenza liver and on boundary-markers set up in his honour. The Romans had Silvanus and the comparison is an old one, but it is a comparison and not an identity.

gods.name: Nortia
gods.description: Goddess of fate at Volsinii, in whose temple a nail was driven into the wall each year — one nail for one year, fixing the year in place and marking it done. To have one's fate 'nailed by Nortia' was to have it settled beyond changing. The Roman Fortuna is a near neighbour and the two are often compared; they are kept distinct here.

gods.name: Culsans
gods.description: The god of the doorway, shown with two faces looking opposite ways, so that nothing may pass in or out unseen. A bronze of him from Cortona shows him young and bearded on both sides. The Roman Janus is two-faced also and the resemblance is plain, but the ancient equation is not treated here as sameness.

gods.name: Tuchulcha
gods.description: The demon of the Tomb of Orcus at Tarquinia, painted with the beak of a vulture, the ears of an ass, and snakes in the hands and hair, standing over Theseus in the underworld. The sex is not settled: the flesh is painted in the pale tone the Etruscans generally used for women, while the dress and bearing have struck others as male, and the name decides nothing. No sex is asserted here.

gods.name: Kamrušepa
gods.description: Goddess of healing and of the spoken charm. When Telipinu vanishes in his anger and the land dries and the beasts stop bearing, it is she who at last purifies him — driving his rage out with fire and water and the burning of brushwood, sending it down through the dark earth to the bronze cauldrons of the underworld whose lids never lift. She stands behind the Hittite ritual texts as the model of the practitioner. She descends from the older Hattian Kataḫzipuri; that is her antecedent, not another name for her.

gods.name: Hedammu
gods.description: The devouring sea-serpent of the Hurrian Song of Hedammu, who lies in the water and eats oxen and men by the thousand until the land is emptied, and whom Šauška at last draws out of the sea by bathing before him and setting beer and drugged food on the shore. The song makes him Kumarbi's offspring by a daughter of the Sea; the tablets are broken and the mother is not securely known, so the parentage is given here in prose and is not entered as genealogy.

gods.name: Ubelluri
gods.description: The giant of the Hurrian Song of Ullikummi, who stands or sleeps in the earth with heaven and earth resting upon him, and who is so vast and so far from the affairs of the gods that when Kumarbi set the stone child Ullikummi on his right shoulder to grow, he felt nothing and knew nothing of it. When at last he is asked, he says only that when heaven and earth were cut apart with a cutter, he noticed a little something on his shoulder.

gods.name: Allani
gods.description: The Hurrian goddess of the underworld — the Sun-Goddess of the Earth, called the Bolt of the Earth, who keeps the gate that does not open outward and sets a feast for the gods in her dark house. She is Hurrian and is housed here on the mixed Anatolian shelf beside the Hittite and Luwian gods. She is not the Sun Goddess of Arinna, the Hittite state goddess of the sky above, and she is not Ištanu, the sun of the day: the sun below, the sun of the state, and the sun of the daylight are three offices and three deities.

gods.name: Runtiya
gods.description: The Luwian god of the hunt and of the wild country, who stands upon a stag and carries the bow, and whose name is written with the sign of the antler. He is Luwian rather than Hittite, and is housed here on the mixed Anatolian shelf; he keeps the game of the open land, and the hunters' offerings are made to him.

gods.name: Mabon ap Modron
gods.description: 'The Divine Son, son of the Divine Mother' — stolen from between his mother and the wall when he was three nights old, and heard of no more until Arthur's men, going back through the oldest animals of the world to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, find him imprisoned at Caer Loyw crying out of a stone wall. Freed, he is the huntsman who takes the razor from between the ears of the boar Twrch Trwyth. The Gaulish Maponos is a cognate of the name and no doubt of the god behind it, but he is not the same figure, and the two are not merged here.

gods.name: Modron
gods.description: 'The Mother' — named in Culhwch and Olwen only as the one from whom Mabon was taken, and appearing in the Triads as the daughter of Afallach and the mother, by Urien, of Owain and Morfudd. She is a great mother-figure of whom very little narrative survives. The Gaulish Matrona, goddess of the Marne, is a cognate of her name; the identification is linguistic and is not treated here as sameness.

gods.name: Gwyn ap Nudd
gods.description: Lord of Annwn and huntsman of the dead, into whom — Culhwch and Olwen says — God put the fury of the demons of the underworld, lest the world be destroyed. He rides out with his hounds, and later tradition sets his hall inside Glastonbury Tor. Every May Day he fights Gwythyr for Creiddylad, and must fight for her until Judgement Day, when the winner takes her. His father Nudd is not catalogued in this archive, and the Irish Nuada — a cognate of that name — is a separate figure on a separate shelf; no link is drawn between them.

gods.name: Ceridwen
gods.description: The enchantress of the Tale of Taliesin, who brews a year-long cauldron of inspiration for her ugly son and loses it to the boy Gwion Bach, who takes the three drops on his thumb and flees. She hunts him through a chase of shapes — greyhound after hare, otter after fish, hawk after bird — and at last swallows him as a grain of wheat, and bears him again as Taliesin. Her story survives only in the late Ystoria Taliesin; she is not attested as a goddess in the medieval Welsh sources, and her standing as one is largely a later interpretation, so she is not catalogued as a deity here.

gods.name: Culhwch
gods.description: Cousin of Arthur, laid under a destiny by his stepmother that he should have no wife but Olwen. He comes to Arthur's court to claim his help, and is set by her father Ysbaddaden the giant to perform some forty impossible tasks — the hunting of the boar Twrch Trwyth chief among them — before he may have her. The tale is the oldest of the Arthurian prose stories.

gods.name: Olwen
gods.description: Daughter of the giant Ysbaddaden, and the woman Culhwch is fated to win. 'Whiter was her flesh than the foam of the wave, and fairer were her hands than the blossoms of the wood anemone' — and where she walked, four white trefoils sprang up behind her, which is why she is called Olwen, 'white-track'. Her father must die when she marries, and so he sets the tasks.

gods.name: Ishkur / Adad
gods.description: The storm — Sumerian Ishkur, Akkadian Adad — who rides the bull and carries the lightning-fork, and whose voice is the thunder. He is a god of two faces: the rain that makes the barley stand, and the flood and the hail that flatten it, so that he is prayed to and feared in the same breath. In the flood story it is his roar out of the cloud that begins the destruction. He is recorded here as one god under both names, as An/Anu, Utu/Shamash and Inanna/Ishtar are on this shelf.

gods.name: Ninshubur
gods.description: Sukkal — vizier and messenger — of Inanna, and the one who saves her: when her mistress goes down to the underworld and does not return in three days, it is Ninshubur who sets up the lament, tears at her eyes and mouth, and goes from Enlil to Nanna to Enki until one of them will act. She is female in the Sumerian tradition, which is the tradition represented here; the later Akkadian material conflates the office with the male Papsukkal, and the sex of the figure shifts with it.

gods.name: Anzu
gods.description: The great bird with the lion's head — a storm made feathers — who stole the Tablet of Destinies from Enlil's chamber while the god was bathing, and flew with it to the mountain, so that the ordinances were suspended and stillness fell on heaven. Ninurta went after him and shot him down with the arrow and the flood-wave, and brought the Tablet back. His parentage is told differently in different versions and is not entered here.

gods.name: Nusku
gods.description: God of fire and of the lamp, and vizier of Enlil, whose word he carries. He is the light lit against the night and against what moves in it, and the burning that purifies — in the incantations, the figures of witches are given to Nusku to consume.

gods.name: Ninkasi
gods.description: The goddess of beer, born — the hymn says — of the sparkling fresh water, and set by Ninhursag to satisfy the desire and sate the heart. The Hymn to Ninkasi is both a praise-poem and a recipe: it goes through the soaking of the malt, the baking of the bappir loaves, the mash and the filtering vat, step by step, and could be brewed from.

gods.name: Baridegi
gods.description: The Abandoned Princess. Seventh daughter of a king who wanted a son, she was put in a box and cast away at birth; and when her parents afterwards fell sick and no one of the six kept daughters would go, it was she who went — through the underworld, and worked nine years for the keeper of the western sky, and bore him seven sons — to bring back the water of life that raised them from their coffins. For this she was made the guide of the dead, and the shamans sing her narrative over the coffin at the funeral rite.

gods.name: Yeomra-daewang
gods.description: Great King Yeomra, who judges the dead and rules the ten courts of the Korean otherworld. The office and the name descend from the Indian Yama by way of the Chinese Yanluo, both of whom are catalogued separately on their own shelves; this record is the Korean figure of the shamanic narratives and the folk tradition, not either of those. He is also not the Jeoseung Saja, the black-robed messengers who fetch the dead and bring them before him — they are his servants and are catalogued apart.

gods.name: Gangnim
gods.description: In the Jeju narrative, a mortal official — a hard man with nine wives — who was sent by a magistrate to summon Yeomra himself, and who went down and, against every expectation, came back with him. Yeomra, admiring the man who had fetched him, took him for his own, and Gangnim became the chief of the messengers who go out for the dead. He passed from man to underworld servant by that errand and not by any birth, and no lineage is recorded here.

gods.name: Haemosu
gods.description: Son of Heaven in the Goguryeo foundation tradition, who came down in a chariot drawn by five dragons and rode back up to heaven at dusk, and who by the river-god's daughter Yuhwa fathered Jumong. He is known from the Samguk Yusa and the Lay of King Dongmyeong; the descent is told there and is left here in prose.

gods.name: Jumong
gods.description: Founder of Goguryeo, and the finest archer of the tradition — the name is said to mean 'good shot'. Born from an egg that his mother Yuhwa bore after the touch of Haemosu's sunlight, he was thrown to the dogs and the pigs and left in the road, and none would harm him; grown, and hunted by the king's sons, he fled to the Eastern Buyeo river, where the fish and the turtles rose to make him a bridge. He is the Goguryeo counterpart of Dangun, who founded Gojoseon and is catalogued here beside him.

gods.name: Baal Hammon
gods.description: Supreme god of Carthage, bearded and ram-horned, enthroned between sphinxes — the god to whom the urns of the tophet were dedicated, and whose worship the Romans and the Hebrew Bible remembered with horror. He is a Punic god of the western colonies, and he is not the Ugaritic Baal Hadad catalogued on this shelf: a different god, of a different city, a thousand years and a sea away, sharing only the Semitic word ba'al, 'lord', which many gods carried.

gods.name: Tanit
gods.description: The great goddess of Carthage, 'Face of Baal', named before Baal Hammon himself in the later inscriptions, and marked everywhere on the stelae by her sign — a triangle, a bar, a disc, standing for a figure with raised arms. The ancients equated her with Astarte and with Juno Caelestis, and modern writers often do the same; she is a Carthaginian goddess with her own cult and her own sign, and she is not merged here with the Astarte catalogued on this shelf.

gods.name: Eshmun
gods.description: God of healing and chief god of Sidon, whose great sanctuary stood outside the city by the river. The story told of him is that he was a beautiful youth whom the goddess Astronoe pursued, and who unmanned himself with an axe to escape her, and died, and was warmed back into life by her — a dying-and-returning god, whom the Greeks matched with Asklepios.

gods.name: Horon
gods.description: West Semitic god invoked against snakes and against the curse — a god of the underworld and of the spells that hold it off. In the Ugaritic tale of Keret the king is cursed by Horon; in an incantation against serpent-venom, it is Horon who goes to the tree and roots out the poison. His name survives in the place-names Beth-horon and Hauron.

gods.name: Pidray
gods.description: One of the three daughters of Baal in the Ugaritic cycle — Pidray of the light, with Tallay of the dew and Arsay of the earth — and called 'daughter of the mist'. She dwells in Baal's house on Mount Zaphon and is named among the goods of it. Her sisters are not yet catalogued here, and the parentage is left in prose rather than entered alone.

gods.name: Sokar
gods.description: Falcon god of the Memphite necropolis and of the workshops that furnished the dead — hawk-headed, swathed like a mummy, standing on the henu-barque that was dragged around the walls at his festival. His kingdom is the Fifth Hour of the night, the deepest and most secret cavern of the underworld, where the sun-boat must be hauled over the sand. The composite figure Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, which fuses him with two other gods, is a later fusion and is not what is catalogued here.

gods.name: Onuris
gods.description: 'He who brings back the distant one' — the hunter-god of This, plumed and spear-carrying, who went into Nubia after the Eye of Ra when she fled there as a lioness, and brought her home to Egypt as his wife Mehit. He became a god of war and of hunting both, and the Greeks matched him with Ares. His Egyptian name is Anhur.

gods.name: Aker
gods.description: The earth as a gate. He is drawn as two lions seated back to back, one facing the sunrise and one the sunset, with the horizon held between them; and it is through him that the sun passes down into the night and out of it in the morning, and through him that the dead go. The two lions are one god in two aspects — Yesterday and Tomorrow, they are named — and he should not be confused with the Akeru, the plural earth-spirits older than the gods, which are a class and not a person.

gods.name: Mehet-Weret
gods.description: 'The Great Flood' — the cow of the primeval water, on whose back the young sun rose out of the waters at the first morning, and who carries him between her horns. She is the water itself made a cow, and the sky imagined as a river. Later theology drew her into Hathor, into Neith, and into Isis, each of whom took on the cow and the flood; those are syncretisms of the later temples, and she is catalogued here as herself, not as any of them.

gods.name: Consus
gods.description: God of the stored grain, whose altar in the Circus Maximus was kept buried under the earth and uncovered only twice a year, at his two festivals — the harvest safely in, and the sowing done. On the Consualia the horses and mules were garlanded and rested, and it was at the games of his feast, the story goes, that the Romans carried off the Sabine women. A purely Italic god with no Greek counterpart.

gods.name: Silvanus
gods.description: God of the woods and of the uncleared ground beyond the farm — of the boundary between the tilled field and what will not be tilled. He had no state cult and no temple, but was worshipped everywhere by farmers, herdsmen and woodcutters, who left him offerings at the edge of the trees. The Etruscan Selvans, catalogued separately here, holds the same ground and the names are related; they are parallel gods of two peoples, and are not treated as one.

gods.name: Liber Pater
gods.description: An old Italic god of the vine and of generative power, and — as his name says — of freedom: he was the god of the plebs, of the free man, and it was at his festival, the Liberalia, that a boy put off the child's toga and took the plain white one of a citizen. He was worshipped with Ceres and Libera on the Aventine, the plebeian triad. The Romans later identified him with Bacchus and Dionysus, and the Bacchus catalogued on this shelf is that Greek god in Roman dress; Liber is the older Italic god underneath, and the identification is a later overlay, not his origin.

gods.name: Carmenta
gods.description: Goddess of childbirth and of prophecy — the two joined because the carmen, the chanted verse from which her name comes, both foretells and brings about. Her flamen was one of the archaic priests, and at the Carmentalia in January the women came to her; leather was forbidden in her shrine, as nothing that had died might come where birth was asked for.

gods.name: Portunus
gods.description: God of the harbour and of the door, who holds the key — the gate of the city and the mouth of the river being one idea to the Romans, a place where what is outside is let in. His temple stood by the cattle-market at the old river port of Rome, and his festival, the Portunalia, fell in August, when keys were thrown into the fire for luck.

gods.name: Fides
gods.description: Good Faith made a goddess — the keeping of the word, in a treaty between states or a bargain between men. Her cult on the Capitol was reckoned among the oldest in Rome, and her priests came to her with the right hand wrapped in white cloth, because the right hand is what is given in pledge and must be covered as a thing holy.

gods.name: Kullervo
gods.description: The most ruinous figure of the Kalevala — a boy whose kin were slaughtered by his uncle Untamo, who was sold into slavery, and who broke everything he was set to do: he cursed the smith's wife and had her torn apart by bears, unknowingly seduced his own sister, who threw herself into a torrent, and at last, having destroyed Untamo's house and his own, asked his sword whether it would eat him, and it said it would. He belongs to the poetry of the Kalevala and is not an older Finnish god.

gods.name: Aino
gods.description: The young sister whom Joukahainen pledged to Väinämöinen to save his own life, and who would not have the old man: she went to the shore, laid her clothes on a stone, and drowned herself, and afterwards swam as a fish that slipped from Väinämöinen's hand. The name and much of the figure are Lönnrot's own, worked up out of fragments of folk poems for the Kalevala; she is a literary creation upon an oral foundation, and not an old goddess.

gods.name: Joukahainen
gods.description: The rash young man of the Kalevala who challenged Väinämöinen to a contest of singing and was sung into the ground — into a bog to his belt, to his mouth — until he bought his life with the promise of his sister Aino. Afterwards, in envy, he shot at Väinämöinen with a crossbow and killed his horse instead, and so drove him into the sea and into the hands of Pohjola. A Kalevala figure, not a god.

gods.name: Antero Vipunen
gods.description: The great dead singer of the Kalevala who lies under the earth with trees grown over him, and in whom the three words Väinämöinen needs to finish his boat are kept. Väinämöinen digs down to him and is swallowed; he sets up a forge in the giant's belly and hammers until Vipunen, in his pain, opens his mouth and sings out all the origins he knows. A figure of the poetry — a body of buried knowledge given a name.

gods.name: Iku-Turso
gods.description: The thing raised out of the sea in the Kalevala — 'Iku-Turso, son of Old Age' — sent by Louhi against the men who stole the Sampo, and hauled up by the ears by Väinämöinen, who makes it swear never to rise again, and it never does. What it looks like is never said, and the name has been read as walrus, as octopus, and as nothing that swims at all.

gods.name: Yu the Great
gods.description: Yu the Great, who tamed the flood. His father Gun had tried to dam it with the stolen self-renewing earth and was executed for it; Yu dredged instead, cutting channels to the sea, and worked thirteen years — passing his own door three times and never going in — until the waters ran off and the land could be farmed. For this he was given the throne and founded the Xia. He stands with Huangdi and Shennong among the sovereigns of the mythic age catalogued on this shelf, and not among the historical figures of the deified-humans shelf.

gods.name: Doumu
gods.description: The Mother of the Dipper — the goddess from whom the nine stars of the Northern Bushel were born, and who is shown many-armed and many-headed, seated on a lotus, holding sun and moon. She keeps the register of life and death that the Dipper stars administer, and is prayed to for the lengthening of life. Her form owes much to the Buddhist Marici, taken into Taoism and made Chinese.

gods.name: Bixia Yuanjun
gods.description: The Lady of the Azure Clouds, goddess of Mount Tai — the holy mountain of the east, where the sun comes up and where, the Chinese held, the dead go. Women climbed it to ask her for children, and she is prayed to at birth and for the sight of the eyes. She is called the daughter of the god of the mountain, and in the popular cult she long ago overtook her father.

gods.name: Yuqiang
gods.description: God of the north and of the northern sea in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, with a man's face and a bird's body, and two green snakes hanging from his ears and two more trodden underfoot. He is the wind of the north when he takes his bird shape, and a fish when he goes into the sea. It is he who sets the fifteen great turtles to carry the floating islands of the immortals on their heads.

gods.name: Wākea
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the sky-father, from whom with Papahānaumoku the islands were born and the chiefly line descends — the taro plant first, and then the human ancestor. He is the Hawaiian counterpart of the Māori Ranginui, catalogued separately here; the two belong to two traditions and the names are cognate, but they are not the same figure and are not merged.

gods.name: Papahānaumoku
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, 'Papa who gives birth to islands' — the earth-mother, consort of Wākea, from whom Hawaiʻi, Maui and the rest were born as children. She is the Hawaiian counterpart of the Māori Papatūānuku, who is catalogued separately on this shelf; the archive keeps the regional forms apart, as it does Rongo and Lono, and Tangaroa and Kanaloa. The consort tie to Wākea is told differently in different genealogies and is left in prose.

gods.name: ʻOro
gods.description: In Tahitian tradition, the great god of Raʻiātea and afterwards of all the Society Islands — a god of war whose feathered images and red girdles were the sign of a chief's right to rule, and who was also invoked as ʻOro-i-te-tea-moe, ʻOro-of-the-laid-down-spear, in time of peace. The ʻarioi, the travelling society of players and dancers, were his. He is called a son of Taʻaroa, who is not catalogued here, so no parentage is recorded.

gods.name: Tāwhaki
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the hero of the climb to heaven — beaten and left for dead by his wife's brothers, he recovered and went up, hand over hand along a vine, past his blind grandmother Whaitiri, whom he cured by restoring her sight, to the topmost sky. Lightning is said to flash from his armpits, and he is called on for it.

gods.name: Ajisukitakahikone
gods.description: Son of Ōkuninushi, and a kami of thunder and of the paddy-field. In the Kojiki he goes to the funeral of Ame-no-Wakahiko, his friend, and is taken by the mourners for the dead man come back — for the two were so alike — and in his fury at being mistaken for a corpse he draws his sword, cuts the mourning-house down and kicks it away, and it flies off and becomes a mountain.

gods.name: Shitateruhime
gods.description: Daughter of Ōkuninushi and sister of Ajisukitakahikone, and the wife of Ame-no-Wakahiko, the envoy who was sent to pacify the land and kept it for himself. Her beauty is said to have shone through her clothes, and it is she who sings the song naming her brother when the mourners mistake him for her dead husband.

gods.name: Ame-no-Hohi
gods.description: The first kami sent down from heaven to demand that Ōkuninushi give up the Central Land. He went, and was so won over by Ōkuninushi that he took his side and sent no word back for three years — and so a second envoy had to be sent, and then a third. The priestly house of Izumo reckoned him their ancestor, and serve that shrine still.

gods.name: Heh
gods.description: God of endlessness — one of the eight of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, paired with his consort Hauhet, and shown as a kneeling man holding a notched palm-rib in each hand, the sign of the years, with the shen-ring of eternity at his elbow. Two of him hold up the sky. He is one god, and is not to be confused with the ḥeḥu, the plural 'millions' — the countless nameless ones — which is a way of counting and not a person.

gods.name: Imentet
gods.description: The West made a goddess — the land of the dead being always the western bank, where the sun goes down. She is shown at the edge of the desert with the sign of the west upon her head, holding out her arms to those who come, and she is called the one who gives bread and beer to the newly dead. In the tombs she stands with Hathor, and the two are often written as one.

gods.name: Shed
gods.description: 'The Saviour' — a young god shown on the household stelae as a boy grasping snakes and scorpions and standing on crocodiles, called upon by ordinary people against the bite and the sting and against whatever else came at them in the night. He rose in the New Kingdom, outside the temple cult, and belongs to the magic that people did for themselves.

gods.name: Fáfnir
gods.description: Son of Hreiðmarr, who killed his father for the gold that Loki had paid as blood-price for Ótr — Andvari's hoard, and the ring that Andvari cursed as it was taken from him. He carried it to Gnitaheiðr, and there he lay upon it and turned into a serpent, and grew so venomous that nothing would come near. Sigurd dug a pit in his path and stabbed him from beneath as he crawled to water, and the dying dragon warned him that the gold would kill him too. It did.

gods.name: Sigurd
gods.description: The dragon-slayer of the Völsungs, who was fostered by Regin, took the sword Gram, killed Fáfnir in the pit, and — tasting the heart-blood on his thumb — understood the speech of birds, who told him Regin meant to kill him; so he killed Regin and rode off with the hoard. This record is the Sigurd of the Norse tradition, of the Eddic poems and the Völsunga saga. The Siegfried of the German Nibelungenlied is the same legend told by another people, and he is not merged here.

gods.name: Brynhild
gods.description: The valkyrie whom Odin pricked with the sleep-thorn and shut in a hall ringed with fire, for giving victory to the wrong king. Sigurd rode through the fire and woke her, and they swore oaths; but he was given a drink of forgetting, married Gudrun, and won Brynhild for another man while wearing Sigurd's shape. When she learned it, she had him killed, and went onto his pyre. This is the Eddic and Völsunga Brynhild — not the mortal queen Brünhild of the Nibelungenlied, and not the historical Brunhilda of the Franks; and though she is a valkyrie, she is one named woman and not the company of them catalogued separately here.

gods.name: Andvari
gods.description: The dwarf who lived as a pike in a waterfall and kept a hoard of gold there. Loki caught him in a net and took it all; and when Andvari begged to keep back one ring, Loki took that too, and Andvari laid on it that it should be the death of whoever owned it. That curse runs through the whole story of the Völsungs and out the other side.

gods.name: Útgarða-Loki
gods.description: The giant-king of Útgarðr, and the greatest deceiver Thor ever met. He beat the gods with illusions: the drinking-horn whose end was the sea, the cat that was Jörmungandr, the old woman Elli who was Old Age herself and whom nobody throws. The huge giant Skrýmir, who travelled with them beforehand and whose glove they slept in and whose head Thor could not crack, was Útgarða-Loki himself in another shape — the same being, not a second one, and no separate record is made of him.

gods.name: Hrungnir
gods.description: The strongest of the giants, with a head and a heart of stone and a shield of stone, who raced Odin on his horse Gullfaxi into Asgard, got drunk, and boasted he would carry off Valhalla and kill all the gods but Freyja and Sif. Thor came and killed him with the hammer, and a shard of Hrungnir's hurled whetstone lodged in Thor's skull and stayed there.

gods.name: Vishvakarma
gods.description: The architect of the gods and the maker of their things — Indra's Vajra, the city of Dvaraka, the flying chariots, the palaces of Lanka. He is called the all-maker, the one who sees everywhere and whose hands shape what the gods use; craftsmen and engineers keep his day. The Rigveda names him as a creator-figure; the later texts make him the celestial builder.

gods.name: Narasimha
gods.description: The man-lion, fourth descent of Vishnu, made to answer a boon that could not be broken: Hiranyakashipu could be killed by neither man nor beast, indoors nor out, by day nor night, on the earth nor in the air. So Vishnu came as neither man nor beast, on the threshold, at dusk, and took him on his lap and tore him open — and so saved his devotee Prahlada, the tyrant's own son. Both Hiranyakashipu and Prahlada are catalogued here. The descent is an incarnation of Vishnu and not a birth from him, and no parentage is recorded.

gods.name: Varaha
gods.description: The boar, third descent of Vishnu, who dived into the cosmic ocean where the demon Hiranyaksha had dragged the earth, killed him, and brought her up again on his tusks and set her on the water. The descent is incarnation, not lineage, and is left in prose.

gods.name: Vamana
gods.description: The dwarf, fifth descent of Vishnu, who came to the sacrifice of the generous demon-king Bali and asked only for as much ground as he could cover in three strides. Bali granted it; and the dwarf grew until he crossed the earth with one step and the heavens with the second, and asked where he should put the third — and Bali, keeping his word, offered his own head, and was pressed down into the underworld, honoured for it. Incarnation, not parentage.

gods.name: Parashurama
gods.description: Rama with the axe, sixth descent of Vishnu — a brahmin who took up arms. At his father's word he beheaded his own mother, and afterwards asked her life back as his boon; and when the kshatriya king Kartavirya killed his father, he swore to clear the earth of that warrior caste, and did it twenty-one times over. He is one of the immortals, and is said to be waiting still. Incarnation, not parentage.

gods.name: Fionn mac Cumhaill
gods.description: Leader of the fianna, the roving warrior-bands, and the centre of the Fenian Cycle. As a boy he was set to cook the Salmon of Knowledge for the poet Finnegas, burned his thumb on it, and put the thumb in his mouth — and so the wisdom went to him and not to the man who had fished seven years for it. Ever after, when he needed to know a thing, he chewed his thumb.

gods.name: Oisín
gods.description: Son of Fionn and the poet of the fianna. Niamh of the Golden Hair — catalogued here — came out of the sea and carried him to Tír na nÓg, where he stayed three hundred years thinking them three; and when he came home and leaned from the saddle, his foot touched Ireland and the years fell on him all at once, and he was an old blind man in a country where the fianna were a story.

gods.name: Medb
gods.description: Queen of Connacht, who began the Táin Bó Cúailnge because her husband Ailill's herd held one bull more than hers, and she would not be the lesser — and so mustered the armies of Ireland to steal the Brown Bull of Cooley, and was held off nearly alone by the boy Cú Chulainn. Scholars have long read behind her a goddess of sovereignty, whom the king must take to rule; that is an interpretation of the figure and not what the saga says of her, and it is noted here without being asserted. In the tale she is a queen, and acts as one.

gods.name: Scáthach
gods.description: The warrior-woman of Alba — of Skye, tradition says — to whom Cú Chulainn went to be taught, and who gave him the feats and the terrible barbed spear, the Gáe Bulg. She is otherworldly and more than human, and she had a rival, Aífe, whom Cú Chulainn beat; but she is nowhere worshipped and is no goddess of the Tuatha Dé, and she is not catalogued as one here.

gods.name: Flidais
gods.description: A woman of the Tuatha Dé Danann in the Lebor Gabála lists, and in Táin Bó Flidais the owner of a great herd whose cow gave milk enough for three hundred at a milking, and who left her husband for Fergus mac Róich. The later habit of calling her a goddess of deer and of wild things rests on very little in the medieval sources, where it is cattle and plenty she is joined to; the wilder characterisation is a modern one and is not adopted here.

gods.name: Bellerophon
gods.description: The hero who tamed Pegasus with the golden bridle Athena gave him, and, flying above the reach of it, shot the Chimera and dropped lead into its throat, which its own fire melted and killed it. He rose on his luck and then above it: he set Pegasus at Olympus itself, meaning to go among the gods, and Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse, and he fell, and went lame and hated for the rest of his life.

gods.name: Ganymede
gods.description: The most beautiful of mortals, a prince of Troy whom Zeus — in the form of an eagle, the later versions say — carried up to Olympus to pour the wine of the gods, and gave immortality and never aging. To his father, in payment, went a pair of divine horses. He was set in the sky as Aquarius, the water-pourer.

gods.name: Triptolemus
gods.description: The man of Eleusis whom Demeter, in her wandering after Persephone, took into her care and taught the sowing of grain; and she gave him a chariot drawn by winged serpents and sent him over the whole earth to teach it to men. He is the chief of the Eleusinian figures after the two goddesses, and is shown between them on the great relief, taking the ears of corn.

gods.name: Piltzintecuhtli
gods.description: The Young Prince — a god of the young sun and of the third hour of the day, joined with Tonatiuh and with the visions of the sacred mushrooms. With Xochiquetzal he is named as the father of Centeotl, the maize-god, in the accounts the Aztecs gave of him.

gods.name: Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli
gods.description: Lord of the House of Dawn — the Morning Star, and the aspect Quetzalcoatl took when his heart rose out of the pyre and became Venus. He is a dangerous god: when the star first appears he hurls his darts at whatever is under it, and the Aztecs reckoned by the Venus tables which days were unlucky for whom. He has his own trecena, his own place in the codices, and his own cult; he is nonetheless filed here as an aspect of Quetzalcoatl, alongside Ehecatl and Xolotl.

gods.name: Ixtlilton
gods.description: 'The Little Black One' — a god of healing, and of the dancing and the feasting that went with it. Sick children were brought to his shrine and given the black water that stood there in jars, and his priests danced for them. He is called a brother of Xochipilli, the flower-prince.

gods.name: Odùduwà
gods.description: The founder at Ile-Ife, from whom the Yoruba kings trace their crowns. The traditions do not agree on what he was. In one, he is the orisha who came down the chain with the sand and the five-toed hen and made the dry land, because Obatala, sent first, drank palm wine and slept. In another, he is a man — a conqueror out of the east who took Ife and founded the dynasty, and was made a god afterwards. And though he is male in the dominant Ife and Oyo tellings, which is how he is filed here, other accounts and much of the diaspora present Odùduwà as female. Creator, ancestor-king, deified man: the tradition holds all three, and this record does not choose between them.

gods.name: Òsùmàrè
gods.description: The rainbow made a serpent — the orisha who arches from earth to sky and back, carrying the water up so that it may fall again, and standing for the going and returning of all things. He is served with the python, and is sometimes said to be male for a season and female for a season. He is catalogued here as the Yoruba orisha; the Fon Dan, on the Fon shelf of this archive, and the Brazilian Oxumaré of Candomblé are related figures of other traditions and are not merged with him.

gods.name: Yewa
gods.description: Orisha of the river Yewa in the west of Yorubaland — a cool and severe goddess, kept apart, associated with virginity and with the ground where the dead are laid out and prepared. Her priestesses were held to strict rule, and she is spoken of quietly.

gods.name: Utnapishtim
gods.description: The man who survived the flood, in Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh. Warned by Ea against the silence the gods had sworn, he tore down his house and built a boat of it, took aboard the seed of all living things, and rode out six days and seven nights until the boat grounded on Mount Nimush and the dove came back and the raven did not. Enlil, relenting, touched his forehead and his wife's and set them to live far off at the mouth of the rivers; and it is there that Gilgamesh finds him, and is told that there will be no second such assembly of the gods, and no immortality for him. Ziusudra, king of Shuruppak in the Sumerian flood story, and Atrahasis, the 'exceedingly wise' of the Old Babylonian poem, are flood-survivors of other compositions, told with other details; they are related figures of the same tradition and are not merged with him here.

gods.name: Adapa
gods.description: The sage of Eridu, priest and fisherman of Ea, who broke the wing of the south wind when it capsized his boat, and was summoned to heaven to answer for it. Ea, meaning to save him, told him to refuse the bread and water he would be offered there, for they would be the bread and water of death. But Anu, appeased, offered him the bread and water of life — and Adapa, obeying his god, refused, and so went back to earth mortal. He had been given wisdom, Ea says, but not life.

gods.name: Isimud
gods.description: The sukkal of Enki — his vizier and his messenger, shown with two faces looking opposite ways, so that he sees where he has come from and where he is going at once. He carries Enki's words, and in the tale of Inanna and the me it is he who is sent again and again after her boat to take the stolen powers back, and fails each time.

gods.name: Lahar
gods.description: The cattle-god, made with the grain-goddess Ashnan so that the Anunnaki might be clothed and fed. The Sumerian debate poem sets the two of them arguing which is the greater — the wool or the bread — until Enlil and Enki judge between them and give it to Ashnan. He is named in the archive's Ashnan record and is catalogued here in his own right.

gods.name: Asag
gods.description: The demon of the mountain in Lugal-e, so hideous that the fish boiled alive in the rivers when he came near, and who begot an army of stone from the mountain itself. Ninurta went up against him, was driven back once, and killed him at last with the mace Sharur; and afterwards he set the stones in their order, cursing those that had fought for Asag and blessing those that had not.

gods.name: Neti
gods.description: Chief gatekeeper of the underworld. When Inanna comes down and beats on the gate demanding entry, it is Neti who goes to Ereshkigal for instruction and comes back with it: to let her in through the seven gates, and at each one to take something from her — the crown, the beads, the breastplate, the ring, the rod, the robe — until she stands before her sister with nothing at all.

gods.name: Taliesin
gods.description: The radiant-browed bard of the Ystoria Taliesin. He began as Gwion Bach, the boy set to stir Ceridwen's cauldron for a year and a day, who took the three drops of inspiration on his thumb and fled — through the shapes of hare, fish, bird and grain of wheat, with Ceridwen after him as greyhound, otter, hawk and hen — until she swallowed him and bore him again, and set him in a leather bag on the water, where Elffin found him and named him for his shining forehead. He is the legendary Taliesin of that tale. A historical poet of the name lived in the sixth century and some poems in the Book of Taliesin are ascribed to him; that man and this figure are not the same, and are not merged here.

gods.name: Lludd Llaw Ereint
gods.description: King of Britain in Lludd and Llefelys, who rebuilt the walls of London and was troubled by three plagues: the Coraniaid, who heard every word the wind carried; a scream on every May-eve that made women miscarry; and the vanishing of a year's provisions from the king's court. His brother Llefelys, king in France, told him the cures — the insects crushed in water, the two fighting dragons buried at Oxford, the giant caught at the feast — and he worked them, and the land was quiet. His name is cognate with that of Nudd, and behind that with the Irish Nuada and the British Nodens; the comparison is one of names and is not treated here as identity. In the tale he is a king, and acts as one.

gods.name: Ysbaddaden Bencawr
gods.description: Chief Giant of Culhwch and Olwen, and the father of Olwen — whose eyelids were so heavy that they had to be lifted with forks before he could see, and who threw a poisoned spear at each of Culhwch's three visits and had it thrown back at him each time. He was fated to die when his daughter married, and so set some forty impossible tasks upon her suitor; and when they were done he was shaved to the bone and beheaded, and said that it was Culhwch's doing and not his own.

gods.name: Creiddylad
gods.description: Daughter of Lludd, called the most majestic maiden in the Island of the Mighty. Gwyn ap Nudd and Gwythyr ap Greidawl both wanted her, and Arthur judged between them: that they should fight for her every May-day until Judgement Day, and whichever was the victor then should have her, and she should stay in her father's house meanwhile. So the summer and the winter contend, and neither wins.

gods.name: Hyfaidd Hen
gods.description: Father of Rhiannon in the First Branch of the Mabinogi. It is at his court that Pwyll comes to the wedding-feast, and there that Gwawl asks his boon and gets Rhiannon promised away from under him; and it is from there, a year later, that Pwyll wins her back with the badger-in-the-bag. Little else is told of him.

gods.name: Yuhwa
gods.description: 'Willow Flower', eldest daughter of the river god Habaek, in the Goguryeo foundation tradition. Haemosu took her by the river and she was cast out by her father for it; and afterwards, shut in a room, she was found by a shaft of sunlight that followed her wherever she moved, and conceived, and bore an egg, from which Jumong came. She sent him away when the king's sons meant to kill him, and gave him seed-grain to take.

gods.name: Habaek
gods.description: God of the rivers in the Goguryeo foundation tradition, and father of Yuhwa.
