When Haemosu carried off his daughter he came after him, and the two fought by changing shapes — carp and otter, deer and wolf, pheasant and hawk — and when neither could win, he tested the man with wine instead, and was outdone. He put the pair in a leather boat to send them to heaven, and Haemosu went up alone.

gods.name: Bak Hyeokgeose
gods.description: Founder of Silla. The chiefs of the six villages, looking for a ruler, saw a light by a well and a white horse kneeling and crying beside a red egg; and when the horse flew up to heaven and the egg was opened, there was a boy in it, whose body shone. They raised him, and made him king at thirteen. His queen Aryeong was born from the ribs of a dragon on the same day.

gods.name: Onjo
gods.description: Founder of Baekje, and a son of Jumong. When Jumong's elder son came from Buyeo and was made his heir, Onjo went south with his brother Biryu and their followers to find land of their own; and Biryu settled by the sea at Michuhol, where the water was salt and the ground poor, and died of shame, and his people came over to Onjo, who had built at Wiryeseong and prospered.

gods.name: Gamunjang-agi
gods.description: Youngest of three daughters in the Jeju shamanic narrative. Asked by her parents whose merit it was that she lived so well, she answered that it was her own — for which she was driven out, while her sisters, who had answered as they were meant to, stayed. She married a poor man who dug stones, and the stones turned out to be gold; and her parents, who had gone blind and beggared, came at last to the feast she set for beggars, and got their sight back at the sound of her voice. She is a goddess of fortune, and of the fortune one makes.

gods.name: Almo
gods.description: God of the little river Almo, which ran into the Tiber just south of Rome — a small god of a small stream, but the stream mattered: it was in the Almo, every March, that the black stone of Cybele and the sacred things of her cult were washed by her priests in the rite called the lavatio. He is father of the nymph Larunda in the Roman telling.

gods.name: Feronia
gods.description: Ancient Italic goddess of the wild ground, of springs, and of the freeing of slaves — at her grove and sanctuary at Lucus Feroniae, at the foot of Soracte, slaves sat on a stone that bore the words 'let the deserving sit down as slaves and rise up free', and went away with the cap of liberty on. The Sabines, the Latins and the Etruscans all knew her, and the market at her grove was famous.

gods.name: Angerona
gods.description: Goddess of silence, shown with her mouth bound and sealed and a finger raised to it. Her statue stood in the shrine of Volupia, and she was sacrificed to at the Angeronalia at the turn of the winter. It was said that she kept the secret name of Rome — the true name, which was never to be spoken, because whoever knew it could call the city's gods away from it.

gods.name: Vejovis
gods.description: An old and obscure Roman god, shown as a beardless youth with arrows and a she-goat beside him. His name reads as an un-Jupiter or a lesser Jupiter, and the Romans themselves were unsure of him: some made him a Jupiter of the underworld, some a god of expiation and of the sick, some a young Jupiter before he came into his power. He had a temple between the two summits of the Capitol, and his victims were offered in the manner of the dead.

gods.name: Wurunkatte
gods.description: The war god of the Hattian layer, whose name means 'king of the land' — the oldest of the Anatolian war gods, taken over by the Hittites and standing in their offering lists with a city and a cult of his own. He is shown on a bull, or with the mace; the scribes wrote his name with the Mesopotamian sign for Zababa, which is a scribal convenience and not an identification.

gods.name: Lelwani
gods.description: Deity of the underworld and of the dark earth, whose temple was the place of the royal dead. The gender is not fixed and the change is real: in the older Hattian layer Lelwani is male, addressed as a king of the underworld, and in the later Hittite texts female — a queen, to whom Puduḫepa prayed for her husband's life, offering statues of him. No sex is asserted here, because the tradition itself moved.

gods.name: Hasameli
gods.description: Hattian god of the smiths and of metalworking, taken into the Hittite pantheon. He is invoked to make a man invisible to his enemies, as the smith's work is hidden in the smoke of the forge; and he is asked to cover the king in battle.

gods.name: Hauhet
gods.description: One of the eight of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad — the four pairs of frog-headed gods and snake-headed goddesses who were the elements of the world before the world: Nun and Naunet the waters, Heh and Hauhet the endlessness, Kek and Kauket the darkness, Amun and Amunet the hidden. Hauhet is the female of the pair of endlessness, and stands with Heh for the limitless extent of time and space. She is named as a member of that eight; that is what she is, and the whole of what the texts give her.

gods.name: Kek
gods.description: Darkness itself, and one of the eight of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, paired with Kauket. He is the dark that lay on the waters before there was any light to be dark against — not evil, and not night, which is a thing that comes after the sun; the dark that was there first. He is called 'bringer-in of the light' as well, being the hour before dawn.

gods.name: Kauket
gods.description: The female of the pair of darkness in the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, standing with Kek. Where he is the dark that precedes the light, she is called 'bringer-in of the night' — the dark that follows it. She is a named member of the eight, and the theology of Hermopolis gives her no story apart from that place in it.

gods.name: Andjety
gods.description: The old god of Busiris in the Delta, shown as a man with the crook and the flail and a high crown of two feathers. He is older there than Osiris, and when Osiris rose at Busiris he took Andjety's insignia and his shepherd's crook, and in time his cult — so that the later texts write of Osiris-Andjety, and Andjety's own name fades. He is the god who came before and was absorbed, not another name for the god who absorbed him, and he is catalogued here in his own right.

gods.name: Wadj-Wer
gods.description: 'The Great Green' — the sea and the standing water of the Delta made a god, shown as a heavy figure with water lines across the body and the belly of one who is well fed, carrying fish and loaves. He is fertility as water: the lagoons and the marshes that fed the Delta, and by extension the Mediterranean beyond them.

gods.name: Mahuika
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the atua of fire, in whose fingers and toes the fire is kept. Māui came to her and asked for fire, and she drew out a fingernail and gave him the flame in it; and he quenched it and came back, and again, and again, until she had given away all but one and understood that she was mocked — and threw the last after him, and set the forest alight, and he fled as a hawk with the fire behind him and was saved by the rain. What she had left she threw into the trees, and that is why fire lives in wood and can be drawn out of it. She is fire, and not merely Māui's grandmother.

gods.name: Whaitiri
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the atua of thunder — a woman of the sky, and a cannibal, who came down for a mortal husband, Kaitangata, having heard his name and taken it for a promise of the flesh she liked. She went back up when he disappointed her, leaving her children behind, and it is her grandson Tāwhaki who climbs to find her. She had blinded herself in her grief, or was blinded; and he restored her sight. Thunder is hers, and is her name.

gods.name: Makemake
gods.description: In the tradition of Rapa Nui — Easter Island — the creator god and the chief god of the island, who made man and is carved everywhere at Orongo with great eyes and a beaked face. His was the birdman cult, the tangata manu: each spring the servants of the chiefs swam out to the islet of Motu Nui through the sharks to wait for the first egg of the sooty tern, and the man whose servant brought it back was birdman for the year, and was tapu, and his patron ruled. Rapa Nui is the eastern-most of the Polynesian islands, and its gods are catalogued on this shelf with the rest.

gods.name: Kamohoaliʻi
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the shark god — the king of the sharks, who may take the form of any fish and of a man, and who is prayed to by fishermen and by those who go on the water. He is said to have guided the canoes of Pele's family to Hawaiʻi, and he keeps the steam of the volcano; the priests would not eat his flesh nor say his name over the water lightly. He is a god of the sharks in his own right, and his kinship with Pele is one fact about him and not the whole of him.

gods.name: Rata
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the hero who went to avenge his father Wahieroa. He felled a great tree in the forest to make his canoe, and came back the next morning to find it standing again; and the second time he hid and watched, and saw the hakuturi — the birds and the insects of the forest, the children of Tāne — putting the chips back and raising it up, because he had cut it without the proper rite. He asked their pardon, and they built the canoe for him in a night.

gods.name: Leizu
gods.description: Wife of the Yellow Emperor, and the one who found silk. A cocoon dropped into her tea, they say, and unwound in the hot water into a thread that ran on and on; and she taught the rearing of the silkworms and the reeling of the thread and the weaving of it, and was worshipped afterwards as the First Sericulturist, to whom the empress sacrificed every spring.

gods.name: Gun
gods.description: The man who tried to stop the great flood and failed. He stole the xirang from the high god — the self-renewing earth, which grows of itself and never runs out — and built dykes of it for nine years; but the water rose over them, and the god sent Zhurong to kill him at Feather Mountain for the theft. His body did not rot for three years, and when it was cut open his son Yu came out of it, who finished the work by dredging instead of damming. He is a figure of the flood myth and of the theft that fails — not a small god, but a man who reached above himself and was struck down for it.

gods.name: Dongwanggong
gods.description: The King Father of the East — the male counterpart of Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West, and made to answer her: she has the west and the yin, he has the east and the yang, and the Han mirrors and the tomb reliefs show the two of them facing one another across the world. He is a real god of that religion and received his own offerings; but he was formed as her counterweight and never had the cult or the stories she had, and he is not catalogued here at her rank.

gods.name: Yinglong
gods.description: The winged dragon — the responding dragon — who fought for the Yellow Emperor against Chiyou at Zhuolu, and dammed the waters against him, and killed him and Kuafu both. Afterwards he could not go back up to heaven, having killed, and settled in the south; and where he lies there is rain, and in drought his shape was made in clay so that the rain would come to it.

gods.name: Cangjie
gods.description: The scribe of the Yellow Emperor, who invented writing. He had four eyes, and looked at the tracks of the birds and the beasts in the dust, and saw that each was different and that a mark could stand for a thing; and he made the characters from that. And on the day he made them the sky rained millet and the ghosts wailed in the night, because from that time nothing could be hidden.

gods.name: Tallay
gods.description: In the Ugaritic Baal cycle, the second of the three daughters of Baal — 'Tallay, daughter of showers'. She is the dew, as her sister Pidray is the light or the mist and Arsay the earth, and she dwells with them in Baal's house on Mount Zaphon and is named among the things that are his. The Ugaritic texts give her little beyond the name and the epithet, and nothing is added here.

gods.name: Arsay
gods.description: The third of Baal's daughters in the Ugaritic cycle — 'Arsay, daughter of the wide world' — whose name is the earth itself, and who is set with the underworld by those who read her epithet that way. She stands with Pidray and Tallay in Baal's house and is named with them, and beyond that the tablets are silent.

gods.name: Chemosh
gods.description: The god of Moab, and the one Moabite god we have in his own words — for on the Mesha Stele, cut about 840 BCE, the king Mesha says that Chemosh was angry with his land and let Israel oppress it, and then that Chemosh said to him, 'Go, take Nebo from Israel,' and he went and took it and slaughtered the town for him. He is a national god of the sort the Iron Age Levant was full of — the god of a people and their land and their wars. He is not Baal, the Ugaritic storm-god catalogued on this shelf, and he is not Moloch: the Hebrew Bible records that a king of Moab offered his son on the wall, but Moloch in this archive is a separate entry, and a name the biblical writers used in polemic, and the two are not run together here.

gods.name: Aqhat
gods.description: In the Ugaritic Epic of Aqhat, the long-awaited son of Danel, to whom the craftsman-god Kothar gave a marvellous bow. The goddess Anat wanted it and offered him silver and gold for it, and then immortality; and he answered that she was lying — that a man dies as all men die, and that a bow is a thing for warriors and what is she doing with one. For that she had him killed by her henchman in the shape of a hawk, and the bow was lost in the water, and the land went dry.

gods.name: Takuhadachiji-hime
gods.description: Daughter of Takamimusubi, wife of Ame-no-Oshihomimi, and mother of Ninigi — so that the line of the emperors runs through her as much as through Amaterasu. Her name has to do with the weaving of bark-cloth on the heavenly loom, and she is given in the sources under other forms as well: Takuhatachiji-hime, and Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime in the Nihon Shoki. When the heavenly grandchild was to be sent down, it was her son who was to go, and he sent his own son instead.

gods.name: Enma
gods.description: Great King Enma, who judges the dead in Japanese Buddhist tradition and rules the hells — red-faced, in the robes and cap of a Chinese magistrate, with the mirror that shows a man his own deeds and the ledger in which they are written, and two attendant heads that see and hear everything. The office descends from the Indian Yama by way of the Chinese Yanluo; both are catalogued separately in this archive, as is the Korean Yeomra, and this record is the Japanese figure of the Buddhist temples and the hell-scrolls, not any of the others.

gods.name: Untamo
gods.description: In the Kalevala, the brother of Kalervo and the ruin of his house: over a quarrel about a fishing ground and a field of oats, he came with his men and killed all of Kalervo's people but one pregnant woman, whom he took, and whose son was Kullervo — who grew up in his uncle's house, was sold away when he could not be killed, and came back at the end and burned the place and everyone in it. He is a figure of the Kalevala's poetry and of the Finnish and Karelian songs Lönnrot worked from, and not an object of any cult.

gods.name: Marjatta
gods.description: In the last canto of the Kalevala, the maid who conceived from a lingonberry she ate off the ground, and was turned out by her mother and bore her son in a stable among the horses. When the child was half a month old he spoke and condemned Väinämöinen out of his own mouth, and was made king of Karelia; and Väinämöinen, seeing his time was done, sang himself a boat of copper and went away over the sea, leaving his songs behind him. The canto is Lönnrot's shaping of Christianised folk songs about a virgin and a berry; it is the poem's ending, and no evidence of an old cult.

gods.name: Sampsa Pellervoinen
gods.description: The sower of the second canto of the Kalevala — 'Pellervoinen, son of the field' — a slight boy whom Väinämöinen sends to seed the empty land, and who goes out with the seeds in a pouch of marten-skin and sows the pines on the hills and the birches in the hollows and the alders on the loose ground, and everything comes up but the oak, which needs a second sowing. He belongs to the Kalevala and to the Finnish folk poetry Lönnrot drew on; whether anything was ever offered to him is not known, and is not claimed here.

gods.name: Mac Cecht
gods.description: One of the three last kings of the Tuatha Dé Danann in the Lebor Gabála Érenn — sons of Cermait, grandsons of the Dagda — who ruled Ireland together, each in turn for a year, until the Milesians came and killed all three at Tailtiu. His name is read as 'son of the plough'. He is catalogued as a king of the Tuatha Dé, which is what the tradition makes him; that his wife was Fódla, who gave her name to Ireland, is a further fact about him and not the reason for it.

gods.name: Mac Cuill
gods.description: One of the three last kings of the Tuatha Dé Danann, son of Cermait and grandson of the Dagda, who held Ireland jointly with his brothers Mac Cecht and Mac Gréine and fell with them before the Milesians. His name is read as 'son of the hazel'. His wife was Banba, one of the three who gave Ireland her names; his standing here rests on his kingship among the Tuatha Dé.

gods.name: Mac Gréine
gods.description: One of the three last kings of the Tuatha Dé Danann, son of Cermait and grandson of the Dagda. His name is read as 'son of the sun'. He held Ireland with his two brothers and was killed by the Milesians in the taking of the land. His wife was Ériu, whose name Ireland still carries — but it is as a king of the Tuatha Dé that he is catalogued, not as her husband.

gods.name: Aoife
gods.description: Second wife of Lir in the Children of Lir, and daughter of Bodb Derg. She married Lir after her sister Aobh died, and grew jealous of Aobh's four children, whom he loved better than anything; and she took them to a lake and struck them with a druid's wand and turned them into swans for nine hundred years. Bodb Derg, learning of it, turned her into a demon of the air. She is not Aífe of Alba, the warrior-woman who fought Scáthach and bore Cú Chulainn's son Connla — a different woman who shares the name, and who is not this record.

gods.name: Áine
gods.description: Goddess of Munster and of the summer, whose hill is Cnoc Áine in County Limerick, where fires were lit on Midsummer Eve within living memory and the torches carried through the fields and the cattle to bless them. She is a sovereignty goddess — the land taken as a woman, who makes or unmakes a king; the FitzGeralds claimed descent from her, and she was said to be seen combing her hair on the bank of the Camóg.

gods.name: Tailtiu
gods.description: Queen of the Fir Bolg and foster-mother of Lugh, who cleared the forest of Breg into open plain so that it could be farmed, and died of the labour of it; and Lugh, at her asking, founded games and a fair in her memory at the place that bears her name — the Óenach Tailten, held at Lughnasa, which went on in some form into the nineteenth century. What the medieval texts give is this: a queen, a foster-mother, a cleared plain and an assembly. The fuller claim of a pan-Irish earth goddess is a modern extension of that, and is not made here.

gods.name: Regin
gods.description: The dwarf smith of the Eddic poems and the Völsunga saga — son of Hreiðmarr, brother of Fáfnir and Ótr — who took Sigurd as his foster-son and forged him the sword Gram, and sent him against the dragon that had been his brother, meaning to have the gold himself. He asked Sigurd to roast the heart for him; and Sigurd, burning his thumb on it and putting it in his mouth, understood the birds in the tree above, who said that Regin meant to kill him. So Sigurd killed him first.

gods.name: Garmr
gods.description: The hound bound before Gnipahellir, the cave at the road to Hel, who howls there — and the refrain of the Völuspá turns on that howling: 'Now Garmr bays loud before Gnipahellir, the fetter will break and the wolf run free.' At Ragnarök he gets loose, and he and Týr kill one another.

gods.name: Geirröðr
gods.description: The giant of Skáldskaparmál and of Þórsdrápa, who got Loki into his hands and made him swear to bring Thor to him without his hammer, his belt or his iron gloves. Thor came, was nearly drowned by the giant's daughters Gjálp and Greip in the river, and broke their backs on the roof-beam; and when Geirröðr threw a bar of molten iron at him with the tongs, Thor caught it in iron gloves he had been lent and threw it back through the pillar the giant hid behind, and through the giant, and through the wall. He is not the mortal King Geirröðr of Grímnismál, who tortured Odin between two fires and fell on his own sword; that is a different figure, and this record is not his.

gods.name: Hræsvelgr
gods.description: 'Corpse-swallower' — the jötunn who sits at the end of heaven in the shape of an eagle, and from whose wings, as Vafþrúðnismál says, the wind comes over all men. He is not an enemy of the gods and does not fight them: he is where the wind is made, a being of the world's working rather than a monster set against it, and he is catalogued accordingly.

gods.name: Brokkr
gods.description: One of the two dwarf brothers of Skáldskaparmál who took Loki's wager that they could not match the treasures of the sons of Ivaldi. Brokkr worked the bellows while his brother Eitri forged; and Loki, in the shape of a fly, bit him on the hand, the neck, and at last on the eyelid so that the blood ran into his eye, and he let go the bellows for an instant — which is why the handle of Mjölnir is short. They won the wager, and Brokkr sewed Loki's lips shut for it.

gods.name: Eitri
gods.description: The dwarf who forged, in the wager with Loki, the boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir, and the hammer Mjölnir — laying the gold and the iron in the fire and going out while his brother Brokkr worked the bellows, and charging him not to stop for anything. This is the name Snorri gives him in Skáldskaparmál, the prose source for the story, and it is the name used here. He is very often called Sindri instead — a name taken from the hall of 'Sindri's kin' in Völuspá and fastened onto the smith by later tradition and by modern retellings. It is the same figure, and there is no separate record for him.

gods.name: Matsya
gods.description: The fish, first descent of Vishnu. He came to Manu as a tiny fish in the water cupped in his hands, and asked to be kept safe; and he grew, and outgrew the jar and the pond and the lake and the river, until Manu understood who he was. He told him the flood was coming, and to build a boat and load it with the seeds of all things and with the seven sages; and when the water rose he came as a great horned fish, and Manu tied the boat to his horn with the serpent for a rope, and he drew them through the flood to the mountain. Manu is catalogued here. The descent is incarnation and not birth, and no parentage is recorded.

gods.name: Kurma
gods.description: The tortoise, second descent of Vishnu. When the gods and the asuras churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, using Mount Mandara for the churning-staff and the serpent Vasuki for the rope, the mountain began to sink into the soft sea-bed; and Vishnu went down under it as a tortoise and took it on his back, and it turned upon him for a thousand years while they churned. Vasuki is catalogued here. Incarnation, not parentage.

gods.name: Dhanvantari
gods.description: The physician of the gods, who rose out of the churned ocean of milk carrying the pot of amrita in his hands — the last and the best of the things that came up out of it. He is the god of Ayurveda and the giver of medicine, and physicians have invoked him at the beginning of their work for as long as there has been a written tradition of it. He is worshipped at Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, and the Puranas count him among the descents of Vishnu.

gods.name: Chitragupta
gods.description: The scribe of Yama, who keeps the account. Every deed of every living thing is written down by him, the good on one side and the bad on the other, in the book called the Agrasandhani; and when a soul comes before Yama, it is Chitragupta's ledger that is read out, and by that the judgment is given. The Kayastha caste hold him for their ancestor.

gods.name: Manasa
gods.description: Goddess of snakes and of the cure for their bite, worshipped chiefly in Bengal and the east, and the subject of the Manasamangal — the long cycle of poems in which she sets out to force the merchant Chand Sadagar to worship her, and he will not, though she kills his sons one after another. The last of them, Lakhindar, dies of a snakebite on his wedding night in an iron chamber built to keep her out; and his widow Behula takes the body on a raft down the river to the gods and wins his life back, and the merchant at last gives her the flower — with his left hand, and without looking.

gods.name: Phaethon
gods.description: Mortal son of Helios, who was taunted with not knowing his father and went to him to be owned; and Helios, glad of him, swore by the Styx to give him whatever he asked, and he asked to drive the chariot of the sun for a day. He could not hold the horses. The chariot ran high and left the earth cold and ran low and burned it black — the Sahara, they said, was made then, and the Ethiopians darkened — until Zeus struck him out of the sky with a thunderbolt to stop him, and he fell into the river Eridanus. His sisters, weeping on the bank, became poplars, and their tears amber.

gods.name: Endymion
gods.description: A mortal — a shepherd on Latmos, or a king of Elis, the accounts differ — whom Selene the moon saw sleeping and loved. She asked Zeus to give him what he wished, and what he wished was to sleep forever, and never grow old, and never die; and he was granted it, and lies in a cave on Latmos in unbroken sleep, and the moon comes down to him. She bore him fifty daughters, the tradition says, while he slept.

gods.name: Syrinx
gods.description: A naiad of Arcadia and a follower of Artemis, who was chased by Pan and, coming to the river Ladon and unable to cross it, begged her sisters the water-nymphs to change her — and was changed into a stand of reeds. Pan, catching only the reeds, heard the wind sigh through them, and cut them into unequal lengths and bound them with wax, and so made the pipes that bear her name and carry her voice.

gods.name: Boreas
gods.description: The north wind — the hard one, bringer of winter, shown bearded and winged and shaggy with frost. He carried off the Athenian princess Oreithyia from the banks of the Ilissos, and the Athenians afterwards counted him a kinsman by marriage and prayed to him; and when the Persian fleet lay off Cape Sepias they called on him, and the storm that broke it was his. He is one of the Anemoi, who are catalogued together as well, and his brother Zephyrus the west wind is catalogued singly, as he is here.

gods.name: Yacatecuhtli
gods.description: 'Lord Nose' — the god of the pochteca, the long-distance merchants who went armed into far countries and came back with quetzal feathers and jade and news. His image was the traveller's staff: on the road the merchants bound their black canes together into a bundle and set it up and made offerings of paper and incense and their own blood to it, and it was him. He is a god of the road and of what is carried on it, and of the profit at the end.

gods.name: Huixtocihuatl
gods.description: Goddess of salt and of the salt water it comes from — an elder sister, Sahagún's informants said, of the rain-gods, who quarrelled with her and drove her out to the salt water, and there she found the salt and the way of making it in the pans. The salt-makers kept her feast in the seventh month with ten days of dancing, the women holding a rope of flowers between them and singing all night, and at the end a woman who had taken her likeness was sacrificed.

gods.name: Chalchiuhtotolin
gods.description: 'Jade Turkey' — a nahual of Tezcatlipoca, one of the shapes the smoking mirror takes, and patron of the day-sign Tecpatl, the flint knife. He is the bringer of plague and also the washer of it: the god who sends the sickness and the one who can be asked to take it away, and to whom the guilt of a man may be given up and cleansed. He is an aspect of Tezcatlipoca and is catalogued as such — one face of that god, in the manner of Ehecatl and Xolotl on this shelf, and not a god standing beside him at his own height.

gods.name: Gwythyr ap Greidawl
gods.description: In Culhwch and Olwen, the rival of Gwyn ap Nudd. Gwyn carried off Creiddylad, and Gwythyr raised an army and went after her, and there was a long and bitter war of it, with prisoners taken and a man made to eat his own father's heart; and Arthur judged between them at last — that Creiddylad should stay in her father's house untouched, and that the two of them should fight for her every May Day until Judgement Day, and whichever won on that day should have her. So they are fighting still, and the summer and the winter turn on it.

gods.name: Elffin ap Gwyddno
gods.description: The luckless prince of the Ystoria Taliesin. He was given the year's catch of his father's salmon-weir on the eve of May, and there was not one fish in it — only a leather bag caught on the poles, and in the bag a child with a shining forehead, whom he named Taliesin and took home and raised. The boy made him rich and, when Maelgwn Gwynedd had him thrown in irons, sang him out of prison again. He is a figure of the tale and not a man of history.

gods.name: Caradog
gods.description: Caradog ap Brân, of the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. When Brân went to Ireland he left seven men to hold Britain, and Caradog his son as chief of them; and while they were gone Caswallawn son of Beli came under a mantle of invisibility and killed six of the seven, and Caradog, seeing the sword and not the man who held it, broke his heart at the sight and died of it. He is not Caratacus, the British chieftain who fought Rome and was taken to it in chains, nor Caradog Freichfras of the Arthurian tales; those are other men who bear the name.

gods.name: Matholwch
gods.description: King of Ireland in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, who came to Harlech for Branwen and married her — and whose horses Efnysien mutilated in spite, so that he went home shamed; and at home he was goaded until he put Branwen out of his bed and set her to cook, and had her boxed on the ear every day by the butcher. That is what brought Brân over the sea, and the ruin of both islands. He is catalogued as a principal actor of the tale, which is what the category means here — not as a man the story admires.

gods.name: Caswallawn
gods.description: Son of Beli, who took Britain while Brân's host was in Ireland — walking among the stewards in a mantle that made him invisible, so that they saw only the sword that killed them, and he spared none but the one he could not bring himself to kill. He carries the name of Cassivellaunus, the British chieftain who fought Julius Caesar; the name is the same and the memory of it lies behind the tale, but the deeds are not that man's deeds, and the two lives are not joined here.

gods.name: Morfran ap Tegid
gods.description: Son of Ceridwen and Tegid Foel, and the reason she set the cauldron of inspiration boiling for a year and a day — for he was so ill-favoured that she meant to make him wise instead, and the three drops went to the servant boy Gwion Bach and not to him. He is called Afagddu, 'utter darkness', for his blackness; that is taken here as his by-name and not another person, and no separate record is made of it — though it should be said that a few manuscript traditions list Morfran and Afagddu as two sons rather than one. In Culhwch and Olwen he is one of Arthur's men, and no one struck him at Camlan, because they all took him for a devil helping.

gods.name: Shamhat
gods.description: The woman of Uruk sent out to the wild man at the watering-hole in the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the one who changes him. She lay with him six days and seven nights, and afterwards the gazelles ran from him and his body would not carry him as it had — but his mind had opened, and he could hear what she said; and she clothed him, and taught him to eat bread and drink beer, and brought him to the city. Dying, Enkidu curses her for it and then, at Shamash's word, takes the curse back and blesses her instead. She is a woman, not a goddess, and she is the hinge of the poem: without her there is no Enkidu to meet Gilgamesh at all.

gods.name: Etana
gods.description: The shepherd-king of Kish in the Sumerian King List — 'the one who went up to heaven' — who had no son, and went looking for the plant of birth. He found an eagle at the bottom of a pit, thrown there for eating the serpent's young, and fed it and healed it; and it carried him up on its back toward the heaven of Anu, and the land grew small below them, and smaller, until he looked down and lost his nerve. The tablets break. The King List says his son reigned after him.

gods.name: Enmerkar
gods.description: King of Uruk in the Sumerian poems, who wanted the gold and lapis of Aratta beyond the mountains and sent his herald back and forth over seven ranges with demands and riddles. The messages grew too long to be remembered, and so — the poem says — he patted clay and set words on it, which had never been done before; and the lord of Aratta looked at the tablet, and it was written, and he could not read it. He is a legendary king, not a god.

gods.name: Mummu
gods.description: The vizier of Apsu in the first tablet of the Enūma Eliš, and a person in that poem: he sits at his master's side, kisses him, and gives him the counsel that begins the war — 'destroy them, and there will be rest by day and sleep by night.' Tiamat would not have it; Apsu took the advice; and Ea put them both to sleep with a spell, killed Apsu, bound Mummu, and took his aura for himself. The word mummu is also used elsewhere in Akkadian as a term and as an epithet — Marduk carries it — but those uses are not this figure, and are not gathered into him here.

gods.name: Nanaya
gods.description: Goddess of love and desire, worshipped at Uruk beside Inanna and afterwards in her own right for two thousand years and more — into the Seleucid age, and eastward as far as Bactria. She is her own goddess, with her own temples and her own hymns, in which she praises her lips and her eyes and her sweetness; but her ground is Inanna's ground, and the two stand very close, so that she is often taken for an aspect of her. She is catalogued here as a distinct goddess of the second rank, and not as another name for the Queen of Heaven.

gods.name: Martu / Amurru
gods.description: The god of the westerners — Sumerian Martu, Akkadian Amurru — who is the Amorite made divine: a god of the open steppe and the tent, carrying the crook, and married in one Sumerian poem to a city girl whose friend warns her against him, saying he eats raw meat and does not bend the knee and never buries his dead. He is recorded here as one god under both names, as Ishkur/Adad and Utu/Shamash are on this shelf.

gods.name: Mater Matuta
gods.description: An old Italic goddess, whose temple in the Forum Boarium is among the earliest in Rome and stood beside that of Portunus at the river port. Her feast was the Matralia on the eleventh of June, kept by women who had been married once only, and to which no slave-woman was admitted; and there the matrons prayed not for their own children but for their sisters'. She is of the morning and of birth and of the harbour together. She is not Aurora, who is catalogued here as the Latin form of the Greek Eos — that is a translated goddess, and this one is Italic and her own.

gods.name: Anna Perenna
gods.description: Goddess of the year that comes round — her name reads as the year lasting through the years — whose feast fell on the Ides of March, which was the old New Year. The people went out to the first milestone on the Flaminian Way and lay about on the grass by the Tiber in tents and huts of branches, and drank as many cups as they hoped to live years, and sang the coarse songs of the day. Ovid did not know who she was and gave four answers. The feast was famous; that is not by itself a measure of rank, and she is catalogued in the second order.

gods.name: Pales
gods.description: The deity of shepherds and of the flocks, whose feast, the Parilia, fell on the twenty-first of April — the day Rome was held to have been founded — when the folds were swept and hung with greenery, the sheep purified with smoke of sulphur and rosemary, and the shepherds leapt through fires of straw. The sex is not settled in the sources: some Roman writers make Pales a goddess, some a god, and some speak of two Pales together. No one of those is chosen here.

gods.name: Summanus
gods.description: The god of the thunderbolts that fall by night, as Jupiter holds those of the day. He is old and obscure and was so already by Ovid's time; but he had a temple of his own near the Circus Maximus, vowed after his image on the roof of the Capitoline temple was struck by lightning, and round wheel-shaped cakes, the summanalia, were offered to him. He is his own god and not a name for Jupiter.

gods.name: Robigus
gods.description: The numen of the red blight that takes the wheat in the ear. At the Robigalia, on the twenty-fifth of April, the flamen Quirinalis went out to a grove at the fifth milestone of the Via Claudia and burned the entrails of a red dog and a sheep, and asked him — in the prayer Ovid gives — to keep his rough hands from the young corn and to scour rusty iron and swords instead. He is the power in the blight, not the name of the festival that placates him.

gods.name: Suro
gods.description: Founder of Geumgwan Gaya. The nine chiefs, at the voice from the sky, sang and stamped on the peak of Guji until a purple cord came down out of heaven with a golden box on it, and in the box six golden eggs; and from the first of them came Suro, who was made king of the greatest of the six Gaya states. His queen, Heo Hwang-ok, came by sea from a country called Ayuta, saying she had been sent in a dream.

gods.name: Aryeong
gods.description: Queen of Bak Hyeokgeose and the first queen of Silla. She was born on the same day as he was — at the Aryeong well, where a dragon or a hen-dragon appeared and she came from its left rib, with a beak for a mouth that fell away when she was washed in the stream. The two were raised together and married at thirteen, and the people called them the Two Saints, and worshipped them together after their deaths. She stands here with the miraculous queens and mothers of the foundation cycles — Yuhwa, and Ungnyeo the bear-woman — and is catalogued as they are.

gods.name: Seok Talhae
gods.description: Fourth king of Silla, and the founder of the Seok line. He was born as an egg to a queen of a country beyond the sea, and set adrift in a chest with treasure and servants; and the chest came ashore in Silla, guarded by magpies, and an old woman opened it. Grown, he took a nobleman's house by burying charcoal and whetstones under it in the night and swearing his people had been smiths there — and afterwards Namhae gave him his daughter, and he came to the throne.

gods.name: Impaluri
gods.description: The sukkal — the vizier — of the Sea in the Hurrian songs of the Kumarbi cycle. He carries the words between his master and Kumarbi, and it is he who is sent to bid the Sea come to the feast, and who stands at his lord's side when the terms are made for the raising of Hedammu. He is the Sea God's man, not Kumarbi's, and he is not the same figure as Mukishanu.

gods.name: Mukishanu
gods.description: The sukkal — the vizier — of Kumarbi in the Hurrian songs of that cycle. He stands before his master and is sent down to the waters to fetch the Sea to him, so that they may make their compact together; and when Kumarbi lays his plans against the Storm God, it is Mukishanu who is told them first. He is Kumarbi's man, and distinct from Impaluri, who serves the Sea. The two are named figures with their own masters, not one office under two names.

gods.name: Mnevis
gods.description: The living bull of Heliopolis, black, held to be the herald of Ra-Atum and the animal in which that god showed himself on earth — one bull only at a time, chosen by its markings, kept and fed and buried with rites when it died, and another sought. He is not Apis, the bull of Memphis, nor Buchis, the bull of Armant: three cities, three bulls, three gods behind them, and they are not one identity wearing three names. His cult was local to Heliopolis and never had the reach of the Memphite bull's, and he is catalogued at the rank that reflects it.

gods.name: Ash
gods.description: God of the western desert and of the oases in it — of the vineyards of the Libyan sands, and of the people who lived out there beyond the cultivation. He is one of the oldest gods named in Egypt, appearing on seal impressions of the First Dynasty and on wine jars, and he is titled 'Lord of Libya'. He is shown sometimes with the head of Set, whose desert he shares. He is a god with a name and a place, not a title of another.

gods.name: Tayet
gods.description: Goddess of weaving and of the woven cloth — and so of the linen bandages in which the dead were wrapped, which is where she matters most. In the Pyramid Texts it is Tayet who clothes the king, who gathers his head for him and binds it, and whose cloth covers what should not be seen. She is a named goddess of her own and not a description of a craft.

gods.name: Buchis
gods.description: The living bull of Armant, in the south — white-bodied and black-faced, said to change the colour of his hair every hour, and held to be the ba of Montu, the falcon war-god of Thebes. He had his own cult and his own burial ground, the Bucheum, where the bulls were entombed one after another with stelae recording each one's birth and installation and death, for some six hundred years. He is not Apis and not Mnevis; each of the three belongs to his own city and his own god.

gods.name: Mehen
gods.description: 'The Coiled One' — the serpent who winds himself about the shrine of the sun-god in the barque of the night, ring upon ring, so that Apep cannot come at him as he passes through the hours of the dark. He is a protector and not an enemy: in the Amduat and the Book of Gates he is drawn around Ra like a wall. An Old Kingdom board game of a coiled snake is also called mehen, and takes its name from him; the game is not the god, and it is the god who is catalogued here.

gods.name: Danel
gods.description: In the Ugaritic Epic of Aqhat, the man who sat at the gate and judged the cause of the widow and the fatherless, and who had no son — until, after seven days lying in the sanctuary, Baal spoke for him to El and a son was granted. That son was Aqhat, whom Anat killed for the bow; and Danel, finding the pieces of him in the crop of a vulture, buried them, and cursed the towns near the killing, and mourned seven years. He is the Ugaritic Dnil. He is not Daniel of the Hebrew book — a different man, of a different people and a much later text; the resemblance of the names has often been made into an identity, and it is not made here.

gods.name: Pughat
gods.description: Sister of Aqhat in the Ugaritic epic, who knew the courses of the stars and drew water and saddled the ass for her father. When Aqhat was killed she asked Danel's blessing and went after the killer herself: she washed and reddened herself, and put on a woman's clothes, and under them a warrior's dress and a blade; and she came to Yatpan's camp as a guest and poured him wine until he boasted of the hand that did it. The tablet breaks there. She is a principal actor of the poem in her own right.

gods.name: Keret / Kirta
gods.description: King of Ugaritic legend who lost everything — seven wives, and all his children with them, to sickness and war and the sea — and wept until El came to him in a dream and told him to take an army and go and ask the king of Udm for his daughter Hurriya, and not to take gold instead. He did, and she bore him sons; and then he fell ill, having failed a vow to Athirat, and the land dried with him, and his son Yassib came to his sickbed and told him to step down. The name is written Krt, and is read both Keret, the older form, and Kirta, which is now preferred; these are two vocalizations of one king's name, not two men, and one record is made.

gods.name: Yatpan
gods.description: The Sutean warrior whom Anat took into her service in the Epic of Aqhat, and whom she carried in the shape of a bird among a flock of vultures to strike Aqhat down at his meal — and Aqhat's breath went out of him and did not come back. Afterwards Pughat came to his camp and poured him wine, and he boasted in his cups that the hand which felled the brother could fell the sister. The tablet breaks off there, and we do not know what she did to him; the loss is in the clay and not in the man, who is named, and speaks, and acts.

gods.name: Qos
gods.description: The national god of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea. He is real and he was the chief god of a kingdom, but almost everything we have of him is names: Qos-gabr, king of Edom, in the tribute lists of Assyria; Qos-malak; hundreds of Idumaean ostraca with the element in them. There is no myth of him, no story, no certain image. So he is catalogued in the second rank — not because he was minor to the Edomites, who had no greater god, but because the evidence that survives is inscriptional and not narrative. He is not Chemosh, who is Moab's; not Baal; and not Moloch.

gods.name: Kaikilani
gods.description: In Hawaiian tradition, the chiefess whom the god Lono came down and married, and lived with at Kealakekua. A man's voice was heard calling to her from the cliff in a chant, and Lono, believing her false, struck her; and she died telling him she had not been. In his grief and remorse he went up and down the islands challenging all comers to wrestle and box — and those contests became the games of the Makahiki, his festival — and then sailed away, promising to return. Hawaiian genealogies also carry a chiefess of this name, and the two have long been run together; the account here is the traditional one and is not offered as biography.

gods.name: Wahieroa
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the son of Tāwhaki and the father of Rata, killed by the ogre Matuku-tangotango — which killing is the reason Rata goes into the forest for a tree, and builds his canoe, and sets out for revenge. He is chiefly a link and a cause: the death that sets the next story going. Other Polynesian traditions arrange the line differently, and give the names in another order; the genealogy here is the Māori one.

gods.name: Uenuku
gods.description: In Māori tradition, the atua of the rainbow, and a god of war — for the rainbow was read as an omen before a fight, and the way of it, and where it stood, told a war party whether to go on or turn back. He was carried to battle in the form of a small figure of woven fibre and feathers, of which one is still kept in Te Awamutu. There are also men called Uenuku in the tribal genealogies — chiefs and ancestors of that name — and they are not this atua, and are not merged with him here.

gods.name: Hotu Matuʻa
gods.description: In the oral tradition of Rapa Nui, the ariki who brought his people to the island. His navigator dreamed the land, or his scouts found it; and he came from a place called Hiva with his household in two canoes, and landed at Anakena, and divided the island among his sons, from whom the clans descend. This is what the tradition says, as it was told to outsiders in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and written down then; it is a founding story, and it is not offered here as an established history of the settlement.

gods.name: Changxi
gods.description: Wife of Dijun and mother of the twelve moons, one for each month, whom she bathes — as the Classic of Mountains and Seas has it, in the wilds of the west there is a woman bathing the moons. She stands beside Xihe, Dijun's other wife, who bore the ten suns and bathes them in the east; the two are a pair, and both are catalogued here. She is not Chang'e, the woman who drank the elixir and fled to the moon — the names are close, and some have derived the later from the earlier, but they are two figures with two stories, and Chang'e is catalogued separately.

gods.name: Nüba
gods.description: Daughter of the Yellow Emperor, and the drought in person. At Zhuolu, when Chiyou had called up wind and rain and fog against her father's army, she was brought down from heaven in a blue-grey robe, and the wind and the rain stopped where she stood, and Chiyou was beaten. But she could not go back up: her heat had spent her, and wherever she settled afterwards nothing fell, and the people drove her north of the red rivers. She is called Ba, and later Hanba — 'drought Ba' — and those are her names. Later folk usage turned hanba into a whole class of drought-demons; that class is not this figure, and the record here is the daughter of Huangdi in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

gods.name: Yue Lao
gods.description: The Old Man Under the Moon, who sits by night with his book and his bag and ties the ankles of the man and the woman who are to marry with a red cord — and once it is tied it holds, though they are born in warring states or hate each other on sight or never meet until the wedding. He was met, the Tang tale says, by a young man named Wei Gu, who was told his wife would be the three-year-old girl of a one-eyed vegetable seller, and who tried to have her killed, and married her fourteen years later and saw the scar. He is prayed to for matches, and has temples of his own.

gods.name: Kishimojin
gods.description: The Japanese form of the Indian goddess Hariti — historically the same figure, carried east with Buddhism, and not an unrelated being. In the story she was a demoness with five hundred children of her own who stole and ate the children of others, until the Buddha hid the youngest of hers under his begging bowl; and when she had searched the world for it and come to him weeping, he asked whether she now knew what the mothers felt, and she was converted, and became the protector of children and of childbirth and of easy delivery. She holds a pomegranate. She is honoured especially in the Nichiren school, and has her own halls in Japan.

gods.name: Isotakeru
gods.description: Son of Susanoo in the Nihon Shoki, who came down with his father out of heaven bringing the seeds of the trees, and did not sow them in the land they landed in but carried them on and planted them through the Great Eight Islands, so that the country was made green from end to end; and he settled in Kii, where he is enshrined at Itakiso. He is called Itakeru and Isotakeru-no-Mikoto as well; those are readings of the one kami's name, and no separate record is made of them.

gods.name: Osmotar
gods.description: The maid who made the first beer, in the twentieth canto of the Kalevala and in the beer-origin runes of the folk poetry that Lönnrot took it from. She sets barley and hops and water together and they will not work; and she asks a squirrel, and a marten, and a bee, and it is the bee, going over the sea to the islands where the honey is, that brings back what makes the ale rise — and then it rises so hard that the tub bursts and it runs down the hillside. Her name means the daughter of Osmo; the -tar ending is the ordinary Finnish way of making a woman's name of a man's, as in Tuonetar and Kivutar on this shelf, and is not itself evidence of anything more. No cult of her is known, and none is claimed.

gods.name: Deichtine
gods.description: Sister of Conchobar in some tellings and his daughter in others, and the mother of Cú Chulainn. She went with fifty women after a flock of birds that had eaten the plain of Emain bare, and they were benighted at a strange house where a child was born that night and she took it; and the child died, and she drank from a cup and swallowed a small creature that was in it, and dreamed that Lugh came to her and told her she was carrying his son. That son was Sétanta, who became Cú Chulainn. Her name is written Dechtire, Deichtine and Deichtire in the manuscripts — spellings of one woman, not several. She is a woman of the Ulster tales and not a goddess.

gods.name: Emer
gods.description: Daughter of Forgall Monach, and the woman Cú Chulainn wanted — who told him she would have no man until he had done what no man could, and set him tasks in riddles, and sent him to Scáthach in Alba to be taught. She had, they said, the six gifts: beauty, voice, sweet speech, needlework, wisdom and chastity. She is the central woman of the Tochmarc Emire, and she is human: no goddess, and no woman of the síde.

gods.name: Mongán mac Fiachnai
gods.description: In the tales, the son of Manannán mac Lir — who came in the shape of Fiachna's own self to Fiachna's wife while the king was away at war, and got the boy on her, and afterwards took him to the Otherworld to rear. Mongán could change his shape into anything, and knew what had happened long ago because he had been there: he was Fionn mac Cumhaill come back, and settled an argument about where a man had died by saying he had killed him himself. A historical king of the Dál nAraidi bore this name and died about 625, and the legend fastened onto him. This record is the legendary figure — Manannán's son — and it is not that king, and does not stand for him.

gods.name: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne
gods.description: Of the fianna, and the best-loved of Fionn's men — who had a love-spot on his brow that no woman could look at without loving him. Gráinne, betrothed to the ageing Fionn, saw it at her own betrothal-feast and put him under bonds to take her away; and the two were hunted the length of Ireland for sixteen years. At the end Fionn let him die of a boar's tusk on Ben Bulben, carrying water to him in his hands and letting it run out between his fingers, twice.

gods.name: Deirdre
gods.description: Deirdre of the Sorrows, over whom the druid Cathbad prophesied at her birth that she would be the most beautiful woman in Ireland and would bring ruin on the Ulstermen. Conchobar had her reared apart to be his own; but she saw Naoise, and put him under bonds, and fled with him and his brothers to Alba. Conchobar called them home under the guarantee of Fergus and killed them anyway, and Deirdre lived a year without lifting her head, and then dashed it against a stone.

gods.name: Crom Cruach
gods.description: A god, or an idol, said to have stood on the plain of Mag Slécht in Cavan — a figure of gold with twelve of stone about him, to whom, the Metrical Dindshenchas says, the Irish gave a third of their children in return for milk and corn, and before whom they broke their heads and bodies on the ground until three-quarters of them died. St Patrick, in the hagiography, raised his crozier and the idol fell. All of this comes from Christian writers, centuries after any such worship, and its purpose in the telling is to show what Patrick delivered Ireland from. There is no pre-Christian witness to him and nothing in the ground; he is catalogued here at the rank the evidence supports, and the accounts are given as claims and not as history.

gods.name: Skírnir
gods.description: Freyr's servant, and the agent of the whole action of Skírnismál. When Freyr sat in Odin's high seat and saw Gerðr in Jötunheim and sickened for her and would not speak, it was Skírnir who was sent to get her — and who asked for Freyr's sword as his price, and rode into the giants' country, and offered her apples and the ring Draupnir, and when she refused, threatened her with a curse of monstrous ugliness and loathing and lust unsatisfied until she agreed. She agreed. The sword was gone, and Freyr will die without it at Ragnarök.

gods.name: Lofn
gods.description: One of the ásynjur named in Snorri's Gylfaginning. She is gentle and good to call on, and Odin and Frigg gave her leave to arrange unions between men and women even where it has been forbidden or barred — and from her name, Snorri says, comes the word lof, permission or praise. That is what the sources give of her: a name and an office in a list. No cult of her is attested, and none is claimed here.

gods.name: Sjöfn
gods.description: One of the ásynjur of Snorri's list, whose care is to turn the minds of men and women to love; and from her name, he says, the word sjafni is made for affection. She is known from Gylfaginning and from the kennings, and from nothing else — a named goddess with a stated function and no story, and the record claims no more for her.

gods.name: Vár
gods.description: One of the ásynjur named by Snorri. She listens to the oaths and the private agreements that men and women make between themselves — the várar, the pledges from which her name comes — and she takes vengeance on those who break them. It is by her that marriage-vows are sworn, and in the Eddic poem of Thrym's wedding the hammer is brought to hallow the bride 'in the name of Vár'. She is known from the list and from that line, and no cult of her is recorded.

gods.name: Vör
gods.description: One of the ásynjur of Gylfaginning. She is wise and searching, Snorri says, and asks until nothing is hidden from her — so that a thing may be said to be vor, made known, when she has had it out. She is a name and a faculty in a list of names, with no narrative attached, and the record does not invent one for her.

gods.name: Syn
gods.description: One of the ásynjur named in Gylfaginning. She keeps the door of the hall against those who should not come in, and she is set as a defence at the Thing against cases a man wishes to deny — so that to make a syn is to enter a denial. A name, and an office, and a legal figure of speech; the sources give no more, and no cult of her is known.

gods.name: Philyra
gods.description: An Oceanid, daughter of Ocean, whom Cronus lay with — and who, when Rhea came upon them, was turned with him into a horse so that they should not be caught; and the child of it was born half a horse, and that was Chiron. Philyra was so appalled at what she had borne that she begged to be changed out of her shape, and became a linden tree, which is what her name means. Chiron she left behind, and he was raised by Apollo.

gods.name: Deianira
gods.description: Second wife of Heracles, won by him in a wrestling-match against the river-god Achelous. Carrying her over a river, the centaur Nessus tried to take her, and Heracles shot him; and the dying centaur told her to keep his blood as a charm to hold her husband's love. Years later, hearing that Heracles had taken Iole, she smeared the blood on a shirt and sent it to him — and the blood was poisoned with the Hydra's venom from the arrow, and it burned him to death, and she hanged herself when she understood. Other women of the myths bear the name; this is Heracles's wife, of Sophocles's Trachiniae.

gods.name: Hippolytus
gods.description: Son of Theseus by an Amazon, who gave himself wholly to Artemis and to hunting and would have nothing to do with Aphrodite — and Aphrodite, for that, made his stepmother Phaedra fall in love with him. He refused her; she hanged herself and left a letter accusing him; and Theseus, believing it, called down one of the three curses Poseidon had promised him, and a bull came out of the sea and maddened his horses, and he was dragged to death in the wreck of his chariot. Theseus and Phaedra are both catalogued here. A later Italian tradition has Asclepius raise him and hide him in the grove at Aricia as the god Virbius; that is a Roman development and a separate identity, and it is not merged with this record.

gods.name: Autolycus
gods.description: Son of Hermes, and the most accomplished thief alive — for his father gave him the gift of stealing without being caught, and of changing the look of whatever he took, so that a beast's colour or its horns would not be what they had been. He stole Sisyphus's cattle and altered them, and Sisyphus, who had marked their hooves, walked in and knew them. He was Odysseus's grandfather on his mother's side: it was he who named the boy, and on a boar-hunt at his house that Odysseus got the scar by which his nurse knew him twenty years later. He is not the Autolycus of the Argonauts, nor the boxer of that name.

gods.name: Pasithea
gods.description: One of the Charites, and the one Hera promised to Hypnos in the fourteenth book of the Iliad as the price of putting Zeus to sleep — for Hypnos had long wanted her, and would not do it for anything else, and made Hera swear by the Styx. The familiar three Graces, Aglaea and Euphrosyne and Thalia, are catalogued here as a group; but the Homeric tradition knows more Charites than three, and Pasithea is one of them, with a part of her own in the poem. She is added beside that group and does not break it up.

gods.name: Shitala
gods.description: 'The Cool One' — the goddess of smallpox in north India, who both sends the pox and takes it away, and whose worship is the treatment: the fever is her presence in the body, and the sufferer is not sick but possessed, and is kept cool and quiet and given no medicine that would fight her. She rides an ass and carries a winnowing-fan, a broom, a small jar of cool water and a neem branch. She has her own temples and her own festival, Shitala Ashtami, when only food cooked the day before is eaten, and no fire is lit.

gods.name: Ayyappan
gods.description: The god of Sabarimala in Kerala, sitting in the posture of yoga with a band about his knees. He is called Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara — that is, of Vishnu in the form of Mohini and of Shiva; that birth is told here as tradition tells it, and Mohini is not catalogued and no parentage is entered. Pilgrims keep a fast of forty-one days, go barefoot in black, call one another Swami, and climb the eighteen steps with a bundle on the head. The Tamil village-god Aiyanar, who rides a horse and guards the boundaries, is a related figure of another region and is not the same as him here.

gods.name: Airavata
gods.description: The white elephant that Indra rides — four-tusked, seven-trunked in some tellings, who rose out of the ocean when it was churned, and who is the first of elephants and the ancestor of the whole kind. He draws water from the underworld with his trunks and sprays it into the clouds so that Indra may make it rain. He is his master's vehicle and has no cult and no story of his own apart from him, and he is catalogued at that rank — being a mount is not by itself a claim to more.

gods.name: Seolmundae Halmang
gods.description: The giant grandmother who made Jeju. She scooped the earth up in her skirt and let it fall in the middle of the sea, and that is Hallasan; and the soil that ran out through the holes in the apron made the three hundred and sixty oreum, the small hills scattered over the island. She was so tall she washed her clothes with one foot on Hallasan and the other on an islet, and she used the crater for a bowl. In one telling she went to measure the depth of the Mulchat pool, which the island said had no bottom, and it had none, and she never came up. She is the creator of Jeju and belongs to that island's tradition. Halmang and halmoni mean grandmother — a title of respect and age, not an identity: she is not Samshin Halmoni, who gives children, and not Yeongdeung Halmang, who brings the spring wind, and she is not a figure of general giantess folklore.

gods.name: Heo Hwang-ok
gods.description: Queen of Suro and first queen of Geumgwan Gaya, in the account the Samguk Yusa gives. She came by sea with a stone pagoda in the ship to steady it against the sea-god, and told the king that she was the daughter of the king of a country called Ayuta, and that her parents had been told of him in a dream and had sent her; and she was sixteen. She bore him ten sons, and two of them took her surname, and the Gimhae Heo clan trace themselves to her. Where Ayuta was, and whether she came from India as many have argued from the name, is a question the sources do not settle: this is what the tradition says, and it is given as tradition and not as established history.

gods.name: Biryu
gods.description: Elder brother of Onjo in the Baekje foundation cycle, and a son of Jumong. When their elder half-brother came out of Buyeo and was made heir, the two of them went south with their followers to find land; and Biryu would not take the advice of the ministers, and settled by the sea at Michuhol, where the water was brackish and the ground would not bear. Onjo prospered inland at Wiryeseong. Biryu, seeing it, died of shame, and his people went over to his brother.

gods.name: Kim Alji
gods.description: Ancestor of the Kim kings of Silla. A light was seen in the forest of Sirim at night, and a white cock crying under a tree, and hanging from the branch a golden box; and when King Talhae had it opened there was a boy inside, who grew handsome and clever. He was given the surname Kim, which is gold, and the forest was renamed Gyerim, the cock-forest, and afterwards the name was used for the kingdom. His descendants took the throne in time. This is the foundation story of the clan as the Samguk Yusa tells it, and it is not offered as biography.

gods.name: Cheoyong
gods.description: In the legend, a son of the dragon of the East Sea, who came to the court of Silla and was given a wife and an office. Coming home one night he found the plague-demon in the bed with her — and instead of striking, he sang a song and danced out of the room; and the demon threw itself down before him and swore never to enter a door where his face was shown. So his face was pasted on gates. The story is set at the court of King Heongang in the late ninth century, which is a historical frame and not a life of him; and the mask-dance made of it, the Cheoyongmu, is a court ritual of much later date that is still performed. The legendary dragon's son, the Silla setting, and the dance are three things and are kept apart here.

gods.name: Lavinia
gods.description: Daughter of King Latinus, and the woman Aeneas came to Italy to marry — for the oracle had told her father to give her to no Latin, but to a stranger who would come. She had been promised to Turnus, and the war of the second half of the Aeneid is fought over her, and she says almost nothing in it. The town Aeneas founded and named for her, Lavinium, was the mother-city of the Latin rite. She is catalogued here because the archive's own records already name her; that is not a decision to catalogue every figure of the Aeneid or of the Alban king-list.

gods.name: Amata
gods.description: Queen of Latinus, and against the marriage from the start — she wanted Turnus, her kinsman, for her daughter. Juno sent the Fury Allecto to her, who threw a snake into her breast, and the poison worked in her slowly until she ran raving into the woods with Lavinia hidden, calling the other women out after her in the rites of Bacchus, and so lit the war. When the city seemed lost and she thought Turnus dead by her doing, she hanged herself. She is catalogued as a principal actor of the poem — which is what the category means here — and not as a woman the poem approves.

gods.name: Numitor
gods.description: King of Alba Longa, put off the throne by his younger brother Amulius, who killed his son and made his daughter Rhea Silvia a Vestal so that she should bear no heir. She bore Romulus and Remus to Mars, and they were set adrift, and grew up, and came back; and when Remus was brought before Numitor as a captive the old man began to guess who he was. They killed Amulius and put their grandfather back on the throne, and then went off to found a city of their own.

gods.name: Libitina
gods.description: Goddess of burial. Her grove on the Esquiline was where the undertakers had their stand and where the funeral things were hired — the bier, the bearers, the criers — and where a coin was paid for every death in the city, so that the count of the dead was known from her register: Suetonius says thirty thousand were entered there in one autumn of plague. The men of the trade were called libitinarii after her, and in time her name came to mean death itself and the business of it. Some of the antiquarians identified her with Venus — Venus Libitina — and Servius with Persephone; those identifications are noted and not adopted, and she is catalogued as the goddess of the grove.

gods.name: Ishum
gods.description: The herald who walks before Erra, and the voice that holds him back. In the Erra Epic the plague-god wakes and wants slaughter, and Ishum goes with him — and argues with him, and delays him, and after the cities are emptied and Erra sits satisfied among the ruins, it is Ishum's speech that turns him and gets from him the promise that the people will grow again. He is a god of the lamp and the night-fire as well, going before like a torch. Erra is described here as the poem describes him; no record is made of him, and the question of how far he is the same god as Nergal is left alone.

gods.name: Ishtaran
gods.description: City god of Der, on the road east into Elam, and a judge — when Lagash and Umma quarrelled over the border of the Gu'edena, it was Ishtaran who was asked to measure the field and set the boundary stone. His minister is the snake-god Nirah, and he himself is drawn as a serpent on the boundary stones. Der was a small city and his cult was a local one; he is catalogued at that measure, as the other city-gods of this shelf are, and the office of judge does not by itself raise him.

gods.name: Nungal
gods.description: Goddess of the prison, and daughter of Ereshkigal. The Hymn to Nungal, which is hers, calls the prison her house and her lap — a place with a mouth that swallows and does not spit out, where the guilty man is kept in the dark and the mud until he is broken; and then she says that the house is a womb, and that the man who comes out of it is born again clean, and she will take his hand and give him back to the god who made him.

gods.name: Enmesharra
gods.description: 'Lord of all the me' — an old god of the earth and the underworld, who held the powers and the offices before the younger gods took them, and who was bound for it and shut up below with his seven sons. Marduk in one account, Ninurta in another, is the one who overcame him; the texts that speak of him are late and are chiefly concerned with his defeat and his imprisonment. He is an old god beaten and put away, which is not the same thing as a first being: he does not stand with Apsu and Tiamat and the pairs of the Enūma Eliš at the beginning of things, and he is not catalogued with them.

gods.name: Hesat
gods.description: The white cow, whose milk is called in the Pyramid Texts the beer of the blessed and the drink that makes the dead live. She is the wet-nurse of the gods and of the king, and the mother of the Mnevis bull of Heliopolis, and in some texts the mother of Anubis. She is attested on her own from the Old Kingdom, and she is not Hathor, the sky-cow of love and music, nor Mehet-Weret, the cow of the primeval water on whose back the sun rose: three cows, three things. The Egyptians did not make one goddess of them, and neither does this archive.

gods.name: Pakhet
gods.description: 'She Who Scratches' — the lioness of the desert wadis of Middle Egypt, who hunts by night at the mouths of the valleys and tears what she takes. Hatshepsut cut her a temple into the rock at Beni Hasan, which the Greeks afterwards called the Speos Artemidos, the Cave of Artemis, because they matched her with their huntress. She has her own name, her own country and her own sanctuary, and she is not a form of Sekhmet, nor of Menhit of Esna, nor of Maahes; Egypt had many lionesses and kept them apart.

gods.name: Kherty
gods.description: The ram-headed god of Letopolis, of the earth and what is under it, who ferries the dead over the waters of the underworld. He is old — he is in the Pyramid Texts — and he is not safe: the spells ask Ra to keep the dead king from his hands, and set him under guard. He is one ram of several, and each has his own city: Khnum of Elephantine who shapes children on the wheel, Banebdjedet of Mendes, Heryshaf of Herakleopolis — and Kherty, who is not any of them.

gods.name: Ōtoshi
gods.description: The kami of the year's crop — toshi is the year and the grain that ripens in it, and he is the ripening. He is the great harvest-god of the Kojiki, which sets out a long line of kami descended from him, and he is worshipped at the Ōtoshi shrines and welcomed into the house at the New Year, when the year turns and the crop is asked for again. His standing here rests on that — on the harvest and the turning of the year, which are his own — and not on his being Susanoo's son.

gods.name: Mizuhanome
gods.description: The water kami, born — the Kojiki says — from the urine of the dying Izanami when the fire-child burned her; and she is the water that is used, the water of the well and the ditch and the irrigated field, rather than the water of the sea. She is written Mizuhanome, Mitsuhanome and Mizuha-no-me; these are readings of one kami's name, and one record is made. She is not to be confused with Kuraokami and Takaokami, the dragon-kami of rain and snow, who are born at another moment and whose own relation to one another this archive has not settled.

gods.name: Kuebiko
gods.description: The scarecrow of the mountain fields, who cannot walk a step and knows everything under heaven. When a tiny stranger came over the sea in a pod of vine and no one at all could say who he was, Ōkuninushi asked the toad, and the toad said to ask Kuebiko; and Kuebiko said at once that it was Sukunabikona, the son of Kamimusubi. He is one named kami and not a class of scarecrows: the Kojiki gives him a name and a word of his own, and that is who is catalogued.

gods.name: Kuixing
gods.description: The star-god of first place in the examinations. In the story he was a scholar so hideous — lame, and with a face like a demon — that when he came first in the palace examination the emperor would not give him the honour, and he threw himself into the sea, and a great ao, the fish-turtle, carried him up on its back and he was made a star. He is drawn standing one-legged on the ao with a brush in his hand and the other leg kicked back, kicking the Dipper. He is not Wenchang, the stellar god of literature and patron of scholars, who is catalogued here — a different god, a different face, a different office: Wenchang has letters and learning, Kuixing has the top of the list. The two are often set in the same hall, which is not the same as being one. Nor is he merely the Kui stars themselves, or the office of the examination: he is the god the story is told of.

gods.name: Conchobar mac Nessa
gods.description: King of Ulster at Emain Macha in the Ulster Cycle, son of Ness and foster-father of Cú Chulainn. He reared Deirdre in seclusion to take her as his own, and when she fled with Naoise he lured the sons of Uisliu home under Fergus's guarantee and had them killed - breaking the surety, driving Fergus into exile in Connacht, and setting the ruin of Ulster in motion. His decisions shape both the Deirdre tragedy and the war of the Táin. His hero classification marks him as a principal saga actor, not a figure of moral approval.

gods.name: Connla
gods.description: The son of Cú Chulainn by Aífe of Alba, the warrior-woman of the eastern isles whom Cú Chulainn met while training with Scathach. Sent to Ireland under a geis forbidding him to name himself or refuse a challenge, he was killed by his own father at the strand before either knew the other - the recognition coming only as he died. His mother Aífe of Alba is not the Aoife catalogued in this archive, who is the second wife of Lir and the stepmother who turned his children into swans; the two women share a name and nothing else.

gods.name: Naoise
gods.description: Eldest of the sons of Uisliu and the lover of Deirdre in Longes mac nUislenn, the tale of the exile of the sons of Uisliu. Bound by the geis Deirdre laid on him, he took her from Conchobar and fled with his brothers Ardan and Ainnle to Alba, living as exiles until Conchobar coaxed them back with a guarantee of safety and then had them killed on their arrival. His elopement is the act on which the whole tragedy turns.

gods.name: Ferdiad
gods.description: Connacht champion and the foster-brother of Cú Chulainn, trained beside him under Scathach. In the Táin Bó Cúailnge, Medb shamed and bribed him into facing Cú Chulainn at the ford; the two fought for days, tending each other's wounds by night and sharing food across the water, until Cú Chulainn killed him with the gaé bolga and mourned him over his body. The combat at the ford is the emotional centre of the epic.

gods.name: Fergus mac Róich
gods.description: Former king of Ulster, displaced by Conchobar through the bargain struck with Ness, and the guarantor whose word Conchobar broke in the killing of the sons of Uisliu. He went into exile in Connacht and rode with Medb's army against his own province in the Táin, where he acted as guide and as Cú Chulainn's foster-father - and at the crisis chose to yield the field rather than kill him, then persuaded Medb to withdraw. His choices materially decide the course of the war.

gods.name: Gráinne
gods.description: Daughter of the high king Cormac mac Airt and the central actor of Tóraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne. Betrothed against her wish to the ageing Fionn mac Cumhaill, she chose Diarmuid at the wedding feast and laid a geis on him to carry her away - a compulsion he could not refuse. The pursuit that follows across Ireland is set in motion entirely by her act of will.

gods.name: Aobh
gods.description: Daughter of Bodb Derg and the first wife of Lir, mother of Fionnuala, Aodh, Fiachra and Conn - the four children later turned into swans by her sister. She died after bearing the youngest, and her death is what brought her sister into Lir's house. Her name appears as Aobh and Aoibh in Irish and is anglicised as Eve or Eva; these are forms of one woman, and she is distinct from unrelated Irish figures who bear the same name.

gods.name: Crunniuc
gods.description: The Ulster farmer whose boast brought the curse on his province. The woman Macha came to his house and lived with him, and when he boasted at the assembly that his wife could outrun the king's horses, she was forced to race them while heavily pregnant. She won, gave birth at the finish, and cursed the men of Ulster with the pangs of childbirth in their hour of need. His name is written Crunniuc, Crunnchu, Crunnchú and Cruinniuc - spelling variants of one man.

gods.name: Belisama
gods.description: A Gaulish goddess known from a small number of inscriptions, notably a Gaulish dedication at Vaison and a Latin one at Saint-Lizier that pairs her with Minerva as Minervae Belisamae.
