The Roman identification with Minerva suggests a sphere of craft and skill, but no narrative, secure iconography or cult centre survives, and the interpretation of her name remains contested. The pairing of Belisama with Belenus is a modern inference drawn from the shared Bel- element in their names, not a securely attested ancient marriage.

gods.name: Gronw Pebr
gods.description: Lord of Penllyn in the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi. Sheltering at Blodeuwedd's court after a hunt, he became her lover, and together they drew from Lleu Llaw Gyffes the elaborate conditions under which alone he could be killed, then contrived them. Lleu, restored, demanded the same blow in return; Gronw's plea to hold a stone between them did not save him. He is rendered Goronwy Pefr and Gronw Bebyr in other manuscripts - one man under several spellings.

gods.name: Teyrnon Twrf Liant
gods.description: Lord of Gwent Is Coed in the First Branch of the Mabinogi, whose mare foaled every May eve and whose foals always vanished. Keeping watch, he cut off the monstrous claw that reached through the window and found outside the door an infant boy, whom he and his wife raised as their own until the child's likeness to Pwyll revealed him as the lost son of Rhiannon. His restoring the boy ended Rhiannon's unjust penance, and the child was named Pryderi. His epithet appears as Twrf Liant and Twryf Vliant among other spellings.

gods.name: Goewin
gods.description: Daughter of Pebin and the virgin footholder of Math fab Mathonwy, in whose lap the king's feet had to rest except when he was at war. Gwydion and Gilfaethwy contrived a war precisely to draw Math from his court, and Gilfaethwy raped her in the king's own bed. When Math returned, she did not stay silent: she went to him and told him plainly what had been done to her and that she would not conceal it. Math married her, gave her authority over his lands, and made her the wronged party whose word the court had to answer.

gods.name: Gwawl ap Clud
gods.description: The suitor Rhiannon rejected in the First Branch of the Mabinogi. Having been promised to him before she chose Pwyll, he claimed her at the wedding feast by a trick of words; Pwyll, advised by Rhiannon, trapped him in an enchanted bag and had him beaten in the game called Badger-in-the-Bag until he sued for peace. The grudge his kinsmen carried for that humiliation is given as the cause of the enchantment that later falls on Dyfed in the Third Branch. He is not to be confused with unrelated Welsh bearers of the name Gwawl.

gods.name: Matuku-tangotango
gods.description: The man-eating ogre of the Maori Wahieroa and Rata cycle, who killed Wahieroa and carried off his bones, and whom Wahieroa's son Rata hunted down and slew in vengeance before going on to build the canoe and recover his father's remains from the Ponaturi. He is an individually named being of the tale, not to be confused with the ordinary word matuku for the bittern, nor with the unrelated Matuku figures of other Maori and Polynesian traditions.

gods.name: Kupe
gods.description: The navigator of Maori oral tradition credited with the discovery of Aotearoa, said to have pursued the great octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi across the ocean, killed it in the strait that bears the name Raukawa, and named places along both coasts before returning to Hawaiki with sailing directions. The traditions differ widely between iwi on where he came from, what he did and whether he returned, and the accounts of discovery and migration are recorded oral tradition rather than verified history.

gods.name: Paikea
gods.description: The whale-rider of Maori tradition, born Kahutia-te-rangi. When his half-brother Ruatapu scuttled a canoe to drown the high-born sons of Uenuku, he alone survived, calling on the sea-creatures and coming ashore on the back of a whale, and thereafter taking the name Paikea. He is remembered as a founding ancestor on the east coast, and the genealogies attached to him vary by region; those regional lines are not merged here, and other ancestors bearing the name are not folded into this record.

gods.name: Hurriya
gods.description: The daughter of the king of Udm and the bride of Kirta in the Ugaritic epic. Kirta, having lost his entire household, was told by El in a dream to march on Udm and refuse all treasure until her father gave her up; she was the sole object of the campaign, and the blessing pronounced at their wedding promised the sons and daughters who would restore his line. She is a principal actor of the cycle, appearing again at the feast where Kirta's illness and his broken vow to Athirat come to a head.

gods.name: Yassib
gods.description: The eldest son of Kirta in the Ugaritic epic. When his father lay sick and the land failed with him, Yassib came to the sickbed and told him to his face that a king who cannot rise, cannot judge the case of the widow or drive out those who prey on the poor, has forfeited the right to rule, and that he should step down and let his son reign. Kirta, restored by El, answered him with a curse. The confrontation is the cycle's closing judgement on what kingship owes.

gods.name: Cessair
gods.description: Leader of the first taking of Ireland in medieval Irish pseudo-history. Refused a place on the ark, she is said to have sailed for the western edge of the world with fifty women and three men, made landfall in Ireland, and died of grief when Bith and Ladra were dead and only Fintan was left; the Flood then drowned her company. The whole episode is a Christian monastic construction, written to fit Ireland into biblical chronology by making her a granddaughter of Noah, and it is not secure evidence of any pre-Christian Irish tradition. Her name is also written Cesair.

gods.name: Fintan mac Bóchra
gods.description: The one man of Cessair's company to outlive the Flood, and thereafter the memory of Ireland. He endured the ages by changing shape - a salmon, then an eagle, then a hawk, before he was given back his own form - and so saw every taking of the land from Cessair to the Gaels. In the end he testified before the king and the assembled men of Ireland at Tara, settling by his witness the bounds and the ordering of the land. He is a parallel of Túan mac Cairill, who serves the same purpose in another text; the two are not the same man.

gods.name: Partholón
gods.description: Leader of the second taking of Ireland, after the Flood had emptied it. His people cleared the first plains and saw the first lakes burst forth, and he fought the first battle ever fought in Ireland, against Cichol and the Fomorians at Mag Itha. To him is given the first judgement in Ireland, in the affair of his wife and the servant Topa - an etiological tale grown up around the settlement rather than part of its core. His people died of plague in a single week and were buried together at Tallaght, whose name preserves it. Some recensions add that he had killed his father and mother to take a kingship and came to Ireland as an exile for it; that is the account of some texts and not a stable part of the tradition.

gods.name: Nemed
gods.description: Leader of the third taking of Ireland. He came with his people after the Partholonians were dead, cleared plains and saw lakes break out, and won four battles against the Fomorians - who then ground his people under a tribute of two-thirds of their children, their corn and their milk, exacted from the tower of Conand on Tory Island. Nemed's people stormed that tower and Conand fell, but Morc came after with a fleet and destroyed them. Nemed himself died of plague, and the remnant of his people scattered out of Ireland.

gods.name: Túan mac Cairill
gods.description: The sole survivor of Nemed's people, and the long-lived witness of another text than Fintan's. He outlasted the ages in a succession of shapes - a stag, a boar, a hawk, and at the last a salmon - and as a salmon he was taken and eaten by the wife of Cairell, and born again from her as a man, keeping all he had seen. He told the whole history of the takings of Ireland to St Finnian, in the setting of the Church. He and Fintan mac Bóchra are parallel deployments of the same motif, the survivor who remembers; they come from different texts and different genealogies and are not the same person.

gods.name: Conand
gods.description: The Fomorian ruler who held the tower on Tory Island and exacted from Nemed's people the tribute of two-thirds of their children, their corn and their milk, to be delivered every Samain. The stronghold is called Tor Conaind, Conand's Tower, and it is named for him - he is a man who held it, not the name of the place. When the Nemedians rose and stormed the tower he was killed in the taking of it.

gods.name: Morc
gods.description: The Fomorian commander who came after Conand's tower had fallen. His fleet fell upon the Nemedians in the hour of their victory and destroyed them, so that of all Nemed's people only thirty were left alive, and they scattered out of Ireland. He is named in the texts as Morc mac Dela; the five Fir Bolg brothers are likewise called sons of a Dela, but the two fathers are not the same man and the sources should not be read as making them one.

gods.name: Eochaid mac Eirc
gods.description: The last king of the Fir Bolg. In his reign, the texts say, no rain fell but only dew, and there was no year without its harvest; and he was the first in Ireland to establish true judgement, so that his name stands for the just king. When the Túatha Dé Danann came and asked for half the country, he refused to divide it, and fought them at the First Battle of Mag Tuired, where he was pursued to Tráig Eothaile and killed. His wife was Tailtiu. His name is also written Eochu.

gods.name: Sreng
gods.description: Champion of the Fir Bolg, sent to parley with the Túatha Dé before the First Battle of Mag Tuired, where he and Bres laid their weapons side by side and each looked at what the other carried. In the battle he met Nuada and with one stroke cut the arm from him - and by that stroke Nuada lost the kingship, for a king of the Túatha Dé could carry no blemish, and Bres was set up in his place. Everything that followed, down to the second battle, turns on it. Sreng survived, and was offered a province.

gods.name: Amergin Glúingel
gods.description: Poet, druid and judge of the sons of Míl, and the man whose rulings shaped the taking of Ireland. It was he who judged that the Milesians must draw back beyond nine waves and win the land again from the sea; he who answered Ériu, Banba and Fódla, promising each that the island would carry her name; and he who set his foot on the shore and spoke the invocation that begins 'I am the wind on the sea'. He divided the land between his brothers Érimón and Éber Finn. He is not Amergin mac Eccit, the poet of Ulster and father of Conall Cernach, nor any other of the Amergins of Irish tradition.

gods.name: Érimón
gods.description: Son of Míl and one of the two leaders of the Milesians after the conquest. Ireland was divided between him and his brother Éber Finn, Érimón taking the north; but the peace did not hold, and when Éber would not be content with half they met in battle at Airgetros, where Éber was killed and Érimón held the whole island alone. Later genealogical tradition made him the ancestor of the northern dynasties, but it is for the partition and the killing of his brother that he is set down here.

gods.name: Éber Finn
gods.description: Son of Míl and joint leader of the Milesians with his brother Érimón, taking the southern half of Ireland when the land was divided between them. He would not hold to the division, and demanded more; the quarrel came to battle at Airgetros, and there Érimón killed him. Later genealogists traced the southern dynasties to him, but that claim is a later use made of his name and not the reason he is catalogued.

gods.name: Íth
gods.description: The first of the Gaels to set foot in Ireland. From Bregon's tower in Spain he saw the land far off and sailed to it, and found the three kings of the Túatha Dé - Mac Cuill, Mac Cecht and Mac Gréine - quarrelling over the sharing of their inheritance. He judged between them justly, and then praised the country he had come to, so warmly that they took fright at what such a man might want and killed him as he went back to his ship. His kinsmen came to avenge him, and that is how the Milesians took Ireland: his murder is the cause of the invasion.

gods.name: Machaon
gods.description: Son of Asclepius and, with his brother Podalirius, leader of the men of Tricca before Troy. In the Iliad he is the physician who is sent for by name when Menelaus is struck by Pandarus' arrow, and who draws the shaft and treats the wound; later he is himself hit by an arrow of Paris and carried out of the fighting by Nestor, and the Greeks reckon the loss of him a wound to the whole army. Post-Homeric tradition makes him the surgeon of the pair, and gives him a death at the hands of Penthesilea or Eurypylus.

gods.name: Podalirius
gods.description: Son of Asclepius and brother of Machaon, with whom he led thirty ships from Tricca to Troy. In the Iliad he is little more than a name in the catalogue: it is Machaon who acts, and no diagnostic art is credited to Podalirius there. His fuller character belongs to the later Trojan-cycle traditions, which divide the healing art between the brothers and give Podalirius the inward maladies - reading Ajax's madness in his eyes, in the account of the Little Iliad - and which bring him home by way of Caria. The specialisation should not be read back into Homer.

gods.name: Epione
gods.description: Wife of Asclepius, and a goddess of the Epidaurian healing cult in her own right rather than only a name in his family. Pausanias saw her image in the sanctuary at Epidaurus, and she is invoked there with Asclepius and their daughters Hygieia and Panacea. Her name is understood as the soothing or gentling of pain. No narrative attaches to her; her standing rests on cult, and nothing more is claimed here.

gods.name: Troilus
gods.description: A young son of Priam. Homer names him once and only in passing, when Priam mourns his dead sons and calls him a fighter from the chariot; the Iliad tells nothing of how he died. The famous story - Achilles ambushing him at the fountain outside the walls and killing him at Apollo's altar - belongs to the Cypria and above all to Archaic vase-painting, where the ambush is among the most often drawn of all scenes, and the prophecy that Troy could not fall if he lived to twenty is later still, the property of scholiasts and mythographers. A separate tradition makes him a son of Apollo by Hecuba rather than of Priam; the sources give both, and neither can be called the settled one.

gods.name: Linus
gods.description: The musician, son of Apollo by one of the Muses and brother or counterpart of Orpheus, who taught the lyre to Heracles and was killed by his pupil with the instrument itself when he struck him for a fault. He is credited in some accounts with inventing melody and with setting letters to Greek. The sources do not agree which Muse bore him - Calliope in one, Urania or Terpsichore in others. He is to be kept apart from the Argive Linus, the infant son of Apollo and Psamathe who was exposed and torn by dogs, and from the linos itself, the lament or vintage-song that Homer's reapers sing, which may be older than any figure named for it. These are not gathered into one man here.

gods.name: Tyro
gods.description: Daughter of Salmoneus, who loved the river Enipeus and haunted his banks, and whom Poseidon took in the river's own shape. Odysseus sees her among the great women of the dead in the Odyssey. She bore Pelias and Neleus and exposed them, and they were reared apart from her; and she was used cruelly by her stepmother Sidero, until her sons came to know her and Pelias killed Sidero at the very altar of Hera where she had fled. Sophocles made a Tyro of it, now lost.

gods.name: Erichthonius (Athens)
gods.description: The earth-born king of Athens, got when Hephaestus pursued Athena and his seed fell on the ground, so that Gaia bore the child and Athena took him up. She shut him in a chest and gave it to the daughters of Cecrops with a charge not to look; they looked, and went mad, and threw themselves from the Acropolis. He was reared in Athena's own precinct, became king, and is credited with the Panathenaia and with yoking horses to the chariot. He is not the Trojan Erichthonius, son of Dardanus and father of Tros, who is another man entirely; and later writers sometimes run him together with Erechtheus, which is a confusion of two Athenian figures and not an identity.

gods.name: Atalanta
gods.description: The huntress, exposed at birth because her father wanted a son and suckled by a bear. Two regional traditions run under the name and the ancient sources already combine them rather than choosing. In the Arcadian, she is the hunter who draws first blood from the Calydonian boar and is given its hide by Meleager, and who wrestles Peleus at the funeral games. In the Boeotian, she is the runner who will marry only the man who outruns her, and who is beaten at last when Hippomenes drops the golden apples of Aphrodite in her path; afterwards the two are turned into lions. Even her father differs by tradition - Iasus in one, Schoeneus in the other - and this record does not pretend the strands agree.

gods.name: Cyrene
gods.description: A huntress of Thessaly who kept no loom and no company, but guarded her father's herds on Pelion; and Apollo, watching her wrestle a lion bare-handed, asked Chiron who she was and carried her over the sea to Libya, where she bore Aristaeus. The story is told at length in Pindar's ninth Pythian - which is also, and openly, a foundation-poem for the city of Cyrene and for the Battiad kings who ruled it and who traced their right to her. That ideological work should be seen for what it is and not mistaken for history; but the lion is hers, and it is for the hunting and not for the city that she stands here.

gods.name: Turnus
gods.description: King of the Rutulians, and the man Aeneas had to destroy to hold Italy. Lavinia had been promised to him before the Trojans came, and when Latinus gave her instead to the stranger of the oracle, Turnus went to war for her and for his own standing, and drew the Latin peoples after him. He kills Pallas, the son of Evander, and strips his sword-belt; and it is the sight of that belt on his shoulder, at the very moment he is begging for his life, that turns Aeneas from mercy and ends the Aeneid with his death.

gods.name: Dido (Elissa)
gods.description: Founder and queen of Carthage. In the older Phoenician tradition she is Elissa, a princess of Tyre whose brother Pygmalion murdered her husband; she fled overseas with her people, bought as much African land as an ox-hide would cover, cut the hide into strips to take a hill, and founded the city - and, when a Libyan king demanded her in marriage, burned herself on a pyre rather than betray her dead husband. Aeneas is nowhere in that story. The love, the cave, the desertion and the curse are Virgil's, written to give Rome's war with Carthage a mythic wound; and by the conventional dates the meeting could not have happened at all, since Troy falls around 1180 BC and Carthage is founded around 814 BC, some four centuries later.

gods.name: Camilla
gods.description: The Volscian warrior-maiden of the Aeneid, dedicated as an infant to Diana by her exiled father, who is said to have bound her to a spear and hurled her across a flooded river to save her. She was reared to the bow and refused marriage, and she leads the Volscian horse against the Trojans. Book eleven is largely hers: she cuts through the field until, distracted by the gold of a Trojan priest's armour, she is killed by a spear from the coward Arruns - whom Diana's nymph Opis then shoots down in payment for her.

gods.name: Evander
gods.description: An Arcadian exile who settled on the Palatine long before Rome, and the man who gave Aeneas his footing in Italy. He receives the Trojans at the feast of Hercules, walks Aeneas over the ground where the city will stand - the Capitol still wooded, cattle in what will be the Forum - and gives him both an alliance with the Etruscans and his only son. His grief when Pallas is carried home dead is one of the hardest passages in the poem, and it is he who tells Aeneas that Turnus owes him a life.

gods.name: Pallas (son of Evander)
gods.description: The son of Evander, sent out from the Palatine to ride with Aeneas and learn war under him. He fights well and is killed by Turnus, who takes his sword-belt from the body and wears it; Aeneas, who had promised the boy's father to keep him, carries him home to Pallanteum with an escort and a lament. At the end of the poem the sight of that belt on Turnus is what decides his death. He is not Pallas Athena, nor the Titan Pallas who is consort of Styx; the three share nothing but a name.

gods.name: Ascanius (Iulus)
gods.description: The son of Aeneas, who came out of Troy with his father and afterwards founded Alba Longa, from which Rome would come. Virgil calls him Iulus and says the name was his of old, which is the point: the equation gives the Julian house, and Augustus with it, a Trojan ancestor. The traditions do not agree about him. His mother is Creusa in the usual account, but some make him a son of Lavinia; and Livy records that even in his own day it was not settled whether the Alban kings descended from this Ascanius or from a later son born to Lavinia. The uncertainty is old and is left standing.

gods.name: Duryodhana
gods.description: Eldest of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and the principal Kaurava claimant to the throne of Hastinapura. He holds that the kingdom is his by his father's possession of it, and he will not give it up: it is his refusal to yield even five villages to the Pandavas that makes the war certain. He sets Shakuni's dice-game in motion, takes Draupadi's humiliation as his right, and fights to the end, dying at Bhima's hand by a thigh-stroke below the belt that breaks the law of the mace. He is a kshatriya prince who chooses wrongly and knows it, and he is catalogued as a principal actor of the epic - which is a statement about the narrative and not about his conduct.

gods.name: Drona
gods.description: The brahmin master of arms who taught both the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and whose obligation to the house that fed him bound him to fight for Duryodhana against the pupils he loved best. He demanded of the low-born Ekalavya, who had learned by watching, the thumb of his right hand as a teacher's fee. He took command of the Kaurava army after Bhishma fell, and could not be killed while he held his bow; so Yudhishthira was made to say that Ashwatthama was dead - meaning an elephant of that name - and Drona, hearing it, laid down his weapons and was cut down. His name is also written Drona with the retroflex, Droṇa.

gods.name: Dhritarashtra
gods.description: The blind king of Hastinapura, who held the throne because his brother Pandu could not, and who never afterwards let it go. He is not a bystander: it is his consent that allows the dice-game, his silence that lets Draupadi be dragged into the hall, and his refusal to restrain Duryodhana - though he is warned again and again by Vidura, by Bhishma and by Krishna - that carries the whole house to the war. He grieves for his hundred dead sons, and Sanjaya narrates the battle to him because he cannot see it. His name is also written Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

gods.name: Gandhari
gods.description: Princess of Gandhara and wife of the blind Dhritarashtra, who on learning that the man she was given to could not see, bound her own eyes and did not unbind them again - a vow kept for a lifetime, read as devotion by some and as reproach by others. She is the mother of the hundred Kauravas, and she told Duryodhana plainly that he was wrong and that where there is righteousness there is victory. When the war was over and her sons were all dead, she looked on the field and cursed Krishna, who could have stopped it and did not, that his own clan should perish as hers had and that he should die alone; and it came to pass. Her name is also written Gāndhārī.

gods.name: Shakuni
gods.description: Prince of Gandhara, brother of Gandhari, and the maker of the quarrel. It is Shakuni who proposes the game of dice and who throws for Duryodhana with dice that cannot lose, so that Yudhishthira gambles away his wealth, his brothers, himself and at last Draupadi; and it is that game, not the battlefield, that decides the Mahabharata. Some tellings give him a motive of revenge for the wrong done to his father and his house by the Kurus. He fights in the war and is killed by Sahadeva, who had sworn to do it. His name is also written Śakuni.

gods.name: Ashwatthama
gods.description: Son of Drona, born with a jewel in his forehead and named for the cry of a divine horse. When his father was killed by a lie he did not forgive it. After the war was decided and the fighting done, he went into the sleeping camp of the Pandavas by night with two companions and killed the men in it as they lay, including Draupadi's five sons - a massacre outside the law of battle - and then loosed a celestial weapon at the womb of Uttara to end the line altogether. Krishna revived the child and cursed him: the jewel torn from his head, and no death, but to wander with his wound unhealed for three thousand years. The birth, the jewel and the curse do not make him other than a man of the epic; he is a human actor who chose what he did. His name is also written Ashwatthaman or Aśvatthāman.

gods.name: Kheredu-ankh
gods.description: The divine mother of Imhotep in the later Egyptian cult. She is not attested in the Old Kingdom, when the historical Imhotep lived, but appears only when he had long been a god - in Ptolemaic and Roman material, where she is honoured beside him, given a divine father in Banebdjedet, and treated as a mother of a god rather than as a woman who had lived. Whether the name preserves anything of the actual mother of the architect of the Step Pyramid cannot be recovered, and is not claimed here. She belongs to the growth of his worship, and it is on that late cultic standing, and not on her place in a genealogy, that she is entered.

gods.name: Iah
gods.description: The moon itself, and a god of it from at least the Middle Kingdom - the word for the moon and the name of the god are the same, and it is carried in royal names such as Ahmose, 'Iah is born'. He is distinct from Khonsu, the moon-god of the Theban triad, and from Thoth, who has the moon among his offices but is the god of writing and reckoning; that Iah could be joined to each of them, as Iah-Djehuty and Iah-Khonsu, shows that he was a separate god available to be joined. The older Egyptological rendering of his name is Aah.

gods.name: Opet
gods.description: A hippopotamus goddess of Thebes, also rendered Ipet, who appears as a nurse-goddess as early as the Pyramid Texts and who had her own temple at Karnak beside that of Khonsu. In the theology worked out there she is the mother who bears and renews Osiris. She overlaps with Taweret and the sources sometimes run the two together; what separates them is that Taweret is a protector of women in childbirth, at home and everywhere, with no great temple, while Opet is fixed at Thebes and set in an Osirian frame. The Opet Festival, the procession of Amun from Karnak to Luxor, is named not for her but for Ipet-resyt, 'the Southern Sanctuary', which is the old name of Luxor temple; the shared root does not make the goddess and the building one thing.

gods.name: Taishang Laojun
gods.description: The Most High Lord Lao, third of the Three Pure Ones with Yuanshi Tianzun and Lingbao Tianzun, and the member of the three who turns toward the world and teaches it. He is not simply the sage Laozi promoted after death. From the second century onward the Daoist texts make him a cosmic power older than heaven, who takes flesh in age after age to give the teaching to men - and the man Laozi, who is separately catalogued here among the deified humans, is understood as one of those appearances. Religious Daoism holds the two together and this archive keeps both records, the man and the god, without pretending either that they are unrelated or that the god is only the man's ghost.

gods.name: Sigmund
gods.description: The Völsung. When a one-eyed stranger drove a sword into the Barnstokkr at his sister's wedding and said it was for whoever could draw it, Sigmund alone drew it out, and Siggeir, who could not, took the insult and paid it back by killing his father Völsung and taking his brothers. Bound in the forest and left for the wolves, he alone lived, and he lay hidden in a wood for years afterwards working toward the payment of that debt - and got Sinfjötli on his own sister to do it with him, for no half-Völsung would serve. He burned Siggeir in his hall at the last. He fell in old age against the sons of Hunding, when the one-eyed man came against him again and the sword broke on the raised spear; and he would not be healed, saying he had lived as long as Odin would have it. The shards were kept for his son.

gods.name: Signy
gods.description: Daughter of Völsung, married against her will to Siggeir, and the maker of the vengeance that follows. She warned her father and he came anyway and was killed; and when her husband had taken her brothers she stayed in his house for years, not as a captive waiting but as a woman working. She sent her two sons by Siggeir to Sigmund to be tested, and when they failed the test she told him to kill them, and he did. Then she changed shapes with a sorceress and went to her brother in the wood, and lay with him unknown, and bore Sinfjötli, who did not fail. When the hall was burning at the end she came out and told them plainly what she had done and whose son the boy was - and then went back into the fire and died with the husband she had destroyed, saying she had done everything to bring the killing about and could not live gladly after it.

gods.name: Sinfjötli
gods.description: Son of Sigmund by Signy his sister, got and reared for one purpose. His mother sewed the sleeves of his shirt to his arms to try him and he did not cry out; and he passed the tests her other sons had failed. He went into the wood with Sigmund, and there the two of them put on wolf-skins they could not take off for a time and lived as wolves, and Sigmund bit him in the throat before the days were up. He helped burn Siggeir in his hall, and afterwards fought a long and violent career. He was poisoned at the last by Borghild, Sigmund's wife, whose brother he had killed - she offered him the horn three times, and the third time he drank. He is not to be confused with later saga men of similar name.

gods.name: Gudrun Gjúkadóttir
gods.description: Daughter of Gjúki, wife of Sigurd, and the centre of the cycle after his death. She was given him by her mother's potion and loved him, and when he was killed in his bed by her brothers' contriving she sat over the body and would not weep until the sheet was drawn back. Afterwards she was married to Atli, who wanted the Niflung gold - and when he had killed her brothers for it she took the vengeance the poems remember: she killed the two sons she had borne him, gave him their blood to drink and their hearts to eat, told him what he had eaten, put a sword in him and set the hall alight. She is Guðrún Gjúkadóttir of the Eddic and Völsung tradition, and is neither Guðrún Ósvífrsdóttir of Laxdæla saga nor Kriemhild of the Nibelungenlied - Kriemhild is her German counterpart, but there the vengeance is taken for a husband and against brothers, which is the reverse of this, and the two are not made one here.

gods.name: Gunnar Gjúkason
gods.description: Son of Gjúki and king of the Niflungs. He wanted Brynhild and could not ride the fire to her, so Sigurd took his shape and rode it for him and lay three nights beside her with a drawn sword between them; and when the deception came out, Gunnar and his brothers had Sigurd killed - not by his own hand, for he had sworn oaths to him, but by the one brother who had sworn none. He kept the Niflung gold and would not say where it was sunk, though Atli sent for him and his brother on a false invitation and took them both; and when he was thrown bound into the snake-pit he played the harp there with his toes until one adder reached him. He is not Gunnar of Hlíðarendi, nor is he Gunther of the Nibelungenlied, who is his German counterpart and not his double.

gods.name: Grimhild
gods.description: Wife of Gjúki, mother of Gunnar and Gudrun, and the hand behind the marriages. She is called the fierce-hearted woman and a sorceress, and it is her drink that turns the story: she gave Sigurd the ale of forgetting so that he lost Brynhild out of his memory, and married him to her daughter, and then set Gunnar to win Brynhild in his place - and everything that follows, the deception at the fire, the quarrel of the queens, the killing in the bed, comes out of that cup. Later she brewed for Gudrun too, to make her forget her grief and marry Atli. She is not Kriemhild of the Nibelungenlied; the names are cognate but the women are not.

gods.name: Atli
gods.description: King in the Eddic poems who married Gudrun after Sigurd's death and wanted the Niflung gold that her brothers held. He sent them a false invitation, and when they came he took Gunnar and Högni and killed them for the treasure they would not give up - Gunnar into the snake-pit, and Högni's heart cut out. Gudrun killed the sons she had borne him, fed them to him, and burned his hall over him. The name descends from Attila the Hun, and the German tradition has him as Etzel; but the Etzel of the Nibelungenlied is an innocent host and the Atli of the Norse poems is the man who does the killing, and neither of them is the historical king. This record is the literary Atli of the Eddic and Völsung poems.

gods.name: Conall Cernach
gods.description: The great champion of Ulster beside Cú Chulainn, and his foster-brother. In Bricriu's feast he is one of the three who contend for the champion's portion and one of the three who go to Cú Roí for judgement. He had sworn that if Cú Chulainn were killed before him he would avenge him before the day was out, and he kept it: he hunted down Lugaid mac Con Roí and fought him - fairly, tying one of his own hands behind him because Lugaid had lost a hand - and killed him, and took his head, and the heads of the others who had a share in the killing. In the tale of Mac Da Thó's pig he claims the carving by throwing the head of Cet's brother at him. He is a first-rank hero of the cycle in his own right and not one of a crowd of Ulster warriors.

gods.name: Cú Roí mac Dáire
gods.description: King in Munster in the Ulster tales, and a man with the otherworld about him - his fort turned on its axis at nightfall so that its door could not be found, and he went out of Ireland for long stretches and could take other shapes. It is he who settles the contest of the champions in Fled Bricrenn: he comes to Emain as a hideous churl with an axe and offers to let a man behead him if the man will bend his own neck the next night, and only Cú Chulainn keeps the bargain and is named first among them for it. The tale is the earliest form of what later becomes Gawain and the Green Knight. He was killed by Cú Chulainn after his wife Bláthnat gave away the secret in which his life was kept. He is catalogued as a hero, which is what the tales make him; the guess that he was once a god is not the basis of the entry.

gods.name: Bláthnat
gods.description: Wife of Cú Roí, taken in the raid on the Fir Falga, and the one who brought him down. She is not simply a woman fought over: it is her decision that kills him. She found out where his life was kept - in an apple inside the belly of a salmon that appeared only every seventh year - and she told Cú Chulainn, and she told him when the fort would be open and the warriors away. She gave the signal by pouring milk into the stream that ran from the fort so that the water turned white and the Ulstermen knew the hour; and Cú Roí was killed in his own house. Cú Roí's poet Ferchertne took her afterwards over a cliff with him. The betrayal is hers, and it is the reason she is here.

gods.name: Ailill mac Máta
gods.description: King of Connacht and husband of Medb, and one half of the quarrel that starts the Táin. The war begins in their bed: they lie counting what each brought to the marriage and what each holds, and everything matches until the bull Finnbennach is found in Ailill's herd and there is nothing of hers to set against it - so she sends for the Donn Cúailnge, and when she cannot get it she takes the army of Ireland to fetch it. He rules with her, judges and rewards through the campaign, and at the end has Fergus killed for going with her. His name must be given in full, for Irish tradition has several Ailills and they are not one man.

gods.name: Bricriu Nemthenga
gods.description: Bricriu of the poison tongue, who made trouble as other men make things. He built a hall and gave a feast and would not be refused, and he went to each of the three champions of Ulster in turn - Cú Chulainn, Conall Cernach, Lóegaire - and told each privately that the champion's portion was his by right; and then he did the same with their three wives, so that the women raced each other to the door and the men broke the house apart. The whole of Fled Bricrenn comes out of his deliberate work, and it is his by design and not by accident. He is malicious, but he is a man and an actor in the tales and is not set down here as a monster for it.

gods.name: Goll mac Morna
gods.description: Leader of clan Morna and the man who killed Cumhall, Fionn's father, at the battle of Cnucha - and so held the leadership of the fianna until Fionn grew up and took it from him. He served under Fionn afterwards for many years and fought beside him, and is given as the second warrior of the fianna and a generous man; but the feud never closed, and in the end it broke out again and Goll was hunted onto a rock in the sea, where he refused water and food and died. He is not a step in Fionn's genealogy but a rival, an enemy and an ally in his own right.

gods.name: Caoilte mac Rónáin
gods.description: The swift-footed man of the fianna, who could run down a deer and who fought through the Fenian tales beside Fionn. He matters most for what he does afterwards. In Acallam na Senórach he and Oisín have outlived the fianna by centuries and meet St Patrick on the road, and Caoilte goes about Ireland with him, and at every hill and ford and cairn tells him what happened there and how the place got its name - so that the whole vanished world of the fianna is set down through his mouth, and Patrick's scribe writes it. He is not an attendant of Fionn; he is the voice through which the Fenian past survives its own ending.

gods.name: Oscar
gods.description: Son of Oisín and grandson of Fionn, and the hardest fighter of the fianna in its last days. When the fianna and the High King Cairbre Lifechair came to the battle of Gabhair, it was Oscar who met Cairbre in the middle of it: they killed each other, Cairbre driving the spear through him and Oscar striking him down as he fell. The fianna broke at Gabhair and did not come together again, and Fionn's lament over Oscar's body is one of the set pieces of the cycle - the destruction of the fianna turns on that combat. He is the Fenian Oscar, and not any of the later or modern bearers of the name.

gods.name: Rostam
gods.description: The chief hero of the Shahnameh and the man on whom Iran leans for seven generations of kings. He rides Rakhsh, whom no other man can mount, and it is he who goes into Mazandaran alone to bring back Kai Kavus from the White Div, passing the seven labours to do it. He serves king after king, and is not obedient to them: he tells Kai Kavus to his face what he is worth. In the great grief of the poem he fights three days against a young Turanian champion he does not know, and throws him at last and puts the dagger in - and the boy, dying, says that his father Rostam will avenge him, and shows the armlet; and it is Sohrab, his own son. He is killed in the end by his half-brother's treachery, in a pit set with spears.

gods.name: Sohrab
gods.description: Son of Rostam by Tahmina of Samangan, born after his father had gone. He grew huge and strong very young, and set out at the head of a Turanian army with the intention of finding his father, putting him on the throne of Iran in Kai Kavus's place, and ruling with him. He asks after Rostam at every turn and is lied to - by the Iranians who do not want the two brought together, and by his own side. He fights an unnamed Iranian champion for three days and throws him once and spares him; the second time he is thrown himself, and the dagger goes in before either has spoken his name. He tells the man who has killed him that his father Rostam will come for him, and shows the armlet his mother tied on his arm. He is not merely Rostam's son; the tragedy is that he spent his whole short life looking for him.

gods.name: Zal
gods.description: Son of Sam, born with hair white as an old man's, and exposed on the mountain of Alborz for it because his father took the whiteness for a mark of the demons. The Simurgh found him and carried him to her nest and reared him among her young; and when Sam repented and came for him she gave him back, and gave him three of her feathers, telling him that if he burned one she would come. He grew into the wisest of the Iranian nobles and the counsellor of kings, and he chose Rudaba of Kabul against the will of both their houses and married her. When she could not bring Rostam to birth he burned the feather, and the Simurgh told them how to open her side and close it again. He is a man, and his rearing by the Simurgh does not make him otherwise.

gods.name: Rudaba
gods.description: Daughter of Mehrab of Kabul, of the hated line of Zahhak, and the woman who chose Zal. She heard what he was and decided on him before she had seen him; and when he came she let down her hair from the tower for him to climb, and would not be turned by her father's fear or by the Iranian king's objection to the match, and the two of them held to it until the houses gave way. She carried Rostam so long and so hard that she was dying of it, and Zal burned the Simurgh's feather; and the bird came and told them to cut her side and take the child out and lay the herb and the feather on the wound - which they did, and she woke and lived. She is not entered here as Rostam's mother but as the woman who made the choice the line depends on.

gods.name: Siyavash
gods.description: Son of Kai Kavus, and the purest man in the Shahnameh. His stepmother Sudabeh tried to take him, and when he refused her she accused him of forcing her; and to prove himself he rode between two mountains of burning wood and came out the other side with his horse's coat unsinged and his white clothes unmarked. He would not stay after that. He went over to Turan, where Afrasiyab received him and gave him his daughter and let him build a city; and then the king's brother Garsivaz poisoned Afrasiyab's mind against him, and Siyavash was taken and his throat cut over a basin, and where the blood fell a plant came up. His death is the wound the rest of the poem turns on - his son Kai Khosrow is raised to avenge it, and the long war between Iran and Turan is fought for it.

gods.name: Afrasiyab
gods.description: King of Turan and the enemy of Iran across the length of the Shahnameh - the antagonist of three generations, not of one episode. He fights Iran under king after king, is driven back and returns; he takes Siyavash in when the young man flees his father's court, gives him his daughter and treats him as a son, and then is worked on by his brother Garsivaz until he lets him be killed - the one act from which the rest of the war grows. He is hunted at last by Kai Khosrow, Siyavash's son, dragged out of a cave where he had hidden, and killed. He is a king and a man, and he is set down here as a hero of the narrative in the sense of a principal actor; his enmity is political and not a matter of his nature.

gods.name: Esfandiyar
gods.description: Prince of Iran, son of Goshtasp, the champion of the new faith of Zoroaster, and made invulnerable in body by Zoroaster's blessing - all but his eyes. He passed his own seven labours to free his sisters from the Turanians. His father, who had promised him the throne and did not want to give it, sent him to bring Rostam back in chains, which he knew was a thing that should not be asked; and he went, because he had sworn obedience. The two of them fought for two days and Rostam could not hurt him and was dying, until Zal burned the Simurgh's feather and the bird told him where to find the tamarisk and how to cut the double-headed arrow and where alone the man could be struck. Esfandiyar took it in the eyes and died knowing his father had sent him to it. He is a man, and neither a god nor a monster.

gods.name: Aži Dahāka / Zahhak
gods.description: The great adversary of the Iranian tradition, under names that changed while the figure did not. In the Avesta he is Aži Dahāka, the aži or dragon, three-mouthed and three-headed and six-eyed, made by Angra Mainyu for the ruin of the world; in Middle Persian he is Dahāg or Aždahāg; and in Ferdowsi he is Zahhak - a prince who murders his own father for a throne, and whom Iblis kisses on the shoulders, so that two serpents grow there that must be fed on human brains. He takes the kingship from Jamshid and holds Iran a thousand years, until the smith's revolt and Fereydun bring him down. He is not killed: he is bound in a cave beneath Mount Damāvand, and the Zoroastrian eschatology has him break those bonds at the end of days and ravage the world once more before Keresaspa rises and kills him at last. These are successive forms of one inherited figure and not separate beings - the serpent is not removed when he is given a man's shape, only moved inside it - and one record is made, with Zohak, Aždahāg, Dahāg and the epithet Bēvarasp among the names it has carried.

gods.name: Fereydun
gods.description: The king who threw down Zahhak. He is the Persian form of the Avestan Θraētaona, who overthrows Aži Dahāka in the older tradition - the same hero under an evolved name, as his adversary is the same adversary, and no separate record is made for the Avestan form. Hidden as a child from Zahhak's men and suckled by the cow Barmayeh, he came out at the head of the rising that Kaveh the blacksmith began, with the smith's leather apron carried before him as a banner; and he took Zahhak and did not kill him, but bound him in the cave under Damāvand. He ruled long and well, and then divided the world among his three sons - Rome and the west to Salm, Turan and the east to Tur, Iran to the youngest, Iraj - and the two elder killed the youngest out of envy, and out of that killing came the war of Iran and Turan that runs through the rest of the poem.

gods.name: Tohil
gods.description: The patron god of the K'iche' in the Popol Vuh, and the god around whom the second half of that book turns. When the first men were cold in the darkness before the first dawn he gave them fire - and when the other tribes came shivering to ask for it, he gave it to them too, but at a price: that they should give him their sides and their armpits, that he should suckle at their breasts, which is to say the hearts of men. The K'iche' carried him on their backs out of Tulan, and set him at last on the mountain, and made war and took captives and gave them to him; and it is from him that their lords held their right to rule. His name is also written Tojil. He is the god of one people, not a supreme deity of all the Maya, and he is not presented as one here.

gods.name: Llefelys
gods.description: Brother of Lludd and king in France, and the man who solves the three plagues of Britain. When Lludd's kingdom was afflicted - by the Coraniaid, who heard every word the wind carried, so that nothing could be plotted against them; by a scream on every May eve that made women miscarry and the land barren; and by the disappearance of a year's provisions in a night - Lludd went to him over the sea, and they spoke through a bronze horn so that no word could be caught. He gave the remedies: insects crushed in water and thrown over the assembly, which killed the Coraniaid and left the Britons unharmed; the measuring of the island to its exact centre and a vat of mead sunk there, into which the two fighting dragons whose battle made the scream would fall asleep; and a vat of cold water for Lludd to leap into to keep himself awake for the giant who was carrying off the food. The counsel is his, and the tale is named for them both.

gods.name: Jocasta
gods.description: Queen of Thebes, wife of Laius and then of Oedipus. When the oracle said the child would kill his father she gave the infant up to be exposed on Cithaeron with his ankles pinned, and afterwards told herself that the oracle had failed and that prophecy was worth nothing. She married the stranger who answered the Sphinx and bore him four children. In Sophocles she reaches the truth before he does - she works it out from the place where Laius was killed and the number of the roads, and she stops trying to persuade him and begins begging him to ask nothing more, and tells him that many a man has lain with his mother in dreams and it is better to live at random. He will not stop, and she goes into the house and hangs herself.

gods.name: Laius
gods.description: King of Thebes, and the man whose choices set the whole catastrophe going. Warned by Apollo that a son of his would kill him, he had the child pierced through the ankles and given to a herdsman to leave on the mountain - and the herdsman pitied it and gave it away instead. Years later, driving to Delphi, he met a young man at the place where three roads meet, and would not give way, and struck him with his goad; and the young man killed him and everyone with him but one. It was his son. He is not a name in a genealogy: the exposure and the quarrel at the crossroads are both his own doing.

gods.name: Polyneices
gods.description: Son of Oedipus. He and his brother Eteocles were to hold Thebes in alternate years, and when his year came Eteocles would not come down; so Polyneices went to Argos, married Adrastus's daughter, and brought back the army of the Seven to take the city by force. He and his brother met at the seventh gate and killed each other with their own hands. Creon then forbade his burial - he had come against his own city, and was to lie unburied for the dogs - and it is that decree, and his sister Antigone's refusal of it, that makes the tragedy. His name is written Polyneices and Polynices; the form used here is the older.

gods.name: Eteocles
gods.description: Son of Oedipus, and the brother who kept the throne. By the agreement the two were to rule Thebes in turn, a year each; Eteocles took the first year and at the end of it refused to give it up, and drove Polyneices out. He held the city through the assault of the Seven, and in Aeschylus he sets a champion at each of the six gates and takes the seventh himself, knowing who is coming to it - and goes to it anyway, saying the curse of his father is on them both. The brothers killed each other there. He was buried with honour and his brother was not, which is where the next tragedy begins.

gods.name: Creon of Thebes
gods.description: Brother of Jocasta, and the man left holding Thebes after each of its disasters. When Eteocles and Polyneices had killed each other he took the rule and made the decree: Eteocles to be buried with honour, Polyneices to lie where he fell, and death to anyone who covered him. Antigone buried her brother anyway, and Creon had her walled up alive, and would not hear his son Haemon, and would not hear Tiresias, until at last he gave way - and came too late, and found Antigone hanged, and his son dead over her body, and his wife dead by her own hand in the house. He is a man who governs badly, not a monster, and he is set down here as a principal actor. He is not Creon of Corinth, the father of the bride in the Medea, who is another man.

gods.name: Pelops
gods.description: Son of Tantalus, and the founder of the line that bears his curse. In the old story his father cut him up and served him to the gods, and they put him back together and gave him an ivory shoulder where Demeter had eaten. Grown, he came to Pisa for Hippodamia, whose father Oenomaus had killed thirteen suitors in the chariot race and nailed their heads to his house; and Pelops went to Myrtilus, the king's charioteer, and bought him with a promise - and Myrtilus took the linchpins out of the axle, and Oenomaus was thrown and killed. Then Pelops threw Myrtilus into the sea to be rid of him; and Myrtilus, going down, cursed the house of Pelops. Everything that Atreus and his sons do afterwards is that curse working.

gods.name: Atreus
gods.description: Son of Pelops, king of Mycenae, and the author of the act the house is remembered for. He and his brother Thyestes contended for the throne; there was a golden lamb in Atreus's flocks that carried the kingship with it, and Thyestes got it through Atreus's wife Aerope and took the rule by it. Atreus won it back, and then pretended reconciliation, and invited his brother to a feast - and killed Thyestes's children and cooked them and served them to their father, and brought in the hands and the heads afterwards to show him what he had eaten. The sun is said to have turned back in its course. He is catalogued as a principal actor of the cycle, which is a statement about the narrative and not about the man.

gods.name: Thyestes
gods.description: Son of Pelops and brother of Atreus, and not merely the victim of the feast. He seduced Atreus's wife Aerope and through her got the golden lamb that carried the kingship, and took the throne of Mycenae with it. Driven out, and then called back and fed his own children, he went to the oracle to ask how he could be avenged - and was told to father a son on his own daughter Pelopia. He did it, in the dark and unrecognised, and the son was Aegisthus, who was reared in Atreus's own house and grew up to kill him. The vengeance is his, executed by the child he made for the purpose.

gods.name: Clytemnestra
gods.description: Daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, wife of Agamemnon, and his killer. He took their daughter Iphigenia to Aulis on the promise of a marriage and cut her throat there to buy a wind for the fleet, and Clytemnestra did not forget it in the ten years he was gone. She held Mycenae in his absence and took Aegisthus, his cousin and his enemy, and when Agamemnon came home she spread the crimson cloth for him to walk on and killed him in the bath, tangled in a robe he could not get his arms out of. In Aeschylus she stands over the body and claims the act and says she feels no shame; other tellings make her more the instrument of Aegisthus, and the sources do not agree on where the weight of it lies. Her son killed her for it.

gods.name: Aegisthus
gods.description: Son of Thyestes by his own daughter Pelopia, got for one purpose: to be the instrument of the vengeance on the house of Atreus. He was reared in Atreus's household not knowing whose son he was, and was sent to kill Thyestes - and learned the truth at the last moment and killed Atreus instead. He took Clytemnestra while Agamemnon was at Troy and ruled Mycenae with her, and had a hand in the killing when the king came home; how large a hand depends on which poet is telling it, for in Homer the murder is largely his and in Aeschylus it is largely hers. He held the throne seven years, and was killed by Orestes. He is not simply Clytemnestra's lover; he is the curse of Pelops arriving on time.

gods.name: Orestes
gods.description: Son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, sent away as a boy and come back a man to do what Apollo told him to do. He killed Aegisthus, and then he killed his mother - and she bared her breast to him and asked him to remember it, and he did it anyway. The Erinyes took him for it and drove him mad and hunted him across Greece; he went to Delphi, and Apollo would not free him of them, and sent him to Athens. There Athena set up a court on the Areopagus and the case was heard and the votes were equal, and she cast for him, and he was acquitted - and the Furies were turned into the Kindly Ones and given a place under the city. The Oresteia ends with law put in the place of blood.

gods.name: Electra (of Mycenae)
gods.description: Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, who kept her father's death alive in the house for years while his killers ruled in it. She was left in Mycenae, unmarried or married off beneath her to keep her sons harmless, and she would not be quiet: she mourned openly, and hated openly, and waited for her brother. When Orestes came back she knew him by the lock of hair and the footprint at the tomb, and it is she who hardens him to the matricide - in Sophocles she stands at the door while he does it and calls to him to strike again. Euripides gives her a larger share still and has her lay hands on the sword herself; other tellings keep her outside. The sources vary in how much of it is hers, and this record does not settle it. She is not the Oceanid Electra, the consort of Thaumas, who is another and unrelated figure.

gods.name: Iphigenia
gods.description: Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, brought to Aulis on the false promise of a marriage to Achilles and killed there so that the fleet could sail - the act from which her mother's revenge and the whole ruin of the house follow. The traditions do not agree on what she was in it. In Aeschylus she is a victim and nothing else: they lift her over the altar like a goat, and gag her so that she cannot curse the house, and her eyes go to each of the sacrificers in turn. In Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis she refuses at first and pleads for her life, and then changes her mind and goes to the altar of her own will, saying that Greece is worth her death. And in a third tradition Artemis takes her from the altar and leaves a deer there, and carries her to Tauris to be her priestess, where she nearly sacrifices Orestes before she knows him. Voluntary sacrifice is one telling and not the general one, and it is not presented as such here.

gods.name: Lucretia
gods.description: A Roman noblewoman, wife of Collatinus, raped by Sextus Tarquinius, the king's son, who came to her house as a guest and threatened to kill her and lay a slave beside her body if she resisted. What follows in Livy is hers. She sent for her father and her husband and told them to bring a trusted man each, and when they came she told them plainly what had been done and who had done it, and made them swear to punish him; and then, refusing the absolution they offered her, she drew a knife she had hidden and killed herself in front of them. Brutus took the knife from the wound, and the body was carried into the forum, and the Tarquins were driven out and the Republic made. The Roman writers use her death as a founding proof, and the code of honour that made her think she had to die is theirs and is not endorsed here; the assault was done to her, and the testimony is what she chose.

gods.name: Lucius Junius Brutus
gods.description: Founder of the Roman Republic in the Roman tradition. He had lived at the Tarquin court playing the fool - brutus, the dull one - because his kinsmen had been killed and stupidity was safe; and when Lucretia died he took the knife from her body and swore by her blood to drive the kings out, and was not a fool any longer. He led the rising, expelled Tarquinius Superbus, and was made one of the two first consuls. Then his own sons were found in a conspiracy to bring the kings back, and he sat in judgement on them himself and had them beaten and beheaded in front of him and did not look away. He fell fighting the Tarquins' cavalry. He is not Marcus Junius Brutus, who killed Caesar four centuries later and claimed descent from him.

gods.name: Horatius Cocles
gods.description: The Roman who held the Sublician bridge. When the Etruscan army of Lars Porsenna broke through and the way into Rome lay open across the river, Horatius - called Cocles, the one-eyed - told the others to cut the bridge down behind him and stood at the far end of it with two companions, and then alone, and kept the whole army off the narrow crossing while the timbers went. When it fell he called on the river and went into it in his armour and swam across, and Rome gave him as much land as he could plough in a day. Livy tells it and doubts parts of it, and the story is a Roman exemplum of what a citizen owes - it is not secure history, and is not offered as such.

gods.name: Gaius Mucius Scaevola
gods.description: The Roman who put his own hand in the fire. During Porsenna's siege he crossed into the Etruscan camp to kill the king, and, not knowing which man was which, stabbed the royal secretary instead and was taken. Brought before Porsenna and threatened with burning, he thrust his right hand into the flame on the altar and held it there while it burned, and did not change his face, and told the king that three hundred Romans had sworn the same oath and were coming after him one by one. Porsenna, the story says, let him go and made peace; and he was called Scaevola, the left-handed, ever after. It is a Roman exemplum of resolve, told to explain a name, and is not offered as certain history.

gods.name: Cloelia
gods.description: A Roman girl given to Lars Porsenna as one of the hostages in the peace, and the one who got away. She led a group of the other girls out of the Etruscan camp, and they swam the Tiber under the enemy's missiles and came back into Rome. Porsenna demanded her back and the Romans returned her, keeping the treaty; and he, the story says, was so struck by what she had done that he freed her and let her choose others to take with her, and she chose the youngest of the boys, as the ones most at risk. Rome set up an equestrian statue of her on the Sacred Way. The escape is hers, and it is for that and not for her use as a symbol that she stands here.

gods.name: Coriolanus
gods.description: Gnaeus Marcius, called Coriolanus for the taking of Corioli, and the best soldier of his generation in the Roman account. He set himself against the plebeians and the tribunes and would have had the corn withheld until they gave up their rights, and was tried and driven out of the city for it; and he went straight to the Volsci, Rome's enemies, and took their army and brought it back to the gates of Rome, and would hear no embassy - not the envoys, not the priests. Then his mother Veturia came out to him with his wife and his children and the women of Rome behind her, and told him what he was doing; and he gave way, and turned the army round, and the Volsci killed him for it. He is a man who chose wrongly, and is set down here as a principal actor.

gods.name: Numa Pompilius
gods.description: The second king of Rome in the tradition, a Sabine, chosen after Romulus and remembered as the opposite of him: where the first king made the city by war, the second made it by religion. To Numa the Romans attributed nearly the whole apparatus of their public worship - the calendar with its fixed and forbidden days, the pontiffs and the flamens, the Salii with their dancing and their shields, the Vestals and the perpetual fire, the temple of Janus whose doors he closed and which stayed shut for the whole of his reign. He is said to have taken his counsel from the nymph Egeria at her spring. These are attributions made by Roman writers looking back at institutions whose beginnings they did not know, and they are given here as the tradition and not as biography. He was not deified.

gods.name: Kaveh
gods.description: The blacksmith who began the rising against Zahhak. Seventeen of his sons had been taken for the serpents that grew from the tyrant's shoulders and had to be fed on the brains of men, and when they came for the last one he went to the court itself. Zahhak had drawn up a testimony for the great men to sign, declaring that he had never ruled but justly; and Kaveh, standing in front of the throne, asked for his son and then tore the paper across and threw it down and walked out. In the street he put his leather apron on the point of a spear and raised it, and the people came to it; and that apron, hung with jewels by the kings after him, became the Derafsh Kaviani, the standard of Iran. He brought the rising to Fereydun and put him at the head of it. His name is also written Kāveh, and he is called Kaveh the Blacksmith.

gods.name: Kai Khosrow
gods.description: Son of Siyavash by Afrasiyab's daughter, born in Turan after his father's murder and hidden among shepherds, and brought out of Turan at last into Iran to take the crown. He is the king who finishes the long war: he hunts Afrasiyab down for the killing of his father, takes him out of the cave where he had hidden, and has him killed. And then, at the height of it, with the war won and the world quiet, he does the thing that is remembered - he says that he has done what he was raised to do and that a king who stays too long becomes what he destroyed, and he gives the kingdom away and rides up into the mountains with a few companions, and goes into the snow, and is not seen again. He continues the Avestan Kavi Haosravah under an evolved name, and no separate record is made for that form; he is not the historical Sasanian kings Khosrow I or Khosrow II, who are other men entirely.

gods.name: Tahmina
gods.description: Princess of Samangan, and the woman who chose Rostam. He had come to her father's city looking for Rakhsh, who had been stolen while he slept; and in the night she came to his chamber with a candle before her and told him who she was and what she wanted - that she had heard of him all her life, and would have a child of him, and would find his horse. He sent for her father in the morning and married her by the law. He left before the child was born and gave her an armlet to put on it, and she bore a son and tied the armlet on his arm, and told him afterwards who his father was. That armlet is what Rostam sees on the boy's arm when he has already put the dagger in him. She is not entered here as Sohrab's mother but as the woman who came in the dark and said what she wanted.

gods.name: Keresaspa / Garshasp
gods.description: The great club-bearing hero of the Iranian tradition, under names that changed while the figure did not. In the Avesta he is Kərəsāspa, the club-bearer, who kills the horned dragon Srvara - so large that he cooked his meal on its back and did not know until the beast moved beneath him - and Gandarewa, and the monsters of the wilderness; in the later Persian tradition he is Garshasp, and a whole book of his deeds is written for him. Because he killed a fire, or slighted one, his soul is held back at the last, and the tradition gives him this at the end: when Aži Dahāka breaks the bonds that Fereydun laid on him beneath Damāvand and comes out at the end of days to ravage the world, it is Keresaspa who is roused from his long sleep and rises and kills him at last. Kərəsāspa, Keresaspa and Garshasp are successive forms of one inherited hero, and one record is made; he is not to be confused with unrelated men of similar name.

gods.name: Bran mac Febail
gods.description: The voyager of Immram Brain. A branch of silver with white blossom was found in his hand, and a woman none of them had seen come in stood in the house and sang to him of the islands over the sea, of the plain where there is no want and no sorrow and no death, and told him to come; and when she had gone the branch went with her, and Bran took three companies of nine and put out. He met Manannán driving his chariot over what was a flowering plain to the god and the sea to him, and came to the Island of Joy and to the Land of Women, and stayed there what seemed a year. When they grew homesick they were warned to touch no land, and they came back to Ireland and called their names from the water - and the people on the shore said they knew Bran mac Febail only from the old stories. One man leapt out of the boat, and the moment he touched the ground he fell to ashes, as though he had been dead for hundreds of years. Bran told them what had happened, and put out again, and was not heard of after. He is not Brân the Blessed of the Welsh tales, nor Saint Brendan.

gods.name: Máel Dúin
gods.description: The voyager of Immram Maele Dúin, who set out to kill the men who had killed his father and did not do it. He built the boat and was told the number to take, and took three foster-brothers besides, and for that the voyage was driven off its course; and they came to island after island - the ant island, the island of the horse-races, the island of the burning boar, the crystal bridge, the woman who threw them a thread that stuck to the hand, the old hermit who had gone out on a sod of earth that grew into an island under him. The text as it survives has been worked over by Christian hands and reads the wandering as a penance, and that framing is part of what we have and is not stripped out here. At the end they came to the very island where the killers were, and were welcomed in, and Máel Dúin sat down at their table and made peace with them and went home. The turning of the tale is that he chose not to take the vengeance he had gone out for.

gods.name: Tiresias
gods.description: The blind seer of Thebes, who saw seven generations of it. He was blinded, the stories say, and given prophecy in exchange - by Athena for having seen her bathing, or by Hera, when he was called to settle whether the man or the woman has the greater pleasure in love and answered the woman, having been both, for he had struck a pair of coupling snakes and lived seven years as a woman before striking them again. In Oedipus Tyrannus he will not say what he knows, and is goaded into saying it, and names Oedipus as the killer - and Oedipus does not believe him, and accuses him of conspiring with Creon; the discovery comes afterwards through Jocasta and the herdsman, and not through him. In Antigone he does change the outcome: Creon insults him and accuses him of taking bribes, and Tiresias tells him he will pay with one out of his own loins and walks out - and Creon, who has refused his son and the chorus and the girl herself, gives way at last, and goes to free her, too late. In the Odyssey he alone among the dead has kept his mind, and tells Odysseus the way home. Also written Teiresias.

gods.name: Amphiaraus
gods.description: Seer and warrior of Argos, and the one man of the Seven who knew before they set out that they would all die but Adrastus. He would not go; but he had sworn to abide by whatever his wife Eriphyle decided in any quarrel with Adrastus, and Polyneices bought her with the necklace of Harmonia, and she sent him. He went knowing it, and charged his sons to avenge him on their mother. He fought well and, fleeing along the river at the end, was not killed - Zeus split the earth in front of him with a thunderbolt and he went down into it, chariot and charioteer and all, alive. He was worshipped afterwards at Oropos, where the sick slept in his precinct for a dream. He is a man who acted against his own knowledge, and is not entered here only as a prophet or as Eriphyle's husband.

gods.name: Eriphyle
gods.description: Sister of Adrastus and wife of Amphiaraus, and the woman who sent the Seven to Thebes. Amphiaraus had bound himself to abide by her judgement in any dispute with her brother, and when Polyneices came asking for the expedition and Amphiaraus - who could see the end of it - refused, Polyneices gave her the necklace of Harmonia, and she gave the decision for the war. She did it knowing he would die of it. The sources do not make her the necklace's victim but its buyer: the choice is hers, and it destroys her house. Her son Alcmaeon killed her for it afterwards, at his father's charge, and was hunted by the Furies as Orestes was.

gods.name: Tydeus
gods.description: An exile out of Calydon, taken in by Adrastus of Argos and married to his daughter, and one of the Seven. He was small and enormously violent; sent alone to Thebes as an envoy, he challenged the Cadmeians to contests and beat them all, and killed the fifty men they laid in ambush for him on the road home, all but one. At the wall he was mortally wounded by Melanippus; and Athena, who loved him, was coming down with a drug that would have made him immortal. What she found is the thing he is remembered for: Amphiaraus, who hated him, cut off Melanippus's head and threw it to him, and Tydeus split it and was eating the brain when she arrived, and she turned away and let him die. That last detail is the property of the later epic and the mythographers rather than of every telling of the war, and is given here as theirs. He is a man and a warrior, not a monster; he is the father of Diomedes.

gods.name: Adrastus
gods.description: King of Argos, and the man who made the expedition of the Seven against Thebes. An oracle had told him to yoke his daughters to a boar and a lion, and when two exiles - Polyneices and Tydeus - fought on his porch by night in the skins of those beasts, he read the sign and married his daughters to them and swore to restore them both to their countries. He raised the army and led it, against Amphiaraus's warning; and of the seven who went, he alone came home, carried out of the rout on the immortal horse Arion, who is catalogued here separately. Ten years later he sent the sons of the dead - the Epigoni - back to Thebes, and they took it; and his own son was the only one of them to fall, and Adrastus is said to have died of the grief of it.

gods.name: Haemon
gods.description: Son of Creon and betrothed to Antigone. When his father had condemned her for burying her brother, Haemon came to him and argued - carefully at first, saying that the city was grieving for her in secret and that a man who thinks himself the only wise one is found to be empty when he is opened - and Creon would not hear it, and told him he was a woman's slave; and Haemon left saying his father would never see his face again. He went to the vault where she had been walled up. Creon, when he came to release her, found her hanged and his son with his arms round her; and Haemon spat in his face and drew on him and missed, and then turned the sword on himself and fell on it, and died holding her. His mother Eurydice killed herself when she was told, cursing Creon over the body of the second son she had lost. The sources differ over the exact scene at the tomb, and it is given here as Sophocles has it.

gods.name: Myrtilus
gods.description: Charioteer of Oenomaus of Pisa, and the man who threw the race. His master had killed thirteen suitors in the chariot-course, and Pelops came for the fourteenth; and Myrtilus took the bronze linchpins out of the axle and put in pins of wax, so that the wheels came off at speed and Oenomaus was dragged to death in the reins. Why he did it the sources will not agree: some say Pelops bribed him with half the kingdom, some that Hippodamia, who loved Pelops, persuaded him because he loved her, and some that he had been promised a night with her. Pelops, having won, threw him into the sea to be rid of the debt - and Myrtilus, going down, cursed him and his line. That curse is what works itself out through Atreus and Thyestes and Agamemnon, and it is the reason he is entered here as an actor and not as a tool.

gods.name: Oenomaus
gods.description: King of Pisa in Elis, who had been told that his daughter's husband would kill him - or who wanted her himself, the sources give both - and who therefore made a contest of her marriage. Any suitor might take Hippodamia and drive off with her, and Oenomaus would follow with a spear; and his horses, which were the gift of Ares, always caught them, and he killed each man on the road and nailed the heads up on the pillars of his house. Thirteen had died so when Pelops came. He lost that race because his own charioteer had drawn the linchpins, and was dragged in his own reins and killed - and in some tellings he cursed Myrtilus with his last breath, and the curse was passed on. He is not entered here as Hippodamia's father but as the man who built the thing that killed him.

gods.name: Hippodamia (of Pisa)
gods.description: Daughter of Oenomaus of Pisa and wife of Pelops. What she does depends on who is telling it, and the difference matters. In Pindar's ninth Olympian ode she is the prize and no more: Pelops prays to Poseidon by the grey sea and is given the winged chariot, and the girl is what he wins with it. In Apollodorus and the tradition behind him she is an actor: she has fallen in love with Pelops, and it is she who works on Myrtilus - who wants her himself - and gets him to draw the linchpins from her father's axle. Her admission here rests on that second tradition, and the first is not suppressed to make room for it. A further and later strand has her fear that Chrysippus, Pelops's son by another woman, will be preferred to her own, and set Atreus and Thyestes on to kill him, or kill him herself with Laius's sword; that belongs to the mythographers and the tragedians and is given as theirs. She is not Hippodamia the wife of Pirithous, over whom the centaurs fought, nor the Hippodameia whose patronymic is Briseis.

gods.name: Aerope
gods.description: Cretan wife of Atreus, and the hinge on which the house of Pelops turns. A golden lamb had appeared in Atreus's flocks, and the kingship of Mycenae went with it, and Atreus killed it and hid the fleece away in a chest. Aerope, who was Thyestes' lover, gave it to him - and Thyestes stood up in the assembly and produced it and was made king by it. Everything follows from that transfer: the exile, the recall, the children served at the table, the curse that comes down to Agamemnon. How much of it is her own act the sources will not settle. Apollodorus says she had been debauched by Thyestes and gave him the lamb; the tragedians treat her sometimes as the mover of the scheme and sometimes as the instrument of it. She is entered here because the throne changes hands by her hand, and the question of how freely is left where the sources leave it. Atreus is said to have drowned her in the sea, which is a further tradition and not in all of them.

gods.name: Niobe
gods.description: Daughter of Tantalus and queen of Thebes, who had many children and said so. Standing against the worship of Leto, who had borne only two, she told the women of Thebes to stop the sacrifices and turn to her instead, being the better mother by the count of them. Leto's two were Apollo and Artemis, and they came and shot the children down - the sons in the field and the daughters in the house - and the sources differ on how many there were, giving six and six or seven and seven or more, and on whether one was left alive. Niobe went to Sipylus and was turned to stone there, and the stone still weeps: the water runs down the rock face in the summer.
