She is not entered for what was done to her but for what she said; the boast is the cause and the killing is the consequence.

gods.name: Servius Tullius
gods.description: The sixth king of Rome in the Roman account, and the one to whom they credited the shape of the state. He was born a slave in the palace, the tradition says, and a flame played about his head as he slept and did not burn him; and Tanaquil read the sign and reared him, and put him on the throne when her husband was murdered. To him the Romans traced the census and the division of the people by property into classes and centuries, which decided how they voted and how they served - so that the assembly that elected their magistrates was his design - and the wall and the enlargement of the city, and the temple of Diana on the Aventine. He was murdered at the instigation of his own daughter Tullia and her husband Tarquinius Superbus, thrown down the steps of the senate house; and Tullia drove her carriage over his body in the street that was called the Street of Crime afterwards. These are the attributions of the annalists to a king they could not document, and are given as tradition and not as biography.

gods.name: Tanaquil
gods.description: An Etruscan noblewoman, and the maker of two Roman kings. She was skilled in reading portents, as Etruscan women were said to be; when an eagle took her husband's cap as they came in sight of Rome and set it back on his head, she told him what it meant and would not let him settle for less, and he became king as Tarquinius Priscus. When he was struck down by assassins she did the thing she is remembered for: she had the doors shut, and told the crowd from an upper window that the king was only stunned and would recover and had appointed Servius Tullius to act for him in the meantime - and kept the death secret, and kept Servius giving judgement in the king's name, until his hold was firm enough that the truth could be told and he simply went on ruling. She is not entered here as anyone's wife.

gods.name: Veturia
gods.description: The mother of Coriolanus, and the only person who could stop him. When he had brought the Volscian army to the gates of Rome and turned away the envoys and then the priests, the women of the city went to her, and she went out to the camp with his wife and his children and the matrons of Rome behind her. She would not embrace him until she knew whether she came as his mother or his prisoner, and she asked him whether the city he was about to destroy had not borne him; and she said that he could not reach Rome except over her body. He gave way, and drew the army off, and the Volscians killed him for it. The names in the sources conflict and are not reconciled here: Livy calls the mother Veturia and the wife Volumnia, while Plutarch reverses it, giving Volumnia to the mother and Vergilia to the wife - and Shakespeare followed Plutarch, which is why the mother is generally called Volumnia today. The earlier Roman name is used here.

gods.name: Verginius
gods.description: A Roman centurion, and the man whose act brought down the Decemvirate. Appius Claudius, one of the ten, wanted his daughter, and had a client claim her in court as a slave born in his household, so that a judgement could give her to him; and Verginius came from the army and stood in the Forum and could get no hearing, and Appius gave the girl to the claimant. Then he asked leave to speak to her one last time, and took her aside among the shops, and picked up a butcher's knife and killed her with it, saying it was the only way he had left to make her free. He carried the knife bloody through the city to the camp, and the army rose, and the Decemvirate fell and the tribunes were restored. The act is set down as the tradition gives it and is not praised here; and his daughter, who was killed and did not act, has no record.

gods.name: Cincinnatus
gods.description: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, the Roman exemplum of power laid down. The story is that the senate's messengers found him at the plough on his four-acre farm across the Tiber, and that he wiped off the sweat and put on his toga to hear them tell him he had been made dictator; and he crossed over, raised a levy, and in a single night surrounded the Aequi who had trapped a consular army at Mount Algidus, and made them pass under the yoke the next day. He held the office sixteen days, and then resigned it and went back to the farm, with the remainder of the six months still to run. The Romans told it against their own later politicians, and it is a moral tale about the relinquishing of power rather than a documented life; the resignation, not the victory, is the whole of it.

gods.name: Camillus
gods.description: Marcus Furius Camillus, called the second founder of Rome. He took Veii after a ten-year siege, and was then prosecuted over the division of the spoil and went into exile, and cursed the city as he went. When the Gauls came and broke the army at the Allia and took Rome and were besieging the Capitol, the Romans made him dictator in his absence; and the tradition has him arriving as the gold was being weighed out to buy them off, and saying that Rome ransoms herself with iron and not with gold, and driving them out. Afterwards, when the people wanted to abandon the ruins and move to Veii, he argued them out of it and kept the city where it was - and that, more than the fighting, is what the title was for. The accounts are annalistic and were shaped to answer the shame of the sack; how much is his is not recoverable.

gods.name: Kai Kavus
gods.description: King of Iran in the Shahnameh, and the source of most of what goes wrong in it. He is not a passive fool: he decides, and the decisions cost. He invades Mazandaran against every warning because a div sings to him about it, and is blinded and taken with his whole army, so that Rostam must come alone through the seven labours to get him back. He is persuaded that he can reach heaven, and has a throne built and four eagles tied to it with meat on poles above them, and rises until the birds tire and drops out of the sky into a wood. He believes his wife Sudabeh against his own son and sends Siyavash into the fire to prove himself, and so drives him out of Iran to his death. He quarrels with Rostam and orders him bound, and is only saved from the consequence by Rostam's forbearance. He continues the Avestan Kavi Usan under an evolved name, and no separate record is made for that form.

gods.name: Sudabeh
gods.description: Queen of Iran, wife of Kai Kavus, and the woman whose lie starts the long war. She wanted her stepson Siyavash and contrived to have him brought to the women's quarters, and made her offer, and he refused her - twice, and gently, and would not expose her. So she tore her own clothes and clawed her face and cried out that he had forced her; and when that was doubted she produced a dead child and said it was hers by him. Kai Kavus believed her far enough to put Siyavash to the ordeal, and he rode between two mountains of burning wood and came out unmarked; and the boy would not stay in Iran after it, and went over to Turan, and was murdered there. She is killed at last by Rostam, who comes into the palace and takes her out of the king's own arms and cuts her in two, and Kai Kavus does not stop him. She is an actor and not a monster, and she is not entered here as anyone's wife.

gods.name: Piran
gods.description: Vizier and commander of Turan under Afrasiyab, and the best man on the wrong side. He does not merely advise: he acts, and against his own king's interest, again and again. He receives Siyavash when he comes over the border and stands surety for him, and marries him to Afrasiyab's daughter Farangis, and gets him land to build a city on. When Garsivaz poisons the king's mind and Siyavash is taken, Piran rides to intercede and comes too late; and then he saves what is left - he stops Afrasiyab from killing the pregnant Farangis, takes her into his own house, and when the child Kai Khosrow is born he hides him among shepherds and keeps him alive, knowing what that child will grow up to do to Turan. He fights for Turan to the end and is killed by Gudarz in the great battle, and the Iranians bury him with honour.

gods.name: Rakhsh
gods.description: Rostam's stallion, and the only horse in Iran that did not sink under his hand when he pressed it on the back to test them. What he does he does himself. In the first of the seven labours, while Rostam sleeps in the reed-bed, a lion comes; and Rakhsh does not wake him but fights it alone, striking with the forehooves and biting through its head, and kills it - and is scolded for it afterwards, Rostam telling him he should have been woken. In the third labour Rakhsh knows the dragon is there and wakes him three times, and twice the beast is gone and Rostam threatens to kill him for it, and he wakes him a third time anyway, and this time it is seen; and when they fight, Rakhsh tears at the dragon's shoulders with his teeth while Rostam cuts off its head. At the end, before the pit that Shaghad has dug and lined with spears, he balks and will not go on - and Rostam, angry, drives him forward, and they go in together and die. He is stolen from Rostam at Samangan while he sleeps, which is what brings Rostam to Tahmina's city; but that is done to him and is not his doing, and it is for the lion, which he killed alone and which would have killed his rider, that he stands here.

gods.name: Grani
gods.description: Sigurd's grey stallion, of the stock of Sleipnir. An old one-eyed man met Sigurd as he went to choose a horse and told him to drive the whole herd into the river; and one alone swam it and came out on the far side, and that was Grani, and the old man was Odin. In the Völsunga saga he does the thing that turns the story. Gunnar wants Brynhild, who will have no man that cannot ride the fire round her hall; and Gunnar's own horse Goti will not go into it. So he asks for Grani - and Grani will not stir a foot for Gunnar. Only then do Sigurd and Gunnar change shapes, and Grani goes forward at once under Sigurd wearing Gunnar's face, and carries him through; and out of that deception comes the quarrel of the queens, and the oath-breaking, and Sigurd dead in his bed. The horse-refusal is the saga's telling and is not spelled out in the same way in every Eddic source, and it is given here as the saga's. In Guðrúnarkviða II it is Grani who brings the news: he comes back from the Thing with his head hanging and no rider on him, and Gudrun knows by that what has happened.

gods.name: Diomedes (of Argos)
gods.description: Son of Tydeus, lord of Argos, and after Achilles the best of the Achaeans at Troy. The fifth book of the Iliad is his: Athena takes the mist from his eyes and he goes through the Trojan line, and when Aphrodite comes down to carry Aeneas off he cuts her across the hand so that she drops her son and runs crying to Olympus - and then, with Athena herself in the car beside him holding the reins, he drives the spear into Ares, and the war-god bellows like nine or ten thousand men and goes up into the sky. He meets Glaucus between the lines and, finding their grandfathers were guest-friends, exchanges armour with him, bronze for gold. In the tenth book he goes out by night with Odysseus, takes Dolon, and kills Rhesus and twelve of his Thracians in their sleep. He wins the chariot race at Patroclus's games. The rest is later and is given as later: the taking of the Palladium out of Troy with Odysseus, his place in the horse, and the return in which Aphrodite pays him back, so that he cannot stay in Argos and goes to Italy, where cities are founded for him and he is given a cult on the Adriatic. He is not Diomedes of Thrace, who kept man-eating mares and was fed to them by Heracles, and who is another man entirely.

gods.name: Philoctetes
gods.description: Keeper of the bow and arrows of Heracles, given to him for lighting the pyre. On the way to Troy he was bitten in the foot by a snake at Chryse, and the wound would not close and stank, and he cried out so that the sacrifices could not be made; and the Greeks put him ashore on Lemnos and left him there and sailed on, and he lived nine years alone with the bow, shooting birds to eat. Then it was foretold that Troy could not be taken without the bow, or without the man, and Odysseus came back for it with Neoptolemus, and the whole of Sophocles' play is the struggle over whether it will be stolen, or begged, or given. He refuses; he is offered a passage home and takes it; and it is only at the end, and in Sophocles only when Heracles appears to him, that he changes his mind and consents to go to Troy - and it is that consent, and not his ownership of the bow, that he is entered here for. At Troy he was healed and killed Paris with it. The traditions differ over who came for him and how he was persuaded.

gods.name: Neoptolemus
gods.description: Son of Achilles, called also Pyrrhus, and fetched from Scyros because Troy was not to fall without him. He came late and did what his father had not lived to do. He was in the horse, and in the sack he killed Priam - the old man had fled to the altar of Zeus in his own courtyard, and Neoptolemus killed his son Polites in front of him and then dragged him through the blood of it and cut his throat at the altar, which is the act the Greeks themselves were said to have been punished for. He threw Astyanax from the wall, or was said to have done; and at Achilles' tomb he cut the throat of Priam's daughter Polyxena over it, which is the later tradition and is given as such. Afterwards he took Andromache, Hector's wife, as his prize, and was killed at Delphi in a quarrel over the sacrifices. His savagery is not softened here, and the classification of him as a principal actor is not praise.

gods.name: Pelias
gods.description: King in Iolcus, who had taken the throne from his half-brother and held it, and who had been warned by the oracle to beware of a man coming with one sandal. Jason came down from the mountain having lost one crossing a river, and Pelias knew him; and rather than kill him openly he sent him for the Golden Fleece in Colchis, at the far end of the sea, expecting he would not come back. That order is the Argonautica: the ship, the crew, the whole voyage exists because Pelias gave it. He came back, and with Medea. She showed the daughters of Pelias an old ram cut up and boiled in a cauldron with herbs and springing out a lamb, and told them they could do the same for their father; and they cut him up and boiled him, and he did not come out. He is not a background king of the Argonautic story - he is its cause, and he is a man and not a monster.

gods.name: Meleager
gods.description: Prince of Calydon, and the killer of the great boar that Artemis sent when his father forgot her at the sacrifice. He gathered the heroes of Greece for the hunt, and it was Atalanta who drew first blood, and Meleager who killed it - and he gave her the hide, for the wound was hers first, and because he loved her. His mother's brothers took it from her, saying no woman should carry it off, and he killed them for it. What follows differs by source. Homer has him withdraw from the fighting in a rage when his mother curses him, and come back only when his wife begs him, and get nothing for it. The later tradition has the firebrand: his life burned in it, and his mother Althaea, when she heard whom he had killed, took it out and put it on the fire, and he died as it burned through, far off and untouched. The two accounts are not the same story and are not made one here.

gods.name: Althaea
gods.description: Queen of Calydon and mother of Meleager, and the woman who killed her own son on purpose. When he was seven days old the Fates came to her hearth and said he would live as long as the brand then burning on it; and she snatched it out and quenched it and put it away in a chest, and kept it there for years. Then Meleager killed her brothers in the quarrel over the boar's hide - and she took the brand out of the chest and set it on the fire and stood and watched it burn, and her son died as it went. She had to choose between her brothers and her child and she chose her brothers, and the sources dwell on the choosing. Afterwards she hanged herself. She is not entered here as a mother who grieved but as one who decided.

gods.name: Agave
gods.description: Daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and mother of Pentheus. She would not have it that her sister Semele had lain with Zeus, and said the child was got by a mortal and the story was a lie - and Dionysus, coming back to Thebes, drove her and the women out onto Cithaeron in his frenzy. Pentheus went up to spy on them, and they took him for a lion in the pines; and Agave got him first, and set her foot on him, and tore his arm out of the shoulder while he was touching her face and telling her who he was, and the others pulled the rest of him apart. She came down carrying the head on her thyrsus and boasting of her hunting, and it was her father who made her look at it and see. The frenzy is the god's and the hands are hers, and the play does not let her off on either count; she was sent into exile after. Her disbelief is where it begins.

gods.name: Ino / Leucothea
gods.description: One being under two names and in two conditions - a woman of Thebes who became a goddess of the sea, and Homer says so himself. As Ino she was a daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and the second wife of Athamas, and she hated her stepchildren: in the usual account she got the women of the country to parch the seed-corn so that nothing came up, and then bribed the men sent to the oracle to bring back word that Phrixus must be sacrificed to end the famine - and it was to save him and his sister Helle that the golden ram came, which is where the Fleece comes from. She took in the infant Dionysus, her sister Semele's child, and Hera did not forgive it: Athamas was driven mad and killed their son Learchus, and Ino took the other, Melicertes, and went off a cliff into the sea with him in her arms. There she was made a goddess, and he with her - she Leucothea, the white goddess, and he Palaemon, whom the Isthmian games honour. In the fifth book of the Odyssey she comes up out of the water to Odysseus drowning on his raft and gives him her veil to keep him up, and Homer names her plainly: Ino Leucothea, daughter of Cadmus, who was once a mortal of human speech and now has her share of honour among the gods. That is the identity, and it is one, and no separate record is made for the goddess. The motives given her as a mortal vary from source to source and are not harmonised here. Roman writers came to identify Leucothea with Mater Matuta, but that is a later equation, and Mater Matuta is catalogued here as the Italic goddess she is, in her own right.

gods.name: Alcmaeon
gods.description: Son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle. His father, going to the war his mother had sold him to, left it on him: to avenge himself on her and to lead the sons of the dead back to Thebes when they were grown. He did both. He took the Epigoni to Thebes and it fell to them, which it had not to their fathers; and then he came home and killed his mother, and the Erinyes took him for it as they took Orestes, and drove him mad and out of Argos. He wandered a long time and was purified at last, on new land the river had thrown up that the sun had not shone on when the crime was done. But he had taken the necklace of Harmonia - the thing she had been bought with - and it went on doing what it did: he gave it to one wife and then wanted it back for another, and her brothers killed him for it. The killing of his mother is his own act, done under orders and chosen, and the record rests on it.

gods.name: Laocoön
gods.description: The Trojan priest who tried to stop the horse. In Virgil he comes running down from the citadel and tells them to trust nothing the Greeks leave behind, and throws his spear into the flank of it - and the belly booms hollow, and Virgil says that had the gods not been against them, he would have driven them to open it with steel, and Troy would be standing yet. Then two serpents come over the sea from Tenedos and take his two sons, and him with them when he goes to help, and crush them at the altar; and the Trojans, seeing it, conclude that he was punished for putting iron into a thing sacred to Athena, and pull down their own wall and bring the horse in. So the warning was his, and it nearly worked; and his death, which was not his doing, is what carried the horse through the gate. The earlier Greek tradition is not Virgil's. There he is a priest of Apollo, and the serpents come for an offence of his own that has nothing to do with the horse - that he had married, or lain with his wife in the god's precinct, against the god's will - and in some of those accounts it is only his sons who die, and he is left alive to see it. The two are not made one here.

gods.name: Penthesilea
gods.description: Queen of the Amazons, who brought her women to Troy after Hector was dead and the city had no one left to put in the field. She came, the tradition says, seeking to be cleansed of a killing of her own - she had shot her sister Hippolyte by accident in a hunt - and she came to fight, and she chose Troy, and she led. She went through the Greeks and drove them back to the ships and killed many of them, and then Achilles came out to her and they fought, and he ran her through and killed her horse under her. What is told afterwards is later, and is given as later: that he pulled off her helmet and saw her face and fell in love with the dead woman, and that when Thersites jeered at him for it he struck him dead with his fist. She is not entered here for what Achilles felt but for having raised an army and brought it and commanded it.

gods.name: Tarquinius Superbus
gods.description: Lucius Tarquinius the Proud, the seventh and last king of Rome in the Roman account. He came to the throne over his father-in-law's body - Servius Tullius, whom he had thrown down the senate-house steps and had killed in the street, with his own wife Tullia driving her carriage over the corpse afterwards. He ruled without the senate and without the law, put men to death for their property, and is remembered for the answer he sent his son by the messenger, walking in the garden and striking the heads off the tallest poppies with his stick and saying nothing. It was his son Sextus who raped Lucretia; and when she had told her family and killed herself, Brutus took the knife from the wound and the city rose, and the Tarquins were shut out and the Republic made. He spent the rest of his life trying to get back - through Lars Porsenna, and at Lake Regillus - and died at Cumae. This is the annalists' king, shaped to be everything the Republic was not, and it is given as tradition and not as biography.

gods.name: Sextus Tarquinius
gods.description: Son of Tarquinius Superbus, and the man whose crime ended the monarchy. He had been a guest in the house of Collatinus, his kinsman, and came back to it alone at night while Collatinus was with the army, and was received as a guest again; and in the night he came to Lucretia's room with a sword and told her that if she would not have him he would kill her and kill a slave and lay the body beside hers and say he had found them together - so that she would die shamed and could not even be pitied. She yielded to that and not to him. In the morning she sent for her father and her husband, told them what had been done and by whom, made them swear to punish it, and killed herself in front of them. Her death is not his exoneration and it is not a resolution of what he did to her. The city rose on it; the Tarquins were expelled; and the Republic dates itself from that. He was killed afterwards at Gabii in a private quarrel.

gods.name: Tullia Minor
gods.description: The younger daughter of Servius Tullius, and not to be confused with her sister. Servius had two daughters and both were called Tullia; he married the fierce one, Tullia Minor, to the mild Arruns Tarquinius, and the mild one, Tullia Major, to the fierce Lucius - and the pairing held nothing. Tullia Minor went to Lucius and told him she wanted a husband and not a partner in servitude, and the two of them made away with the spouses that stood between them - her own sister among them - and married. She pushed him to take the throne, and when he had gone to the senate house and thrown the old king down the steps, she drove into the Forum in her carriage and was the first to call him king; and going home she came on her father's body lying in the street, and told the driver to go on over it, and did, and carried the blood back on the wheels. Livy says the street was called the Vicus Sceleratus after it, the Street of Crime. Dionysius tells the murders differently, and the later writers make more of the carriage; the outline is Livy's.

gods.name: Appius Claudius
gods.description: Appius Claudius Crassus, the decemvir - one of the ten appointed to write down the law, who then would not lay the office down, and who is the one of the ten the tradition fastens on. Roman history is full of Appii Claudii and this record is that man and no other. He wanted Verginia, a centurion's daughter who was betrothed elsewhere, and could not have her; so he had a client of his claim in court that she was a slave born in his own household and had been passed off as free - and then sat as the judge on the case himself, and gave her to the claimant. Her father Verginius, brought from the army and given no hearing, asked leave to speak to her, took her aside among the shops of the Forum, and killed her with a butcher's knife rather than let the judgement stand. The army and the plebs rose, the Decemvirate fell, and Appius was thrown into prison, where the tradition has him kill himself before the trial. He is set down here as a principal actor, which is not praise.

gods.name: Lars Porsenna
gods.description: King of Clusium in Etruria, and the enemy of Rome in the year the Republic was born - Lars is an Etruscan title, lord, and it has stuck to his name. The exiled Tarquins came to him and he took up their cause and marched, and the Roman tradition then puts three things in his way: Horatius Cocles holding the wooden bridge alone while it was cut down behind him; Gaius Mucius, taken in his camp having killed the wrong man, thrusting his right hand into the fire in front of him and not moving his face; and the girl Cloelia, given as a hostage, swimming the Tiber with the others and getting away. And in the Roman telling it is Porsenna's own decisions that end it - he lets Mucius go, he gives Cloelia back her freedom and lets her choose companions, he makes peace and takes his army off, and Rome is never taken. That is the patriotic version and it should not be taken as settled history. Tacitus and Pliny preserve another: that Porsenna took the city, and that the terms he imposed forbade the Romans the use of iron except to till the ground. The three heroes may be what was told instead of a defeat.

gods.name: Decius Mus
gods.description: Publius Decius Mus, consul in 340 BC, who gave himself to the gods below to win a battle. Three generations of the family bore the name and the tradition gives the same act to more than one of them; this record is the consul of 340, at the Veseris in the Latin war, and the later Decii are not folded into him. He and his colleague Manlius had each dreamed that the general of one side and the army of the other were owed to the dead; and when his wing began to give way, Decius called the pontifex to him and repeated after him the words of the devotio, standing on a spear laid on the ground, in the toga girt in the Gabine fashion, and dedicated himself and the enemy's line together to Tellus and the Manes. Then he rode into the thick of the Latins and was killed there, and the Romans won, and believed they had won by it. This is the annalists and the priestly books, not documented history; what it records reliably is what the Romans believed a consul could do with his own death.

gods.name: Marcus Atilius Regulus
gods.description: Roman consul of the First Punic War, and the great Roman exemplum of a man keeping his word to his own destruction. The firm part is short: he was consul twice, he carried the war into Africa and won at first, and then his army was broken near Tunis by the Carthaginians under the Spartan Xanthippus, and he was taken alive. The famous part is later. The Romans told that Carthage sent him home on parole to argue for an exchange of prisoners, having sworn to return if it failed - and that he stood up in the senate and argued against the exchange, on the ground that Rome should not buy back a used-up old man at the price of young Carthaginian officers, and so argued away his own freedom; and that he then went back, as he had sworn, and was tortured to death, his eyelids cut away and himself kept from sleep, or rolled downhill in a barrel driven full of spikes. Polybius, who is the best source for the war, has none of this. The torture and the parole are later moralising, and are given here as that. It is for the choice, as Rome told it, that he stands here.

gods.name: Ragnar Loðbrók
gods.description: The great legendary viking of the Norse and Danish tradition. He killed the serpent that lay coiled about Thora's bower and won her by it, going against it in breeches boiled in pitch and rolled in sand - and it is from those shaggy breeches that the by-name loðbrók is said to come. Afterwards he married Aslaug. At the last, hearing that his sons had won more fame than he had, he had two ships built and sailed on England with them alone, out of pride and against his wife's warning; and he was wrecked and taken by King Ælla of Northumbria, and thrown into a pit of snakes. What he said there is what he is remembered for - that the piglets would grunt if they knew what the old boar suffered - and his sons came for the vengeance, and the tradition makes that the beginning of the great army. He is a legendary composite. The sagas gather to his name traditions that seem to belong to more than one ninth-century leader, and there is no single Ragnar who can be securely identified in the historical record; what is set down here is the saga tradition, and it is not offered as history. He is also written Ragnarr loðbrók and, in English, Ragnar Lothbrok.

gods.name: Aslaug / Kráka
gods.description: Daughter of Sigurd the dragon-slayer and Brynhild in the Ragnar tradition, and so the one figure who joins the Völsungs to the Ragnar cycle. Her foster-father Heimir hid her, an infant, inside a harp and carried her out of the wreck of that house; and the peasants who killed him for the gold found her, and reared her as their own, and called her Kráka, the crow, and kept her beauty hidden with tar and a hood. Ragnar's men saw her washing and told him, and he set her a test to come to him neither clothed nor naked, neither fasting nor fed, neither alone nor in company - and she came wrapped in a fishing-net with her hair down over it, biting an onion, with a dog at her heel; and he took her. She told him afterwards who her father was, and proved it when their son was born with the mark of a serpent in his eye. She warned him against the English voyage and he went anyway, and when he was dead she drove her sons to the vengeance. Kráka is the name she was hidden under and not another woman; she is also called Áslaug, and Randalín in the saga after she takes up arms.

gods.name: Hervör Angantýrsdóttir
gods.description: Daughter of the berserker Angantýr, born after his death, and no kind of woman her mother's house could keep. She would not learn embroidery; she took to weapons and to the woods and went out with raiders under a man's name. Then she went alone to Samsey, where her father and his eleven brothers were laid in the howes, and stood among the barrows at nightfall while they opened and the fire came out of them, and called her father up out of the ground and demanded the sword Tyrfing that was buried with him. He would not: he told her the sword was cursed, that it must kill a man every time it was drawn, that it would destroy her line. She stood there and asked again, and would not go without it, and said she feared no fire and no dead man. And he gave it to her. She is not her granddaughter, the later Hervör Heiðreksdóttir who held a fortress and died fighting the Huns; that is another woman and no record is made of her here.

gods.name: Angantýr Arngrímsson
gods.description: Eldest of the twelve berserker sons of Arngrim, and the keeper of the sword Tyrfing. He asked for Ingibjörg, the daughter of the king of Sweden, and Hjalmar the Brave wanted her too, and it came to a holmgang on Samsey: the twelve brothers against Hjalmar and Örvar-Odd. The brothers went into their berserk fit and the twelve fought, and all of them were killed, and Hjalmar with them - Angantýr and Hjalmar killed each other, and Odd alone walked off the island and carried the news. They were laid in the howes on Samsey with their weapons. Long afterwards his daughter Hervör came alone to the barrows and called him up, and he rose in the fire and tried to send her away, and told her the sword was cursed and would be the end of her kin; and when she would not go he gave it up to her. He is not the later Angantýr Heiðreksson who fought the Huns, who is another man of the same name in the same saga.

gods.name: Heidrek
gods.description: Grandson of Hervör and a king with Tyrfing, and a violent man from the beginning - he killed his own brother with a stone as a boy and was driven out for it, and his father's parting counsels he broke one by one, on purpose. He came to a kingdom in the end. A man called Gestumblindi, who had offended him, came to buy his peace, and Heidrek offered him the choice of trial or riddles; and the two of them sat and the riddles went on, and Gestumblindi asked them and Heidrek answered them all - until the last, which was what Odin whispered in Baldr's ear before he was laid on the pyre. Then Heidrek knew who was sitting across from him, and struck at him with Tyrfing, breaking the peace he had given; and Odin turned into a hawk and went out, and cursed him as he went, that the meanest of slaves should be his death. And so it was: his own thralls came on him in the night and killed him and took the sword. The sources are not identical in what they narrate and the account here is the saga's. He is written Heiðrekr in the normalized Old Norse.

gods.name: Hrolf Kraki
gods.description: King at Lejre in the Danish legendary tradition, of the line of the Scyldings, and the centre of a court of champions as Arthur is of another. He is the Hrothulf of Beowulf. He went into Sweden to get from King Adils the gold that was owed him and the treasure his father had lost there; and coming away, pursued, with Adils's riders behind him, he sowed the gold out of his hand across the Fyrisvellir as he rode, and the Swedes got down to pick it up, and let him go - and when Adils himself stooped for the ring Sviagris, Hrolf cut at him and left him bowed. The end came from inside: his half-sister Skuld and her husband Hjörvarð brought an army against him at Lejre with sorcery behind it, and the champions fought until the dead came back up out of the ground against them, and Hrolf was killed in his own hall with his men round him. He is also written Hrólfr kraki.

gods.name: Bodvar Bjarki
gods.description: The greatest of Hrolf Kraki's champions, and a man - the bear is in him and about him, but he is not one. His father Björn had been cursed into a bear's shape by a queen he refused, and hunted and killed in it, and Bodvar was got before that. He came to Lejre and killed the winged troll-beast that had been coming on the hall at Yule, and then took the coward Hott, who had been pelted with bones in the corner, and made him drink the beast's blood and set him on his feet, and Hott became the warrior Hjalti. In the last battle at Lejre he is not to be seen among the men - and a great bear goes before Hrolf's line, killing more than any two champions, taking spears without falling. Then Hjalti misses him and goes into the hall and finds him sitting there, still, and wakes him and reproaches him - and Bodvar says that he has done the king more good sitting than he can now do standing; and the bear is gone from the field, and the line breaks, and they all die. Whether the bear is his fylgja, his sent-out spirit, or another thing again, the sources do not agree. He is written Bǫðvarr bjarki, and Böðvar.

gods.name: Starkad
gods.description: The old warrior of the north, given three men's lives and cursed to disgrace himself in each. In the saga he is brought before an assembly of the gods on an island, and Odin gives and Thor takes away, turn for turn: three lifespans, and a shameful deed in every one of them; victory in every battle, and a wound in every battle; poetry, and no memory of what he composes; the favour of the great, and the hatred of the common people. Then the first of the deeds is done - King Vikar's men draw lots for a sacrifice and the lot falls on the king, and it is arranged as a mockery, a calf's gut for a rope and a reed for a spear; and Starkad strikes and says the words, and the reed is a spear in his hand and the gut is a withy, and the king is hanged in earnest. He served kings all his long life and betrayed some of them, and at the end, old and half-blind and weary of living, he carried gold about his neck and offered it to a man to take his head off, and one did. Saxo Grammaticus has him too, as Starcatherus, and the same core is there - the giant blood, the enormous age, the killing of Wikarus - but Saxo makes him a stern old moralist raging against soft living and foreign fashions, where the saga makes him a man the gods have ruined. They disagree on his ancestry, on how many arms he was born with or had cut from him, on which kings he served and on how the shameful deeds are counted. They are one figure under two tellings and one record is made; the disagreements are set down and not smoothed away. He is written Starkaðr.

gods.name: Örvar-Odd
gods.description: Odd of Hrafnista, called Örvar-Odd - Örvar is the arrows, for the three that never missed and always came back to his hand, and Odd is the man's name. A völva came to the farm when he was young and went round the house saying what would come to each of them, and he would not have his told and hit her with a stick; and she told him anyway: that he would live three hundred years and travel far, and that he would die at home at Berurjóðr, and that his horse Faxi would be the death of him. So he took the horse out and killed it and buried it under a cairn of stones, and left, and did not come back. He was three hundred years about the world - a viking, a giant-slayer, a man among Bjarmians and Permians and in Ireland and the Holy Land, at the holmgang on Samsey where Hjalmar died. And at the end, an old man, he came back to Berurjóðr to look at the place, and walked over the ground where the cairn had been, and struck his foot against a horse's skull sticking up out of it; and an adder came out of the skull and bit him in the leg, and he lay down and made his death-song and died. Everything he did to escape it was the road to it. He is written Örvar-Oddr, and in English Arrow-Odd; the English is a translation and not his name.

gods.name: Peleus
gods.description: King of the Myrmidons, and a man twice exiled for a death. With his brother Telamon he killed their half-brother Phocus - by a discus at the games, the accounts say, though they differ on whether the throw went wrong or was meant - and their father drove them both out. He was purified in Phthia and married there; and then at the Calydonian boar-hunt he threw his javelin and killed his own host Eurytion, who had purified him, and was exiled a second time for it, and had to be cleansed again. He was left on Pelion by Acastus without his sword and nearly killed by the centaurs, and Chiron gave him the sword back. And he took Thetis, who was a goddess and did not want him: he caught her on the shore and held on while she turned in his arms into fire and water and a lion and a serpent, and did not let go until she gave way and took her own shape and consented. It is not as Achilles's father that he is entered here.

gods.name: Helenus
gods.description: Son of Priam, brother of Hector, and the seer of Troy - and he is entered here not for foreseeing but for what he chose to do with it. After Paris was dead he asked for Helen and she was given to Deiphobus instead, and he left the city in anger and went up onto Ida; and there Odysseus took him. What follows is what matters: he told the Greeks the conditions on which Troy could be taken - that they must fetch Philoctetes and the bow of Heracles from Lemnos, that they must bring Neoptolemus out of Scyros, and, in the tellings that include it, that the Palladium must be taken out of the citadel. They did those things and the city fell. The sources do not agree whether he was captured and made to speak, or came over of his own will and offered it, and that difference is not settled here. Afterwards he was Neoptolemus's man and had Andromache and a share of Epirus, which is the later tradition and is given as such.

gods.name: Laomedon
gods.description: King of Troy before Priam, and the man who twice would not pay what he had promised. Apollo and Poseidon served him for a year and built the walls of the city, and when the year was up he refused them their wages and threatened to cut off their ears and sell them; and the two gods sent a plague and a sea-monster on him for it, and the oracle said his daughter Hesione must be chained on the shore for the beast. Heracles came by and offered to kill it for the immortal horses that Zeus had given the house in payment for Ganymede - and killed it, and Laomedon refused him too. So Heracles came back with ships and took Troy and killed Laomedon and all his sons but one, and gave Hesione to Telamon; and the boy he left alive was ransomed by his sister and was called Priam after it, the bought one. The city that falls in the Iliad was sacked once already, and the enmity of the gods it goes down under begins with this man. He is not entered here as anyone's father.

gods.name: Amphitryon
gods.description: Son of Alcaeus, and the general of the war against the Taphians. He killed his uncle Electryon by accident - he threw his club at a cow that had broken from the herd and it came back off her horns and struck the old man dead - and was driven out of Mycenae for it, and went to Thebes and was purified by Creon. Alcmene, betrothed to him, would not have him until her brothers, whom the Taphians had killed, were avenged; so he built the alliance and made the war. He bought Creon's help by ridding Thebes of the Teumessian fox, which could not be caught, with the hound Laelaps, which could not fail to catch - and Zeus turned them both to stone rather than settle it - and he brought in Cephalus and Panopeus and Heleius and took the fleet out. The war was not won by his arms. Pterelaus could not be killed while one golden hair grew on his head, and his own daughter Comaetho, who had fallen in love with Amphitryon, pulled it out; and the islands fell. Amphitryon took them - and then put Comaetho to death for the killing of her father, though it was her act that had given him the victory. He came home to find Alcmene already with child by Zeus, who had come in his shape. His admission here rests on the war and on that judgement, and not on his marriage or on the boy he reared.

gods.name: Nestor
gods.description: The old king of Pylos, who had outlived two generations of men and ruled among the third, and who at Troy is the voice the kings listen to. He remembers the men who came before - the Lapiths, the fight with the centaurs, the cattle-raid on the Epeans - and he is always telling them so, and the poem lets him, and lets him be a little long about it. But he is not there for decoration. When the Greeks are being beaten back on the ships and Achilles will not come out, it is Nestor who takes Patroclus aside and puts it to him: that if Achilles will not fight, he should send Patroclus out in his armour, so that the Trojans might take him for Achilles and give ground. Patroclus goes to Achilles with it, and gets the armour, and goes out, and is killed - and it is Patroclus dead that brings Achilles back into the war and Hector to his end. The whole turn of the Iliad comes out of that counsel. He came home from Troy safely, one of the few, and Telemachus finds him at Pylos in his old age, sacrificing on the shore.

gods.name: Sarpedon (of Lycia)
gods.description: King of the Lycians and the best of Troy's allies, a son of Zeus by Laodamia the daughter of Bellerophon in Homer's account. He speaks the clearest statement in the Iliad of what a lord is for: he asks Glaucus why it is that they are given the best seats and the full cups and the great estate by the river, and answers himself - that they are given them so that they will stand in the front rank where the fighting is worst, and that since no man escapes death in any case they may as well go forward and give glory to another or take it themselves. He is first over the Achaean wall, tearing the battlement down with his hands. Patroclus kills him; and Zeus, watching, thinks of snatching his son out of the battle, and Hera tells him that if he does it every god will want the same, and he lets him die - and rains tears of blood on the ground for him, and has Sleep and Death carry the body home to Lycia to be buried. He is not the Cretan Sarpedon, the son of Europa and brother of Minos and Rhadamanthus, who was driven out of Crete after quarrelling with Minos and went to rule in Asia Minor; the mythographers, noticing the two, tried to make them one by giving the Cretan a life of three generations, or else strung them out over several men of the name. This record is the Iliadic Lycian, and the Cretan is left as he is.

gods.name: Beowulf
gods.description: The Geat who came over the sea to Heorot because he had heard what was happening there. He would not use a weapon on Grendel - the thing fought with its hands and had no skill of arms, and so he would meet it as it came, and it seemed to him no honour to do otherwise - and he lay awake and waited and took its arm off at the shoulder with his grip. When the mother came for her son and took Æschere, he went down into the mere after her, a whole day's swim to the bottom, and his own borrowed sword would not bite; and he took an old sword from the wall of her hall, made by giants, and killed her with it, and the blade melted afterwards in her blood like ice. Then he went home, and the poem leaves fifty years out. He was king of the Geats when a dragon woke, and he was old and he went to it anyway - and killed it, with Wiglaf beside him and no one else, and died of the wound. What is set down of him is not his strength only but what he chose: to fight unarmed, to go down into the water, and at the end, knowing what it would cost, to go out to the barrow himself.

gods.name: Grendel
gods.description: The thing that came out of the moors against Heorot. The poem calls him of the kin of Cain, of the race God cast out for a brother's killing, and says it was the sound of the hall that he could not bear - the harp and the singing and the men glad together - and that he came in the night for it. For twelve winters he took men out of that hall and no one could stop him and no one could come to terms with him, for he would take no wergild and would not treat. Beowulf waited for him in the dark and caught the hand he put out, and held it until the sinews sprang; and Grendel tore loose and went off over the moor with his arm gone and died in his mother's water. What he looked like the poem does not really say. It calls him a shadow-walker and a fen-dweller and a man-shape, larger than a man, and leaves the rest; and he is not made into a troll or an ogre or one of a kind here, because the poem does not.

gods.name: Grendel's Mother
gods.description: The mother of Grendel, and no name of her own in the poem - which does not make her less one being. She is of the same cast-out line, and she lives under the water in a hall the fire does not go out in, and she comes to Heorot the night after her son is dead. She takes one man and takes him on purpose: Æschere, who was Hrothgar's closest counsellor and dearest friend, and she takes back her son's arm from where they had hung it, and goes. That is a feud-killing done by the same rules the men of the poem live by - a life for a life, and the best one they had - and the poem does not pretend not to know it. In her hall Beowulf's borrowed sword Hrunting would not cut her, and she had him down with a knife out before he got up and found the giants' sword on the wall and killed her with that. The Old English calls her ides aglæcwif, which is not 'hag' - ides is a lady, and aglæca is a word the poem also uses of Beowulf himself. She is set down as a monster because the poem makes her a being not of mankind, of Grendel's kind; not because avenging a son is monstrous, which in that world it is not.

gods.name: Hrothgar
gods.description: King of the Danes, of the Scylding line, who built Heorot - the best of halls, and the gift-giving and the singing in it are what brought Grendel out of the moor. Twelve years he sat in it by day and could not hold it by night, and gave what he had and took counsel and got nothing for it, and the poem does not spare him: he wept, and he was old. When Beowulf came he knew him and took him and gave him everything for the killing, and gave more when the mother was dead; and then he said the thing that is remembered of him, standing with the hilt of the giants' sword in his hand - the long speech about the man who is given everything and grows so full of himself that he cannot see the end coming, and about how sickness or the sword or age take it all back, and how the young man now standing in his hall should think of it. He is uncle to Hrothulf, who sits beside him and who is the same figure the archive catalogues as Hrolf Kraki; no second record is made of him.

gods.name: Wiglaf
gods.description: The young kinsman of Beowulf who did not run. When the old king went to the barrow against the dragon he took eleven men with him, and when the fire came they went into the wood - all of them but one. Wiglaf had never been in a battle beside him before. He stood and said what he said to the others, that they had taken his gifts and his mail and his rings and had promised him this, and that he would rather burn beside his lord than carry his shield home; and he went into the smoke. His shield went in the flame and he took cover behind Beowulf's, and he struck the dragon low, under the head where it was soft, and the fire went out of it; and Beowulf got his knife into it and it died. Then Wiglaf washed him and heard his last words and took the ring and the collar from him. He told the ones who came back out of the wood what they were, and said the Geats had lost more than a king. The record rests on the choosing, and not on his being anyone's man.

gods.name: Hygelac
gods.description: King of the Geats, Beowulf's lord and his mother's brother, and the man whose death sets up everything that comes after in the poem. He took a fleet against the Frisians and the Franks and was killed there, and the raid failed; and Beowulf swam home out of it with thirty suits of armour on his arm, and was offered the kingdom and would not take it over Hygelac's son, and served the boy until he was killed too. Then Beowulf reigned fifty years, and at the end the Geats look at the feuds Hygelac's raid opened and know what is coming for them when their king is dead. The raid is the one place where the poem seems to touch a datable event. Gregory of Tours records a ruler he calls Chlochilaicus who came against Frankish territory in about 521 and was killed there, and the Liber Monstrorum speaks of a Huiglaucus, king of the Geats, whose bones were kept as a wonder because of their size; scholars commonly take these to be the same tradition. It is an identification made by readers and not a statement any of the sources make, and it is given here as that.

gods.name: Kriemhild
gods.description: The centre of the Nibelungenlied, and the exact reverse of the woman she descends from. She married Siegfried and he was murdered - speared in the back at a spring by Hagen, with her brothers' knowledge - and she found the body at her door in the morning; and then she sat in Worms for thirteen years while they took the Nibelung hoard from her and Hagen sank it in the Rhine. She married Etzel to reach them. She brought her brothers and their men to his court, and would not be turned from it, and the hall was set alight and the Burgundians were killed to a man in it; and at the end she took Siegfried's sword and struck off Hagen's head with her own hand, and old Hildebrand killed her for it. Siegfried is the continental form of the hero this archive catalogues as Sigurd, Gunther is the figure catalogued as Gunnar Gjúkason, Brünhild the one catalogued as Brynhild, and no second records are made for them. Kriemhild and Gudrun Gjúkadóttir come out of the same heroic matter and have gone opposite ways: Gudrun avenges her brothers upon her husband, and Kriemhild avenges her husband upon her brothers. The loyalty, the motive and the act are inverted, and they are two records.

gods.name: Hagen von Tronje
gods.description: Gunther's man, and the dark engine of the Nibelungenlied. He is not the king's brother but his vassal, of Tronje, and he serves the house and not the man. It was he who got out of Kriemhild where Siegfried could be killed - the one spot on his back the linden-leaf had covered when he bathed in the dragon's blood - and had her sew a cross on the coat over it, and speared him there at the spring while he stooped to drink, and had the body laid at her door. He took the Nibelung hoard from her and sank it in the Rhine, and no one has had it since. When Kriemhild called them to Etzel's court he knew what it was and told them so and went anyway, and threw the chaplains overboard on the way to see if the prophecy would hold. In the hall he killed her child in front of her. Taken alive at the end, he would not say where the gold was while a lord of Burgundy lived; and when Gunther's head was brought to him he said now no one knew but he and God, and she should never have it - and she killed him with Siegfried's sword. He descends from Högni of the Norse poems, who is not separately catalogued; but the brother has become a vassal, the accomplice has become the murderer himself, the gold has become the centre of the thing, and he dies at the hands of a woman Högni never faced. Enough has changed to make a second record.

gods.name: Skuld Helgadóttir
gods.description: The half-sister who destroyed Hrolf Kraki. In Hrólfs saga kraka she is the daughter of King Helgi by a woman of the elves, and there is that in her - she is called a sorceress, and cruel, and not altogether of this world. She was married to Hjörvarð, who held his land of Hrolf and paid tribute for it, and she would not have it; she worked on him for years until he would move, and then they came to Lejre with an army at Yule. What she brought was not only men. The saga has her sitting in a black tent working the seiðr while the fighting went on, and sending against the champions a boar the size of a bull and men who had been killed already and got up again; and Bǫðvar Bjarki's bear went from the field, and the line broke, and Hrolf and his champions were killed in the hall. Saxo tells the fall of the king without so much of the sorcery, and the two accounts are not made one here. She is not Skuld of the Norns, who is the third of the three at the well and is catalogued with them; the name is the same and the woman is not. Hostility and sorcery do not make her a monster; she is an actor, and set down as one.

gods.name: Sanasar
gods.description: The first of the four generations of the Armenian oral epic called Sasna Tsrer, the Daredevils of Sassoun. He and his twin Baghdasar were born to Tsovinar - who is catalogued here as a goddess of the waters - after she drank from a spring, and the caliph who had married her would have killed the boys for it; and they went north into the mountains and would not be brought back. Sanasar went down under the sea, in the way of the epic, and found there the horse Jalali, that comes to no one else, and the Lightning Sword, and the armour; and he came up with them and chose the place among the crags and built Sassoun, and the line and the house and the name all begin with him. He is not one half of a pair of twins here: it is his going down and his coming up and his choosing of the place that makes the epic possible. The cycle was carried by singers for centuries and was not written down until 1873; it is set against the Arab caliphate and it is not a chronicle of it.

gods.name: Mher the Great
gods.description: Մեծ Մհեր, Mets Mher, and called Lion-Mher for what he did: he met the lion that was holding the road and had been eating the people who came along it, and took its jaws in his two hands and tore it in half, and went through. He is the son of Sanasar and the father of David, and the second of the epic's four generations - the one that holds Sassoun by main strength while it can. He fought Msra Melik, the lord of Msr in the epic, and made a peace with him and afterwards went to Msr and stayed there, and the country was left open behind him, and it is that leaving that his son has to come back and undo. His name is not an accident: Mher comes from Mihr, the Armenian form of Mithra, and the god Mihr is catalogued in this archive separately as an Armenian deity. The hero of the epic is a man, and a late one, in a Christian-era oral poem; he is not the god under a later name and the two are not merged here.

gods.name: David of Sassoun
gods.description: Դավիթ Սասունցի, Davit Sasuntsi, and the centre of the whole epic - the one the cycle is named for in most of the telling of it. Born after his father Mher had gone to Msr, he was reared among people who did not know what to do with him, a boy too strong to be safe, breaking what he touched and killing what he hunted; and he came into himself when the tax-gatherers of Msra Melik came to Sassoun for forty years of arrears and he threw them out. Then Msra Melik came with an army, and David went out to meet him alone, and would not strike him while he slept, and gave him his three blows first because that was the bargain - and took his own, and split him and the seven mattresses and the millstone he had hidden under. He is not a general and the epic is not a campaign: he is impulsive and generous and easy to trick, and the poem loves him for it. The Sassoun cycle is oral tradition, written down from singers in the nineteenth century, and is not offered here as the history of the Arab wars it remembers.

gods.name: Mher the Younger
gods.description: Փոքր Մհեր, Pokr Mher, David's son and the last of the four generations, and the one the epic ends on. He is as strong as any of them and there is nowhere for it to go. He quarrels with his father and they fight and are parted; and afterwards, riding, he finds that the ground will not hold him - the earth opens under his horse's feet wherever he goes, because it is worn out and full of injustice and cannot bear a man of that weight any longer. So he rides to the Raven's Rock at Van and speaks the word and the rock opens, and he goes in with his horse and it shuts behind him. He is there still, in the telling, and comes out once a year to see whether the world has grown honest enough to carry him; and finding it has not, he goes back in. He is not Mher the Great, who is his grandfather and two generations away from him, and no record joins them. His name, like his grandfather's, descends from Mihr, the Armenian form of Mithra, who is catalogued here as a god and is not this man.

gods.name: Moremi
gods.description: Moremi Ajasoro of Ile-Ife, who ended the raids by walking into them. The Ugbo were coming out of the forest against Ife and taking whatever they wanted, and no one would stand to them, because they came covered head to foot in raffia and grass and were taken for spirits and not men. Moremi went to the river and vowed to the spirit Esimirin that if she were shown how to save the city she would give whatever was asked of her. Then she let herself be taken. She was carried off among the captives and made much of, and she stayed with them and watched and learned what she had gone to learn - that under the raffia there were men, and that grass burns. She got away and came back to Ife and told them, and when the Ugbo came again the people met them with torches and the disguises went up and the raiders were seen for what they were, and it was finished. Then she went back to the river to pay, and what was asked of her was her only son, Oluorogbo. The traditions do not all end the same way: some say the boy was given and died, and some that he went up out of the world afterwards, or came back, and the Edi festival at Ife keeps the memory of the debt and the paying of it every year. The Ugbo are a forest people of the Ife region and are not the modern Igbo of southeastern Nigeria, with whom the name is often and wrongly confused.

gods.name: Sundiata Keita
gods.description: The hero of the Mande epic, the boy who could not walk. His mother was mocked for it, and when she was refused a handful of baobab leaves and came back weeping, he called for the iron rods, and they bent under him like bowstrings; and he stood, and went out and pulled up the baobab whole and set it down at his mother's door so that she would never ask anyone for leaves again. He was driven into exile with her and wandered for years among the kings of the Sahel, and while he was gone Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso took the Mande country. He came back at the head of an alliance and broke him at Kirina, and out of that the Mali of the epic is made. A historical Sundiata almost certainly lies under this - a thirteenth-century ruler who founded Mali - but what is set down here is the epic and not a chronicle of him: the crippled childhood, the iron rods and the baobab belong to the tradition, which is sung and not written, and which no two jeliw tell alike. He is also called Sunjata, Son-Jara, Sundjata, and Mari Djata.

gods.name: Sogolon Kedjou
gods.description: Sundiata's mother, and not the Buffalo Woman. The two are distinct and the epic is careful about it: Do Kamissa, the buffalo woman of Do, was an old woman cheated of her inheritance who took a buffalo's shape and ravaged the country - and when the hunters came for her she told them herself how she could be killed, on the condition that when the king offered them their reward they should refuse every beauty in Do and ask for the ugliest girl in it. That girl was Sogolon, hunchbacked and unlovely, and the tellings say variously that she carried the buffalo's wraith, or its power, or its inheritance, or was joined to it in spirit; but she is not Do Kamissa and no telling makes her so. What she does is her own. She bore the mockery of Sassouma Bérété for years and the shame of a son who could not walk; and it was her weeping, when she was refused the baobab leaves, that put him on his feet. She took her children into exile and kept them alive through the long wandering from court to court; and it was her death at Mema, and the ground he had to buy to bury her in, that freed him to go home. She is not entered here as anyone's mother. She is also called Sogolon Condé and Sogolon Kèdjou.

gods.name: Soumaoro Kanté
gods.description: King of Sosso, and the man Sundiata had to break. He took the Mande kingdoms one after another while Sundiata was in exile, and he ruled them hard; and the epic makes him a great sorcerer - he kept a chamber of fetishes with the heads of the kings he had killed in it, and a balafon no one else could play, and he could put on other shapes. He took Sundiata's griot Balla Fasséké and would not give him back. And he took Fakoli's wife, who was his own nephew's wife, and lost Fakoli to the other side for it, which cost him the war. At Kirina he was struck with an arrow tipped with the spur of a white cock, which was the one thing his power could not stand against, and his hold broke and he was gone. He is a man, and a king, and a sorcerer; sorcery is something he does and not something he is, and he is set down here as a human antagonist and not as a monster. A historical ruler of Sosso may lie under him, but the documentation is thin, and the epic is not his biography. He is also called Sumanguru Kanté and Sumaworo.

gods.name: Nana Triban
gods.description: Sundiata's half-sister, and the one who found out how Soumaoro could be killed. When Sosso came against the Mande her brother Dankaran Touman sent her to Soumaoro to buy peace, and she was made his wife and kept at his court. She did not sit there. She worked on him and drew him out and got from him, little by little, the thing no one else had - the secret of his tana, the taboo his power rested on, and what could undo it. Then she got out. She came across country to Sundiata in exile with Balla Fasséké, and told him what she had, and the arrow that killed Soumaoro at Kirina was made on what she said. She is not a sister handed over in a bargain; she is the intelligence the war was won on, and the record rests on that.

gods.name: Balla Fasséké
gods.description: Sundiata's jeli - his griot, his voice and his memory - given to him as a boy so that the two should belong to each other. Soumaoro took him, and kept him, and it is in Sosso that the great scene happens: he found his way into the fetish chamber and to Soumaoro's balafon, which no one but the king might touch, and he played it, and played it so well that Soumaoro, coming in furious, could not kill him for it and kept him instead as his own praise-singer. He stayed in that house and used his eyes. He escaped with Nana Triban and came to Sundiata, and what the two of them carried between them was what brought Soumaoro down at Kirina. The tellings divide the discovery differently - some give the secret to Nana Triban, some to Balla Fasséké, some to the two of them together - and that variation is part of the tradition and is not resolved here. He is also written Bala Faséké Kouyaté.

gods.name: Fakoli
gods.description: Soumaoro's own nephew and his best general, and the man whose going over decided the war. He had served Sosso and fought its battles and was reckoned to have power of his own; and Soumaoro took his wife from him. That was the end of it. Fakoli left, and took his men with him, and went to Sundiata; and the alliance that beat Sosso at Kirina was built with him in it. The epic makes a great deal of what he was worth - a small man with an enormous head, who could eat what nine men ate and fight what nine men fought - and the point of the story is that Soumaoro's own act made an enemy of the one man he could not afford to lose. He is given various clan names in the tellings, Fakoli Koroma and Fakoli Doumbia among them, and the jeliw of different lines claim him differently.

gods.name: Manas
gods.description: The hero of the Kyrgyz epic that bears his name, and the figure the whole tradition is built on. He is born to a childless couple late and comes into strength impossibly early; he gathers the scattered Kyrgyz and the forty tribes under one hand and brings them back to the Ala-Too; he takes the choson, the forty companions, and makes war on the Kitay and the Kalmak; and at the height of it he leads the Great Campaign east, as far as Beijing in the fullest tellings. He is wounded to death on the way back from it and dies at home, and his tomb is hidden or built false so that his enemies cannot find it. He is a legendary figure, not a documented king: no Manas can be securely identified in the historical record. And there is no one Manas: the epic is sung by manaschi, and the great recensions differ enormously - Sagymbay Orozbakov's and Sayakbay Karalaev's are not the same poem - so no single sequence of events can be given as the version. The Islamic colouring belongs to the later layers of transmission and not to every part of the poem.

gods.name: Kanikey
gods.description: Manas's wife, and the reason there is a second book. She is not there to be married. She is the one with the judgement in that house: she equips the forty companions out of her own wealth when they go to war, she sees what Manas will not see about the men around him, and she says so - she warns him against the kinsmen who will betray him, and is not listened to. When he is dead and those same kinsmen come for what is left, she does the thing the whole rest of the epic depends on: she takes the infant Semetey and goes, out of the country and into Bukhara to her father's people, and keeps the boy alive there for years while the usurpers hold the land. The Semetey cycle exists because she ran. Also written Kanykei.

gods.name: Almambet
gods.description: The prince who came over. He is born among Manas's enemies - the recensions name his people differently, and the labels Kitay, Kalmak and Chinese are not used consistently across them, so the ethnic terms are best taken as the epic's rather than as ethnography - and he leaves them: he quarrels with his own father, refuses the faith and the loyalty he was born to, and comes to Manas, who takes him as a sworn brother. He becomes the best of the forty, and the most trusted, and the loneliest: he has no people to go back to, and the poem does not let him forget it. He leads the vanguard of the Great Campaign and dies in it. His conversion and his exile are given in the recensions with different weight and different detail, and are given here as theirs.

gods.name: Semetey
gods.description: Manas's son by Kanikey, and the hero of the second of the three great cycles. He was carried out of the country as an infant when his father's kinsmen seized what Manas had held, and he grew up in Bukhara not knowing whose son he was, and was told at last; and he came back. He took his father's horse and his father's arms and his father's men where he could find them, put down the usurpers, and won back Talas and the inheritance; and he hunted down Kongurbay, whom his father had not finished with, and killed him. His own end is dark and the tellings differ - he vanishes, or is betrayed, or is taken away - and his son Seytek carries the third cycle. He is not a coda to his father. The Semetey is a poem in its own right and he is its hero. Also written Semetei.

gods.name: Kongurbay
gods.description: Manas's chief enemy, and a man - a khan of the Kitay in the epic's terms, a great warrior with a great horse, and no monster. He fights Manas across the length of the poem, is beaten and comes back, and commands the forces that meet the Great Campaign in the east. In the major recensions he has a hand in Manas's death: some give him the mortal wound outright, in the fighting or in an ambush on the road home. But the epic does not put it all on him, and the record should not either - the poem is at least as interested in the treachery of Manas's own kinsmen, who turn on him at home, and the tellings apportion the blame between the two differently. He outlives Manas and is hunted down at last by Semetey. Also written Konurbay and Qoñurbay.

gods.name: Amirani
gods.description: The chained hero of the Georgian mountains, known across Kartvelian tradition - in Svaneti, in Khevsureti, in Mingrelia and in the Georgian lowlands - in tellings that do not agree with one another. He is born with extraordinary strength, and in most of them with something on his body that marks him: a sign, or teeth of iron, or a birth cut from his dying mother. He kills the devi and the giants and the serpents, and clears the country of them. And then he goes too far: he defies Ghmerti, God, and challenges him or breaks faith with him, and for that he is chained - to a rock, or inside a cave, in the high Caucasus, with an eagle at his liver or his heart. His dog lies by him and licks at the chain and wears it thin; and every year, on a certain day, the smiths of the country strike their anvils, and the chain is made whole again, and it begins over. Some tellings say he will get free at the end of things. The parallel with Prometheus is real and is worth noting, but he is not derived from Prometheus and is not a Greek import: the Caucasian tradition stands on its own. His parentage varies by region - in the Svan telling his mother is the goddess Dali, and that is the Svan telling and not every one.

gods.name: Dali
gods.description: The goddess of the hunt in Svan tradition, and the owner of the animals that are hunted. She lives high on the crags where men cannot easily go, golden-haired, and the game on the mountain is hers and is not taken without her leave. She takes hunters as her lovers, and while a man has her favour he cannot miss and cannot fall; and the conditions are absolute - he must tell no one, he must not boast, he must not go to his wife while he is hers, he must not take more than she allows. Men who break them are thrown from the rock face, or lose their footing on a ledge they have crossed a hundred times, or simply do not come back. In the Svan telling she is the mother of Amirani, cut from her body by the hunter who fathered him. She is specifically Svan and is not presented here as a deity of all the Georgian regions; hunt-goddesses of related function are known elsewhere in the Caucasus, and she is not merged with them.

gods.name: Kopala
gods.description: A ghvtis-shvili - a child of God, one of the divine beings the eastern Georgian mountain religion sets under Ghmerti and above men - and the great slayer of the devi. He is not a man who was raised to a god; he is of that order from the beginning, and the distinction matters. The devi held the land and the waters and the passes, and Kopala went against them with his mace, and broke them and drove them out and threw them down, and so made the country fit for people to live in; the tradition of Khevsureti and Pshavi is emphatic that men hold their ground because he cleared it. He has his own shrines in those mountains and his own festivals and his own priests, and the tradition is not dead: what is set down here is what is publicly published of it, and no more. His scope is Khevsur and Pshav and he is not a pan-Georgian deity.

gods.name: Iakhsar
gods.description: A ghvtis-shvili of the Khevsur and Pshav mountains, of the same divine order as Kopala and his companion in the war on the devi - and not merely his companion. What is his own is the water. He went down after the devi into the lake, or the pool, into the element they held and men do not hold, and killed what was in it; and being down there he was caught, or defiled by it, and could not come out clean - and had to be brought up and purified before he could stand in his own shrine again. He has shrines of his own in that country and is invoked in his own right. He is entered as minor beside Kopala, who is the primary figure of the pair in the tradition and the one the devi-clearing is chiefly told of; that is a statement about their standing in the eastern mountain religion and not a judgement on him. Also written Iakhsari.

gods.name: Satanaya
gods.description: The mother of the Narts and the mind of them, and the one figure every tradition of the epic has: Satana to the Ossetians, Seteney-Guaša to the Circassians, Satanei-Guasha to the Abkhaz, and the same woman under all of them. She does not age as others do, and she knows what is coming - the story shared across the traditions is that she alone read the winter that was coming and stored against it, so that when the famine came the Narts ate out of her granaries and lived. The other shared story is the one that matters most. A herdsman across the river saw her washing on the bank and was overcome, and his seed fell on a stone; and she marked the stone and had it watched, and when the time was full it was cut open and the boy came out of it glowing, and had to be carried to the smith. That is told in Ossetia and among the Circassians and among the Abkhaz alike. She holds the councils together and gets the Narts out of what they get themselves into, and she does it by knowing more than they do. She is not a goddess and has no shrine in the epic; she is the first woman of the Narts, and the record is made on what she does. Her name has nothing to do with the Christian Satan, whatever the resemblance in English.

gods.name: Soslan / Sosruko
gods.description: The stone-born hero, and one man under many names: Soslan or Sozyryqo in Ossetian, Sosruko or Sawseruquo among the Circassians, Sasrykva among the Abkhaz. The core is the same in all of them and it is a chain of four things. He is born out of the stone that Satanaya marked. He is taken red-hot to the smith, who tempers him in the forge. The smith holds him with tongs - and the part the tongs closed on is the part the fire never reached, so that he is proof against everything in the world except there. And a rolling wheel finds that part at the last and kills him: Balsag's Wheel in the Ossetian telling, the wheel of Jan-Sherkh among the Circassians, and he is cut down at the knees or the hips and dies of it. Which part the tongs held is where the tellings part company - the knees in the main Ossetian forms, the hips or thighs in the Circassian - and other things belong to one region and not to all. The fire-theft, in which he takes fire from a giant and brings it back to the Narts freezing on the mountain, is chiefly Circassian and Abkhaz and is the heart of the story there. The long journey to the Land of the Dead is Ossetian. Not every episode is in every recension, and no separate records are made for Sosruko or Sasrykva, because they are not separate men.

gods.name: Batraz
gods.description: The steel Nart, and the Ossetian cycle is where he lives; what is set down here is the Ossetian Batraz or Batradz. His father Hamyts brought home a wife of the Bycenta, a tiny people, and kept her among the Narts who laughed at her; and when she was insulted at the feast she would not stay, and before she went she put the child she was carrying into Hamyts's own back, into a swelling between his shoulders. It grew there, and Satanaya cut it open at the term, and what came out was a boy of red-hot steel who had to be quenched. He lived afterwards in the sky more than on the ground and came down out of it like a thunderbolt. He killed the men who killed his father. And at the end he turned on the Narts themselves and on heaven, and could not be killed, because his life was in his sword and the sword was in the world; and he would not die until they had dragged it to the sea and thrown it in, and when they had, the water went bloody and boiled, and he died. The Circassians have a Pataraz, a hero of the same name-stock and something of the same cast; but his cycle is not this one, and his episodes are not folded into this record, and no separate record is made of him here.
