A body of steel does not make him a monster; he is a Nart.

gods.name: Uryzmag
gods.description: The eldest of the Narts and the head of their council - Uryzmag in Ossetian, Warzameg to the Circassians - and the record is made on what he decides and not on his years. He is Satanaya's husband, and the two of them together are the government of the Narts: she sees it and he says it, and the young men do it. The story most told of him is the one in the cave. He is taken by a one-eyed giant who shuts him in with his flock and eats the Narts one by one; and Uryzmag heats the spit in the fire and drives it into the eye, and then goes out in the morning under the belly of a ram, or in the fleece of one, while the blinded giant runs his hands over the backs of them at the mouth of the cave. The tale is close enough to the Cyclops of the Odyssey that scholars have argued over it for a century, and they have not agreed - whether the Caucasus took it, or gave it, or both drew on something older - and it is not settled here and not called a copy. He is old, and he is the one they send for when there is nothing else to be done.

gods.name: Syrdon
gods.description: The trouble of the Narts, and Ossetian in the main. He is not one of them and is not loved among them, and he pays it back: he goes among them making mischief, setting them against each other, and they cannot be rid of him and cannot do without him either. Two things are his. The first is the death of Soslan. Balsag's Wheel could not find where Soslan could be cut, and it was Syrdon who told it - the knees, where the tongs had held him - and the wheel came back and took him there. The second is the fandyr. The tellings differ on how it happened and on who did what: in the usual Ossetian account Soslan kills Syrdon's sons and Syrdon, finding them dead, takes the bones of the eldest and the sinews and strings the first fandyr on them and comes to the Nart council playing it; and the Narts, who had every reason to kill him, heard it and let him live and took the instrument, and that is where music comes to them. Grief made into an instrument, by the worst of them. He is no clown; he is a cause, and he is set down as an actor of the epic and not as anything to be admired.

gods.name: Hamyts
gods.description: A Nart of the Ossetian cycle, Xaemyc in the Ossetic, and the father of Batraz - but the record is not made on the fatherhood. It is made on the choice. He took to wife a woman of the Bycenta, a people so small that she could be carried in his pocket or on his palm, and he brought her home among the Narts and kept her there, knowing what they would say, and they said it. What broke it was an insult at a feast - the tellings differ over whose it was and what was said, and some make it Syrdon's - and she would not stay after it; and going, she left the child in a swelling on his back, which Satanaya opened. He was killed afterwards, and the accounts do not agree on by whom, and it is that killing that Batraz spends the rest of his life avenging. The people the wife came from, the reason she left, the words that were said, and how the boy grew in his father's back are all told differently in different places, and are given here as the variants they are.

gods.name: Do Kamissa
gods.description: The buffalo woman of Do, and the epic begins with her. She was the king of Do's own sister, and in the usual telling she was cheated - denied what was hers when the inheritance was shared out, or slighted and put aside - and she had power, and she used it: she took the shape of a buffalo and went through the country killing, and no hunter that went out against her came back. When two hunters came at last, she met them not as the buffalo but as an old woman on the road, and they were kind to her and fed her; and she told them who the buffalo was, and told them how to kill it - the means, and the words, and the moment - which is to say that she gave them her own death. She asked one thing for it: that when the king offered them their reward and paraded the beauties of Do before them, they should refuse every one and ask for the ugliest girl in the country, the hunchback Sogolon. They did it, and Sogolon went to Maghan, and Sundiata was born of that marriage. Everything in the epic stands on a bargain she made. She is not Sogolon Kedjou. Sogolon is said in some tellings to carry the buffalo's wraith or its power or its inheritance, and that is as far as it goes; they are two women, and the tellings do not confuse them and neither does this record. She is a woman who took a shape, and not a beast: what she does is done by choice, and the choice is the reason she is here. She is also written Dò Kamissa. The griots do not all give the inheritance quarrel or the transformation in the same way.

gods.name: Sassouma Bérété
gods.description: Maghan's first wife, and the maker of the exile. When the king took Sogolon on the strength of the prophecy and she bore him a son, Sassouma had a son of her own already - Dankaran Touman - and she meant him to have the throne; and she set herself against the other woman and the other woman's child, and did not stop. Sundiata could not walk until he was seven and she saw to it that no one forgot it. The moment the epic remembers is the baobab leaves: Sogolon came to her door to beg a handful for the pot, having none, and Sassouma gave them to her with the words that her own son had picked them at the age of seven, and Sogolon went home weeping - and it was that weeping that put Sundiata on his feet and sent him out for the tree. When Maghan died she got Dankaran onto the throne over the boy the king had named, and afterwards she made the country too dangerous for the family to stay in, and Sogolon took her children and went. The whole exile - the wandering, the years in Mema, the long absence in which Soumaoro took the Mande - runs from that. The boy who came back to Kirina was made by what she did to him. She acts in her own right and not through her son, who is her instrument in this and not her equal; she is set down as a principal actor of the epic, which is a statement about the story and not about her conduct. The griots tell the persecution differently from one performance to another.

gods.name: Seytek
gods.description: The hero of the third of the great Kyrgyz cycles. The epic is carried in three: Manas, then Semetey, then Seytek, and he is the last of them - Semetey's son, born about the time his father was lost, and reared away from what was his by people who did not tell him whose blood he had. He learns it, as his father learned it before him, and he goes back; and he puts down Kiyaz, who had taken what was Semetey's and held the house and the wife and the land, and he sets the line upright again. It will be seen that this is his father's story told a second time - the hidden heir, the discovery, the return, the vengeance, the restoration - and the Seytek cycle does repeat the Semetey. He is entered here because he is the central man of a distinct cycle that the tradition itself names and carries as the third of the three, and not because his story is a new one. As with the rest of the epic, the manaschi do not tell it the same way twice and no one recension is the version; what is given here is the outline the tradition holds in common.

gods.name: Samdzimari
gods.description: A goddess of the Khevsur and the eastern Georgian mountains - the name is read as the one adorned with cornelian - and she did not begin on that side. The tradition as it is published has her a woman of the Kajis, the people of the other world, taken in the raid the divine sons of God made on Kajeti; and she came over, and stayed, and turned her power to the use of the people who had taken her, and became the one who stands between them and the divinities. She is the one who comes: she appears to men and women, changes her shape, is seen and not seen, and speaks through the oracle-tellers at the shrines, which is her particular office and belongs to no one else in that pantheon. What is asked of her is what is asked of no other there - healing, childbirth, the concerns of women, the finding out of hidden things - and she has her own shrines and her own invocations and is called on in her own name. She is set down as major because she is the first of the divine women of that religious world and holds an office no one else holds, and not as the companion of Kopala or of anyone. The mountain shrines are not a dead religion and are kept still; what is written here is drawn from what has been responsibly published of them and goes no further, and no ritual is described that is not.

gods.name: Nasran
gods.description: The long-bearded chief of the Narts in the Circassian telling - Nasran-zhak'e, Nasren-zhach'e - and this is a Circassian figure and not a shared one; the Ossetians do not have him, and he should not be taken for a pan-Nart hero. He is not Uryzmag, either, whom the Circassians know as Warzameg: their tradition has the two men separately and so does this archive. The story he is remembered for is the fire. The Narts had it and it was taken from them, or was withheld from them by the god who keeps it, and they were freezing on the mountain and there was no one to go; and Nasran, who was their head and answerable for them, took his horse and rode up to force it out of the god - and was taken for it, and chained to a peak of the mountains, where a bird came at him. It is Sosruko who rides out afterwards and gets the fire and brings it back, and the two halves of the story are told in that order and are not to be run together. The chained defier of the sky is a shape the world knows in more than one place, and the resemblance to Amirani in Georgia and to Prometheus in Greece has been remarked on for a long time; but Nasran is his own man in his own epic, and no descent from either is claimed here.

gods.name: Kannagi
gods.description: The woman of the Cilappatikaram, and a human being before she is anything else. She is a merchant's daughter of Puhar, married to Kovalan, and she is left for a dancer and beggared and then taken back without a word of reproach; and when they come to Madurai with nothing she gives him one of her gold anklets to sell, and he is taken for the thief of the queen's anklet and killed on the king's order without a trial. What she does then is her own. She goes into the Pandya court with the anklet that is left to her and she asks the king what was in the anklet he says her husband stole; and his was strung with pearls, and hers is broken open before him and it is full of rubies. The king says that he is the thief, and dies of it. She is not satisfied by that. She tears out her left breast and casts it over the city and calls fire down on Madurai, and the city burns except for the true and the old and the children. The epic then takes her up itself: she goes into the Chera hills and stands fourteen days beneath a venkai tree and is carried up bodily in the sight of the hill people, and Senguttuvan hears of it and raises her a stone and a temple; her deification is narrated inside the poem and is not a later invention laid on top of it. Pattini, the faithful wife, is the title the poem gives her when it makes her a goddess, and it is a title of this same woman and not another name for someone else. What grew afterwards is another matter and is not read backward into her here. The Sinhala traditions of Sri Lanka and the traditions of Kerala carried her far past the poem and gave her ritual cycles of their own and biographies of their own and offices she does not hold in the Tamil epic, and those are related developments and not properties of the woman in the Cilappatikaram; nothing of that is catalogued as her here.

gods.name: Kovalan
gods.description: The husband of Kannagi in the Cilappatikaram, and he is not entered here for being killed. He is entered because he ruins himself, and the ruin is a chain of his own choices. He is a rich merchant's son of Puhar with a wife he does not stay with: he sees Madhavi dance and he goes to her and stays years, and spends what he has on her, and is poor at the end of it; and when a song is sung between them that each takes for a slight he leaves her too. He goes back to Kannagi, who says nothing about any of it, and it is his own decision to leave Puhar for Madurai and begin again there, and his own decision to take her anklet into the goldsmith's street and offer it for sale. The goldsmith who has stolen the queen's anklet sees his chance and names him, and the king does not inquire. Every step onto that street was taken by him. The confrontation that follows and the fire that follows that are Kannagi's; the road to them is his.

gods.name: Madhavi
gods.description: The dancer of Puhar in the Cilappatikaram, of the courtesan line that traced itself to Urvashi, and she is not written here as a seductress or as an obstacle set between a husband and a wife. She dances at the court and Kovalan comes to her and she loves him, and they live together and have a daughter; and what parts them is a misunderstanding and not a betrayal. They sing to each other on the shore, and each hears in the other's song a love meant for somebody else, and he walks away and she does not call him back, and neither of them is lying. What she does after is hers alone. When she is told that he is dead she does not go back to the dancing and she does not go back to the line she was born into: she cuts off her hair, takes the robe, and enters the Buddhist order, and she raises her daughter Manimekalai out of the courtesan's calling and into her own. That decision is the premise of the second epic. Manimekalai is a nun's daughter before she is anything else, and it is Madhavi who made her one.

gods.name: Nedunchezhiyan (of Madurai)
gods.description: The Pandya king of Madurai in the Cilappatikaram. He is the king of the poem and not every historical king of the name: the Pandyas produced more than one Nedunchezhiyan, and the Sangam ruler remembered for Talaiyalanganam is a different man and is not catalogued here. He is entered as a human antagonist and the category carries no praise. His queen's anklet is stolen; a stranger is found offering an anklet for sale; and on the word of the court goldsmith, and without an inquiry that would have taken an hour, he gives the order and Kovalan is cut down in the street. It is his order and no one else's. When Kannagi comes into his hall and breaks the anklet open in front of him and it spills rubies where the queen's spilled pearls, he understands what he has done and says it aloud, that it is he who is the thief and not the man he killed, and he falls dead where he sits. He is not a monster and he is not worshipped, and the epic gives him the one thing it does not give the goldsmith, which is the recognition.

gods.name: Senguttuvan
gods.description: The Chera king of the third book of the Cilappatikaram, and he is not entered for being a king. He is entered for one act. The hill people bring him word that a woman has been carried up into the sky out of their hills, and he hears the whole story of Madurai from them, and he resolves to raise her a stone. He goes north for it himself, against the northern kings who had spoken slightingly of the Tamil country, and he takes the stone from the Himalaya and bathes it in the Ganga and brings it back and sets it up as the image of the goddess, and consecrates the temple to her. He is the reason there is a cult at the end of the poem and not only a burnt city. A Chera Senguttuvan is praised in the Patirruppattu and the literary king is built over that memory, but the poem's Senguttuvan is the figure catalogued here and the historical reconstruction is uncertain and is not given a record of its own. Nor should the whole later history of Pattini worship, in the Tamil country or beyond it, be traced to a single verifiable royal act; the poem tells the founding as its own, and it is told that way here and no further.

gods.name: Manimekalai
gods.description: The heroine of the Manimekalai, the Tamil epic that follows the Cilappatikaram, and the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi. She is entered here as a character of Tamil literature. The poem is Buddhist and it argues Buddhist doctrine at length, and none of that makes this shelf a Buddhist pantheon or her a Buddhist deity; she is a woman in a Tamil poem. The poem is her refusals and her choices. Udayakumaran, the Chola prince, wants her and pursues her and she will not have him, and she hides from him and is carried away from him and holds to it. She takes the robe as her mother did. On the island of Manipallavam she comes to know her former births, and she receives the Amudhasurabhi, the alms bowl that is never empty, and what she does with it is the point of her: she feeds the hungry with it, and goes on feeding them, and takes that as the whole use of her life. She is not the sea goddess Manimekhala, who is a different figure in the same poem and is the deity she is named for, and the two are not merged here; the goddess is not catalogued.

gods.name: Aputra
gods.description: A man of the Manimekalai, whose story is told inside that poem before the bowl comes to Manimekalai. The Tamil is Aputtiran; Aputra is the conventional English display and is used here. The name means the son of a cow, because a cow suckled him where he had been abandoned as an infant, and it began as a description of that; but it is the only name he has and it is his name and nothing else. He is raised in a brahmin house and he throws it all away in one act: he takes a cow that is being led to sacrifice and gets her away from the men who mean to kill her, and for that he is denounced and driven out as a low man, and he does not take it back. He begs in Madurai after that, and he shares what is given him with people hungrier than himself, and he is doing that already, out of a beggar's empty bowl, before anything is given to him. Cintadevi, the goddess of learning, gives him the Amudhasurabhi for it, and he feeds the hungry with it for years. Indra comes and offers him heaven and he will not take it, and says the relief of hunger is the better thing; and Indra's answer is to send rain and end the famine everywhere, so that there is no one left in want and the bowl and the man are alike without a use. He goes to sea looking for people who still need to be fed, and finds them in Savakam, and feeds them; and when there is no hunger left to answer he sets the bowl down at the lake at Manipallavam and starves himself to death beside it. That is where Manimekalai finds it. He is not a lecture with a name on it: he chooses the cow, the exile, the refusal, the voyage and the death. The vessel is not the Akshaya Patra of the Mahabharata, and no identity is claimed between them; an inexhaustible bowl is a motif that more than one tradition has, and a shared motif is not a shared thing.

gods.name: Ayyanar
gods.description: A guardian god of the Tamil country, and one of the great ones. His shrines stand at the edge of village land rather than at its centre, at the boundary and the tank and the field's end, and he is the one who rides the bounds at night and keeps what is outside from coming in; the terracotta horses are his, raised for him to ride, and they are set up at his shrines in numbers and left to weather. He has his own cult and his own name and his own priests, and he is not a local face of somebody else. He is not Ayyappan. The archive's Ayyappan record already says so, and it is said again here: the god of Sabarimala and the horseman of the Tamil boundary are related figures of different regions and they are not the same, and no identity with him, or with Sastha as a general category, is claimed. Neither is he every guardian deity of the Tamil country; the others are their own, and are not folded into him. His worship is living, and this record describes it and does not presume to catalogue it.

gods.name: Madurai Veeran
gods.description: The Warrior of Madurai, a man of the Tamil ballads who is worshipped as a guardian god. The tellings differ, and none of them is the authoritative one, and the differences matter and are not smoothed over here. In the common shape of it he is born to royalty and given away and raised by a cobbler family, and the caste of that upbringing is not an incidental detail of his story but the substance of it, and it stays with him; he grows into a fighting man and takes service under the authority at Madurai and is set to keep order there, and he does it well. Then he takes a woman he was not to take, and the recensions vary as to who she was and what was promised him, and for that the same authority he served has him mutilated and put to death. He is not entered for being executed. He is entered because he chose the fight and chose the woman and chose to stand by both, and because a man who died as a criminal was raised afterwards to a guardian of the place that killed him. He is worshipped now at his own shrines and often at the edge of Ayyanar's, and that nearness is not identity; he is a man who became a god, not a form of Ayyanar and not a member of a guardian class.

gods.name: Alan Gua
gods.description: The ancestress of the Mongol legend as the Secret History of the Mongols tells it; the scholarly transliteration of her name is Alan Qo'a. She is entered here for what she said and taught, and not for having borne anyone. Widowed, she bears three more sons, and her two elder sons whisper between themselves that the children must be the servant's. She learns that they are saying it. What she does then is her own: she seats all five of them in a row and gives each one arrow shaft to break, and each one snaps it easily; then she binds five shafts into a bundle and passes it along the row, and not one of them can break it. Then she names their doubt aloud instead of waiting to be accused of anything, and gives her testimony: that a shining man came in nightly by the light at the smoke-hole and rubbed her belly so that his brightness went into her womb, and went out again on a moonbeam in the likeness of a yellow dog. And she draws the conclusion herself, inside the story: these are the sons of Heaven, and when they are rulers of all, the common people will understand it. That is what her account establishes within the narrative, the heavenly ancestry of the younger sons, and it should not be stretched further; the mandate of Chinggis Khan is asserted elsewhere in the tradition on other grounds and does not rest on her testimony alone. The lesson of the single arrows and the bundle is worth stating plainly for what it is: a migratory motif told of other people in other lands, and not something the Mongols alone possess.

gods.name: Bodonchar
gods.description: The youngest of the five sons in the ancestral legend of the Secret History, called Bodonchar Munkhag, or Munqaq, which is an epithet and means the Simple or the Foolish; it is a name they gave him and not a second person. When the family's goods are divided after their mother's death his four brothers give him no share, reckoning him a fool and hardly kin. He does not fight them for it. He says that he will live if he lives and die if he dies, and rides off down the Onon on a sore-backed grey horse, and builds himself a hut of grass and stays there alone. He sees a hawk take a bird, and he snares her with hair from his horse's tail and keeps her, and lives off what she catches for him; there is nothing miraculous in it and the story does not say there is. A people are camped along the stream nearby and he takes mare's milk from them by day and goes back to his hut at night, and they ask him nothing and he asks them nothing. Then his brother comes down the river looking for him, and it is on the ride home that Bodonchar earns his place here. He says at his brother's back, and says it again when he is told to be quiet, that a body should have a head and a coat should have a collar: those people have no head among them, no great and no small, and they could be taken. The brothers hear him out, go home, and decide together to do it; the decision is theirs jointly and not his alone, and he does not command it, though he is put in the advance when they ride. What is his is the eye and the proposal, and the family's first hold over other people comes out of it, and that is what he is entered for. The Borjigin descend from him, and that is not the reason.

gods.name: Genghis Khan
gods.description: Temujin, the man; Chinggis Khan, the title he took and the figure the legends made of him; and the ancestor who is worshipped. They are one person here, told in the order the tradition made them, and not split apart. The history is not what admits him. Neither is the conquest, nor the empire, nor what he means to a nation now: the archive does not make a god of anyone for being important. What admits him is that he is actually worshipped. The tradition of the Eight White Yurts, the felt shrines that carried his relics and were moved with the people who kept them, has been tended by the Darkhad, whose office is hereditary, and the rites are still performed at Ejen Khoroo in the Ordos. That much is a living cult and not a memory. It should be said as carefully as it is said here, though. His grave was hidden and its place is not known, and no one has found it; the buildings that stand at Ejen Khoroo now are of the last century and are a shrine and not his tomb, and nothing there is his body. Nor has any of it come down untouched: the shrine has been moved, and it has been broken up and put back together again, and what is done there now has been reconstituted more than once. The sulde, the spirit of the standard, belongs to this same cultic complex and is described here as part of it and is not catalogued as anyone. The signs told of his birth, the clot of blood in the fist, belong to the legend and are reported as the legend's and not as things that happened.

gods.name: Hoelun
gods.description: The mother of Chinggis Khan, and that is not why she is here. Three times in the Secret History of the Mongols the story turns on something she does. When her husband is poisoned and the clan rides away and leaves her with small children, she does not accept it: she takes up the standard and goes after the people who are deserting, and turns some of them back, and then keeps her children alive on the Onon on roots and wild fruit and what the river gives. When her sons kill their half-brother Bekter over a fish, she does not excuse it because they are hers; she rounds on them and tells them what they are, and it is the hardest speech in the book and it is aimed at the boy who will be khan. And when Teb Tengri has set her son against his brother Qasar, and Qasar has been seized, she hears of it and drives through the night by camel cart and comes at dawn and unties him herself and shames the khan into letting him go. That is her intervention and it is in the Qasar affair; the later intervention against Teb Tengri, after Temuge is humiliated, is Borte's and not hers, and the two should not be run together. The recensions do not word all of this the same way, and the record does not pretend to a single exact sequence where they differ.

gods.name: Börte
gods.description: She is not entered here as the wife of Chinggis Khan. Not for the Merkit raid that carried her off, which was done to her; not for her sons; not for the quarrel over Jochi's fathering; and not for mattering to a dynasty. She is entered for one thing she does in the Secret History of the Mongols, and it is enough. Teb Tengri and his people have already beaten Qasar and the khan let it pass. Now they take Temuge's followers, and make Temuge kneel behind them and beg, and Temuge comes and tells the khan of it weeping, and the khan does nothing. Then Borte sits up in the bed and holds the blanket against herself and speaks, and what she says is a political argument and not a complaint: what sort of people are these, that they beat one brother and make another kneel; and if they can handle his brothers so while he is alive and standing, then when he falls like an old tree what will they do with his people, and will they leave them to her sons? And straight after she has said it the khan tells Temuge to deal with Teb Tengri as he pleases, and Teb Tengri's back is broken that day. She did not begin the quarrel with him, and this record does not say she did; the Qasar affair came first and it was Hoelun who intervened in that one. What is hers is the argument that moved the khan when nothing else had. The later chronicles enlarge her a good deal, and nothing of that enlargement is drawn on here.

gods.name: Jamukha
gods.description: The anda of Temujin, the sworn brother of his youth, and afterwards the one man on the steppe who was his equal and his rival. He is not written here as an obstacle whose use is to make Chinggis Khan look larger. He is a politician in his own right: the two of them camp together and swear the anda bond twice over, and then Jamukha separates from him, and the tellings of why are cryptic and are left cryptic here; and the people begin to choose between them. He fights him at Dalan Baljut and takes the field. He is raised up by a coalition of the tribes as Gur Khan, khan in his own name and not as anyone's man. And at the end, when his own followers seize him and hand him over to buy their safety, he does not take the gift: he tells Temujin that men who lay hands on their own lord are not to be kept alive, and they are killed, and only then does he ask for himself the death of a nobleman, without his blood being spilled, and it is given him. The Secret History is not a neutral witness and should not be read as one; it was made for the house that won, and its Jamukha is a character it has drawn, whatever the man was.

gods.name: Teb Tengri (Kököchü)
gods.description: A man, and a shaman, and not the god Tengri; nothing in this record touches that one, and the resemblance of the names is a resemblance of words. His name was Kokochu, a son of Munglig, and Teb Tengri was the title he went by, which is to say something like the wholly heavenly. His power was that he was believed when he said what Heaven wanted, and he traded on it. It is the tradition, and Rashid al-Din in particular, that has him proclaim the title Chinggis Khan by Heaven's decree; the Secret History of the Mongols does not tell it that way, and the distinction is kept here rather than folded together. What the Secret History does show is a shaman who had the khan's ear and used it against the khan's brothers. He and his people beat Qasar; and he told the khan that Heaven had said the rule would go first to him and then to Qasar, which was as good as telling him to be afraid of his own brother, and Qasar was seized and came near to being destroyed. Afterwards he took Temuge's followers and made Temuge kneel behind him and apologise for asking. That was the end of him: after Borte spoke, the khan gave Temuge leave, and men were waiting, and his back was broken and he was thrown down. He is catalogued as a human antagonist in a human political and religious quarrel. The category carries no praise and no blame.

gods.name: Sorqan Shira
gods.description: A man of the Suldus, in the service of the Tayichiud, who did one thing and is here for it. Temujin was their prisoner, kept in a wooden cangue and passed from tent to tent, and he got loose in the confusion of a feast and lay down in the river with only his face above the water. Sorqan Shira saw him lying there. He did not raise the alarm. He told him to lie still and that he would say nothing, and he went on; and when the search came round he sent it elsewhere. Later the fugitive came to Sorqan Shira's own tent, which was a thing that could have killed the whole household, and they took the cangue off him and burned it, and hid him in a cart of wool, and when the searchers came and began to pull the wool apart Sorqan Shira turned them back with a word about the heat. Then he gave him a horse and food and let him go. He is not entered for loyalty, which he did not owe and which was not what this was; he was in the other camp. He is entered because Temujin was a slave in a wooden collar and would have stayed one, and this man decided otherwise at his own risk. Nothing supernatural is claimed of him, and the rewards and the standing that the later tradition gives his family are not weighed here.

gods.name: Mwindo
gods.description: The hero of the Mwindo epic of the Nyanga. He is a man of the story and not a god: he is born with power, speaking and walking from the first, carrying his conga-scepter, and none of that is worship. The Nyanga do not sacrifice to him and there is no cult of him, and this record claims none. His father Shemwindo had decreed that his wives were to bear him daughters only, and Mwindo is born in spite of it, out of his mother's middle finger, refusing the ordinary way; and his father buries him alive, and when that fails seals him in a drum and throws the drum in the river, and he lives through both. He goes down the water to his father's sister, and from there he comes back and calls down the lightning and Tubondo is destroyed. His father runs from him into the underworld and he goes down after him, and it is there he has to face Muisa; and when he has his father at last he does not kill him but takes him back, and they are reconciled, and the authority is divided between them. Then he kills the dragon, Kirimu, and for that Nkuba takes him up into the sky and breaks him of what he had become, and he comes home another man and rules with a restraint he did not have before. The child who burned a village and the ruler who gives laws are one person, and the epic is the account of how the first became the second. What is told here follows the performance recited by She-Karisi Rureke in 1956; the epic lives in several recorded performances and they do not agree in their details, and none of them is the original.

gods.name: Shemwindo
gods.description: The chief of Tubondo in the Mwindo epic, and a man, and the antagonist of it. He is not here because he is Mwindo's father. He is here because of what he decides. He gives out the decree that his wives are to bear him daughters and no sons at all, and everything in the epic comes out of that order; and when a son is born to him anyway he does not relent but tries to be rid of him, and has the child buried in a grave, and when the child comes up out of it has him shut in a drum and the drum thrown into the river. When his son comes back grown and his village is destroyed around him he does not stand and face it: he goes down into the underworld and hides there, and has to be hunted. And at the end, brought back up, he neither fights nor is killed; he acknowledges what he did, and the two of them divide the authority between them, and he is left alive. He is a human antagonist and is set down as such, and the tellings differ: the details here follow the Rureke performance of 1956, and other Nyanga performances of the epic order and word these things differently.

gods.name: Muisa
gods.description: The lord of the underworld in the Nyanga epic, the divinity of the world below the ground, and it is into his country that Shemwindo runs when his son comes for him. Nothing is claimed for him here beyond what the tradition records: no shrine of his is described, and no sacrifice and no rite, because none is documented, and he is entered as the underworld divinity that the epic knows and not as a cult that has been proved. He is the one who holds Shemwindo, and he does not give him up for the asking. He sets Mwindo tasks that no one could do, to plant and raise and harvest a banana grove in a day, and to gather the honey; and while Mwindo is at them Muisa sends his belt of cowry shells against him, and the belt falls on him and overcomes him, and he is brought back by his conga-scepter. Whether the text says he was killed outright or only beaten down is not asserted here. Muisa is beaten before Shemwindo is surrendered, and not otherwise. He is his own figure and is not to be read as Owuo, or Osiris, or Yeomra, or any other lord of the dead; that they share an office is not that they share a name. The account follows the Rureke performance of 1956 and differs in other tellings.

gods.name: Nkuba
gods.description: Lightning, and a person: the word means the lightning itself, and in the epic the lightning is somebody, who decides things and has friends and takes offence. That is how a good many gods are named, after the thing they are, and it does not make him less an individual within the story. He is Mwindo's ally first. When Mwindo comes back to his father's village it is Nkuba who answers him, and his seven bolts come down one after another and Tubondo is destroyed with them; the hero asks and the lightning obeys. Then Mwindo kills the dragon, Kirimu, and does not know or does not care that Kirimu was Nkuba's blood-friend, and the lightning turns on him. He takes hold of Mwindo and carries him up out of the world altogether and hauls him through the sky, through the cold and the heat of it, and shows him what he is next to it, and does not let him go until the arrogance is out of him; and then he sends him home, and the man who comes back is not the one who went up. The turning of the whole epic is Nkuba's doing and not the hero's. Nothing is claimed here of worship of him beyond the evidence, and he is not Shango and not Xevioso and not some lightning god of all the Bantu peoples: those are other gods of other nations, and a shared office is not a shared identity. The episode follows the Rureke performance of 1956 and is told otherwise elsewhere.

gods.name: Yamato Takeru
gods.description: A prince of the early chronicles, the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, and what they give is legend and dynastic memory and not a life that can be checked. He is sent away by his own father to fight in the west and then in the east, and the sending is not kindness; the chronicles differ as to how much of it is fear of him. His weapon is his wits before it is his sword. In the west he goes among the Kumaso in a woman's clothes, taken for a girl at the feast, and kills their chief where he sits; and the tellings vary in the detail and in what is said between them at the end. In Izumo he makes a friend of the man he means to kill, and they bathe, and he has left a wooden sword where the other's should be, and then he calls him out to fight; the Kojiki carries this and it is not in every version. In the east he is caught in a burning field, and cuts the grass away from himself with the blade he had of his aunt at Ise, and it is from that the sword is called Kusanagi, the grass-cutter; the sword is a thing of the regalia and is not catalogued here as anyone. He leaves it behind at the last, and goes on without it, and sickens on the mountain and dies far from home, and out of his grave there rises a white bird and is gone. He is a legendary prince and is set down as one.

gods.name: Benkei
gods.description: The warrior monk of the Yoshitsune legends, a huge man of the sohei, and he is not entered here for being loyal. Before he was anyone's man he was his own: the tales have him at the Gojo bridge taking swords from every warrior who crossed it, nine hundred and ninety-nine of them, until the thousandth was a slight young man with a flute who danced away from him and beat him, and that was Yoshitsune, and Benkei followed him afterwards because he chose to. What he is chiefly remembered for is the end. At Koromogawa, with the house surrounded and his lord inside making ready to die, Benkei held the bridge alone so that no one could reach him, and took every arrow they had, and the tradition is that when the attackers at last dared come near they found him dead on his feet and still standing, and that they had been afraid to pass a corpse. That is legend and is given here as legend; it is not an established fact of the fighting at Koromogawa. The Gikeiki and the later tellings have made him larger with every century, and this record follows the legend and says so.

gods.name: Minamoto no Yoshitsune
gods.description: A commander of the Genpei war, and a real man, and also one of the great legendary figures of Japan; the two are not the same and the record keeps them apart. What is history: he fought for his half-brother Yoritomo, and he was brilliant and quick and did not ask permission. At Ichi-no-Tani he is said to have brought his riders down a slope the enemy thought no horse could take, and struck the Taira camp from behind; at Yashima and at Dan-no-ura he finished them. What follows is the ruin, and it is his own doing as much as anyone's: he took honours from the retired emperor without his brother's leave, and Yoritomo, who had won a country and did not intend to share it, turned on him. He ran, and was hunted the length of Japan, and was cornered at last at Koromogawa in the north and killed himself while Benkei held the door. The Gikeiki and the tales that grew out of it made him a boy magician taught by tengu, and gave him a childhood and a hundred exploits, and none of that is history and it is not offered as history here. He is one identity: the boy called Ushiwakamaru, the commander, and the hunted man are the same person and are not divided.

gods.name: Abe no Seimei
gods.description: A real man of the Heian court and afterwards a god. The documented Abe no Seimei was an onmyoji, a specialist of onmyodo, in service to the court in the tenth century and into the eleventh, reading the calendar and the stars and the ominous, and holding office; that much is record. What grew on top of it is enormous and is not record. The tales give him shikigami he commanded like servants, and contests of magic he always won, and prophecies that came true, and a rivalry with one Ashiya Doman that is a thing of the stories and not of the documents; and they give him a mother, Kuzunoha, who was a white fox in a woman's shape and left him when she was found out. Those are legends and are told here as legends, and Kuzunoha is not catalogued. He is set down as a deified human because that is what happened to him: he is enshrined as a kami, and the Seimei Shrine in Kyoto is his, and people go there. Not all of that is old, and the record does not pretend that every shrine custom or every tale about him reaches back to his lifetime.

gods.name: Minamoto no Raikō
gods.description: Minamoto no Raiko and Minamoto no Yorimitsu are the same man; Raiko is the reading the stories use and Yorimitsu the one the documents use, and there is only one of him. The historical Yorimitsu was a warrior and a provincial governor of the late tenth and early eleventh century and there is nothing monstrous in what is recorded of him; the legends are later and they made him the great slayer of things. The chief of them is Mount Oe. Girls were disappearing out of the capital, and the demon Shuten-doji had them, and Raiko went up the mountain with a handful of companions and did not go as a soldier: they went dressed as wandering monks, and asked for shelter, and were given it, and sat down to drink with the oni and gave him the drink they had brought, which was not what he thought it was. And when it had taken hold of him they cut off his head. The stratagem is the point of him and it is his. His four retainers are famous in their own right and are not catalogued in this batch.

gods.name: Shuten-dōji
gods.description: The oni of Mount Oe, and a named one; he is not a general demon and no generic oni is catalogued here. In the cycle he is the chief of a household of them in the mountains north-west of the capital, and he takes people out of Kyoto, women of good family among them, and what is done to them in his hall is told plainly enough in the sources and is not enlarged on here. He is undone by hospitality. Raiko and his companions come to him as travelling monks and he lets them in and drinks with them, and the drink they have brought is poisoned or is a thing the gods gave them, according to which telling is followed, and it holds him; and they cut his head from him while he lies. The head does not stop. It is said to have flown at Raiko and fastened on his helmet and bitten, and that only the helmets he had been given kept him alive. The tellings differ from one region and one century to another, and this record does not make them into a single exact history of him.

gods.name: Tamamo-no-Mae
gods.description: Not a woman who became a fox. She is a fox, and Tamamo-no-Mae is the shape and the name she wore at court: a beautiful and learned lady who was the favourite of the retired emperor Toba, and the beauty and the learning were part of the working. The emperor sickened, and no one could say why, and it was the onmyoji who read it and named her, and she was exposed and fled the palace as what she was, and was hunted down at last on the plain of Nasu by the men sent after her. What is left of her is the Sessho-seki, the killing stone, on the moor at Nasu, which is said to be her, and to have killed what came near it, until a priest broke the power of it; the stone is shown there still and the tradition is old but the tellings of it are not all of one age. The later stories run her together with the fox of the Shang court, Daji, and with foxes of India, and make one long career of it. That identification is something the legend did afterwards, and it is reported here as that and not as a ruling that she and Daji are one being.

gods.name: Kiyohime
gods.description: She begins as a woman. That is the whole of the case and it should be said first: the Dojo-ji legend has her a human girl, an innkeeper's daughter or a landholder's daughter as the version runs, who is promised something by a young monk named Anchin, whether he meant it or was only being kind to be rid of her, and who finds that he has gone. She goes after him. She follows him down the road, and he denies himself to her, and runs; and it is on that road, at the river, that she becomes what she becomes, a serpent or a dragon, and swims it, and comes on. He hides in the temple at Dojo-ji and they lower the great bell over him, and she comes to the bell and winds herself round it, and the heat of her kills him inside it. She is set down as a monster because that is the stable shape the tradition gives her at the end and because the category names what a figure is and not what it deserves; nothing in it is a judgement on a woman who was lied to. The story is told in many forms, in the temple's own picture-scrolls and in the No and in kabuki, and none of them is the only one.

gods.name: Urashima Tarō
gods.description: A fisherman who went to the other world and came back, and the versions of him are old and they are not all the same. The one everybody knows has him rescue a turtle from boys tormenting it on the beach, and the turtle is the sea-god's daughter, and she takes him down to the palace under the water; but the oldest versions, in the Man'yoshu and the Nihon Shoki, have no cruelty on the beach at all, and he catches a turtle himself, or a woman comes to him out of the sea, and the record does not flatten the old tellings into the modern one. What every version has is the return. He is happy under the sea for what feels like a few days and then he wants to see his home, and she lets him go and gives him a box and tells him never to open it. He comes up the beach and the village is not his village, and no one knows the name he gives, and three hundred years have gone by while he was gone. And then, having nothing left and nothing to lose, he opens the box. The years come out of it all at once, and he is an old man in a moment, and in some tellings dust. That opening is his own act and it is what he is entered for.

gods.name: Momotarō
gods.description: The Peach Boy. An old couple who have no children find a peach in the river, and the boy is inside it; in the older tellings the peach is eaten by the old pair and makes them young again and the child is theirs, and the record does not pretend the familiar modern version is the only one. He grows fast and strong, and when he is grown he tells them he is going to Onigashima, the island of the oni, who have been raiding the country, and he asks for millet dumplings for the road. The going is his decision and nobody sends him. On the way he gives a dumpling each to a dog, a monkey and a pheasant, and they go with him, and they are not catalogued and nothing is linked to him here. They take the island and the oni are beaten and he comes home with what the oni had taken from other people. It is a folktale and it has been put to other uses since: it was made into recruiting material in the last century, and the war-poster Momotaro is not the Momotaro of the old books and is not read backwards into him here. No general oni is catalogued.

gods.name: Kaguya-hime
gods.description: The girl of the Taketori Monogatari, the Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, which is about the oldest story Japan has in its own writing. An old bamboo cutter finds a shining stalk and a child inside it no bigger than his hand, and she grows into a woman of such beauty that the whole capital wants her, and she is not of this world and knows it. What she does with the wanting is the story. Five noblemen will not go away, and she does not refuse them outright: she sets each of them a task that cannot be done, the Buddha's stone begging-bowl, a jewelled branch from a tree on Horai, the fire-rat's robe, a jewel from a dragon's neck, a swallow's cowry, and they fail, and those who try to cheat her with forgeries are found out. Then the emperor himself asks, and she refuses him too, and he does not force her. At the end the people of the Moon come down for her, and here the record is careful: the tale does not present the return as a thing she wants. She weeps, and the guards cannot stop them, and she is taken back because she must be, and she leaves the elixir behind her and the emperor has it burned on the mountain. The refusals are hers. The leaving is not.

gods.name: Pentheus
gods.description: King of Thebes, and the man who told a god he was not one. He is human and he is the antagonist of the Bacchae and he is set down as a hero in the archive's sense, which is a category for people and not a compliment. Dionysus comes to Thebes, which is his mother's city, and the women go out to the mountain; and Pentheus forbids the rites and calls the god a fraud and a foreigner and a corrupter of wives, and has the stranger who preaches him arrested and bound, and that stranger is the god. The chains do not hold. And then Dionysus does not kill him, which is the terrible thing: he offers to take him up the mountain to spy on the women, and Pentheus goes, and lets himself be dressed in women's clothes to do it, and by then he is not in his right mind. They see him from the tree. His own mother is the first on him and does not know him, and Agave carries his head down into the city thinking it a lion's. Euripides is followed here; the mythographers and the other tragedies do not all tell it the same way.

gods.name: Alcestis
gods.description: She is not entered here as somebody's wife. Admetus was granted that he need not die at his hour if another would go in his place, and he asked, and his father would not, and his mother would not, and everyone he asked would not; and Alcestis said she would, and did. That is her act and it is unforced and it is the whole of the reason she is in this archive. Euripides is quite clear about the difference between the two of them: she chooses and he accepts, and the play spends its length on how little there is to say for him. She dies, and the house is in mourning, and Heracles comes to it as a guest and is not told, and when he learns what has happened he goes and takes her back from Death at the tomb by main force, and brings her in veiled and gives her to her husband; and she does not speak. The versions differ as to who brings her back and whether Persephone sends her, and this record follows Euripides.

gods.name: Procne
gods.description: The daughter of Pandion of Athens and the wife of Tereus of Thrace, and what she does is not defended here and is not condemned; she is a human being in a tragedy and the category says nothing about her merits. Tereus went for her sister, and raped her, and cut out her tongue so that she could not tell it, and shut her away and told Procne she was dead. Procne believed him for a year. Then the weaving came to her, and she read it, and knew. What she did then was her own: she went and got her sister out, and she killed Itys, her son and Tereus' son, and she cooked him and set him before his father and let him eat, and when he asked for the boy she told him where he was. Tereus came after them with a sword and they were turned to birds as they ran, and he to a hoopoe. Which of the two sisters became the nightingale and which the swallow is not agreed on in the sources. Tereus and Itys are not catalogued here.

gods.name: Philomela
gods.description: She is not entered as a victim, and the distinction matters. Tereus, her sister's husband, raped her, and cut out her tongue so that she could tell no one, and locked her away where no one would come, and gave out that she was dead; and he had reckoned correctly about everything except her hands. She had a loom. She wove what he had done into the cloth, and got it out to her sister, and that is testimony, and it is the reason there is a record here: without the weaving Procne never learns and nothing follows. What follows is terrible and it is chiefly Procne's doing, and it is written in Procne's record and not in this one. They are two women and are not merged. At the end they are birds; which sister becomes the nightingale and which the swallow varies from one source to another, and the record does not decide it. Tereus and Itys are not catalogued here.

gods.name: Lakshmana
gods.description: Rama's brother in the Ramayana, and not entered here for the brotherhood or for being faithful, which is what he is usually praised for. He is entered because he acts. When Rama is sent away it is Lakshmana who will not stay behind: he goes into the forest of his own insistence, and fourteen years of it, and no one commanded him to. In the forest it is his hand that does the thing the war comes out of. Shurpanakha comes to them and will not be turned away, and goes at Sita, and Lakshmana cuts her nose and her ears from her; and she goes to her kin with the blood on her, and after that there is no stopping it. He fights through the whole war and it is he who at last kills Indrajit at Nikumbhila, which nobody else could do, though he is struck down himself before it and has to be brought back. The line he is said to have drawn round the hut, the Lakshmana-rekha that Sita crosses, is worth a word of caution: it is famous, and it is not in the oldest telling of Valmiki, and it belongs to the later tradition. Nothing here is linked to any other record.

gods.name: Kaikeyi
gods.description: The queen whose decision the Ramayana comes out of, and a woman and not a demon; the category is for human beings and it is not praise. Long before, she had saved her husband's life in a battle and he had promised her two boons, and she had not spent them. She spends them on the night before Rama is to be made king. She asks that her own son Bharata be given the throne, and that Rama go into the forest for fourteen years; and Dasharatha, who cannot break a promise and cannot bear what he has promised, gives her both and dies of it. Everything after that, the exile and the forest and the abduction and the war, stands on that hour and on her asking. Her maid Manthara worked on her and put it into her head, and that is in the poem and is not denied here, and Manthara is not catalogued; but it is Kaikeyi who goes into the chamber, and Kaikeyi who names the two things, and Kaikeyi who will not take them back when the king begs. To make her only the instrument of a servant is to take the epic's engine away from the person who pulled it.

gods.name: Bharata (of the Ramayana)
gods.description: Rama's brother, and the son his mother won the kingdom for; and the record is here because he would not have it. He is away when it is done, and comes back to a dead father and a brother in the forest and a throne that is his by his mother's arrangement, and he refuses it, and he says to Kaikeyi's face what he thinks of what she did. Then he goes into the forest himself to fetch Rama home, and Rama will not come, because the fourteen years were promised and he holds to them. So Bharata takes his brother's sandals instead, and carries them back, and sets them on the throne, and rules for fourteen years as their servant and not as a king, living outside the city as an ascetic himself; and when the time is up he gives it all back. The refusal is the whole of him and it is a decision. He is not Bharata Chakravartin, who is on the Jain shelf, and he is not the ancient Bharata whose name the country is said to carry; the three are different men and the identifier keeps them apart.

gods.name: Shurpanakha
gods.description: A rakshasi, and Ravana's sister, and she is set down as a monster for the first of those and not the second: the category follows what she is in the tradition, a being of the rakshasa kind, and it is not a verdict on her wanting something. She finds the brothers in the forest and she wants Rama, and he sends her to Lakshmana, and Lakshmana sends her back, and the two of them make sport of her between them for a while; the versions differ a good deal here, in her words and in theirs and in how much of the mockery is in the text. Then she turns on Sita, and Lakshmana takes her nose and her ears. What she does next is hers and it is what matters: she goes to Khara and his fourteen thousand and sets them on the brothers, and they are destroyed; and then she goes to Ravana and does not ask him for vengeance so much as she describes Sita to him until he wants her. The abduction begins in Shurpanakha's mouth. Khara is not catalogued in this batch. She is not a joke about a rejected woman and the record does not make her one.

gods.name: Vidura
gods.description: The half-brother of the blind king, born of a serving-woman and never eligible for the throne he advised, and he is not entered here as a counsellor; wise men who only speak do not get records. He is entered for the house at Varanavata. Duryodhana has it built of lac and resin and every burning thing, and means to have the Pandavas and their mother asleep in it when it goes up. Vidura sees it. He cannot forbid it and he will not be silent, so he warns Yudhishthira in a language no one else in the hall understands, telling him what a jackal does with many holes to his burrow and what fire does not do to a rat underground; and then he sends a miner to them in secret, and the tunnel is dug, and when the house burns they are already under the ground and away. Every event of the epic that comes after depends on the Pandavas being alive to reach it. He does other things, and refuses the court, and walks out of it at the end; but the tunnel is the reason he is here. Nothing of his is linked to any other record, and no existing record is altered.

gods.name: Ekalavya
gods.description: A boy of the forest people, a Nishada, who wanted to be taught and was refused. Drona would not take him, and the reason is caste and is not disguised in the poem: he was not a kshatriya and Drona was teaching princes. So he went away and made an image of Drona out of clay, and set it up, and taught himself in front of it, and became the best archer of them all, better than Arjuna, whom Drona had promised should be the best in the world. And when they found him and Drona saw what had happened, Drona asked him for his fee, his guru-dakshina, and asked him for the thumb of his right hand; and Ekalavya cut it off and gave it to him, and never drew as he had drawn again. It is not told here as obedience beautifully performed, and it is not a triumph. A teacher who had refused to teach him took the hand that had taught itself, in order that the promise made to a prince should not be broken. That is what the passage says. The later tradition does not agree on what became of him afterwards, and the record does not settle it. `drona` is not modified.

gods.name: Satyavati
gods.description: A fisherman's daughter who married a king and then held the Kuru succession in her own hands. Her father is the one who set the terms of that marriage, that her sons and no others should reign, and it is because of his condition that Bhishma swore never to rule and never to father a child; the record does not put that bargain in her mouth, and the epic does not either. What is hers comes later, and it is considerable. Both her sons die, Chitrangada killed and Vichitravirya of illness, and there is no heir and no one who may lawfully make one, because Bhishma will not break his oath for her and she cannot make him. So she reaches back into her own life before the marriage, to the son she bore Parashara on the river, and she summons Vyasa. And she directs the niyoga: it is by her order that Vyasa goes to her dead sons' widows, and Dhritarashtra and Pandu are born of it, and Vidura of the serving-woman. Every person in the war descends from that decision. She is not entered as a mother or a wife or an ancestress; she is entered because when the line ran out, she is the one who chose what to do about it.

gods.name: Amba
gods.description: Amba and Shikhandi are one person, told in two lives, and this archive holds them in one record; no separate Shikhandi is catalogued. Bhishma carried her and her two sisters off from their own bridegroom-choosing to marry them to his brother, and she told him she had already given herself to Salva; so he sent her to Salva, and Salva would not have her, having been beaten and shamed in front of her. She went back and asked Bhishma to marry her himself, and he would not, because of his oath. So she had no one to blame and no one to go to, and what she did with that is the whole of her. She swore to destroy him. She went to the kings and none would fight him; she went to Parashurama and he fought Bhishma for her and could not win. So she did austerities until the gods gave her the promise of it, and she went into fire to get out of the life she was in and into the one that could kill him. She is reborn in Drupada's house, and here the tradition is not one thing: she is born a girl and raised a boy, or is a girl who becomes a man by an exchange with a yaksha, or is a man from the beginning who remembers, and the versions do not agree and are not made to agree here. What is agreed is the end. On the tenth day Shikhandi stands before Bhishma, and Bhishma will not raise a weapon against what he sees, and Arjuna shoots from behind, and the old man goes down. She said she would do it and she did it.

gods.name: Jarasandha
gods.description: King of Magadha, a man and not a monster; he is born in two halves and joined by a rakshasi who found them, and an unusual birth is not a category. He was the strongest king of his age and he behaved like it. Two of his daughters had been married to Kamsa, and when Krishna killed Kamsa, Jarasandha came for him, and came again, and the tradition has him march on Mathura seventeen times and beat the Yadavas back into the city each time, until they abandoned it altogether and went west to build Dwaraka on the sea. He is said to have held a great many defeated kings prisoner, meaning to offer them, and to have been the standing obstacle to Yudhishthira's Rajasuya, because that sacrifice cannot be made while another king will not bow. So Krishna went to Magadha with Bhima and Arjuna, dressed as brahmins, and Jarasandha received them as a host should and then gave them the choice of combat they asked for, and chose Bhima. They wrestled for days. It was Krishna who saw the answer and gave Bhima the sign, and Bhima tore him in two and threw the halves apart so that they could not join again. The kings came out of his prison and the Rajasuya went forward and the road to the war was open.

gods.name: Tang Sanzang
gods.description: The pilgrim of Journey to the West, called also Tripitaka and the Tang Monk. Underneath him is a real man, the seventh-century monk Xuanzang, who went overland to India for the scriptures and came back and wrote an account of it and translated for the rest of his life; the novel is a thousand years later and it is not his biography and is not offered as one. The two are one inherited identity and are not split. The novel's monk is timid, and weeps, and is captured by nearly every demon he meets, and it would be easy to write him as luggage. He is not. The journey exists because he undertakes it and will not turn back from it, and he holds to a vow of harmlessness that costs him everything and that he never abandons. And he has the one power on the road that matters: the band on Sun Wukong's head, and the spell that tightens it. He uses it. He cannot tell a demon from a beggar and Wukong can, and twice he drives Wukong away for killing what he was right to kill, and both times the road nearly ends there. Those are his decisions and they are the worst ones made on the journey, and they are why he is here.

gods.name: Zhu Bajie
gods.description: Pig of the Eight Precepts, second disciple of the pilgrimage, and once Marshal Tianpeng, who commanded the watery hosts of heaven and was thrown out of it for what he did to the moon goddess when he was drunk; and he was born again into a pig's womb by accident and came out with a pig's head, which he keeps. He is not a monster; he is a fallen immortal on a pilgrimage, and the category here is for what he is in the story and not a compliment to him. He is entered because the journey keeps going wrong on account of him and the going wrong is his own doing. He eats what he should not and takes what he should not and lies about both. He wants to go back to his wife at Gao village and says so at every setback, and proposes at every disaster that they divide the luggage and give it up. He is easily flattered into traps and he leads the others into several. And then, twice or three times, when Wukong has been driven off and the monk is taken and there is nobody else, it is Zhu Bajie who goes and finds him and swallows his pride and talks him into coming back, which he does badly and by lying, and which saves the pilgrimage. Both things are him.

gods.name: Jiang Ziya
gods.description: Lu Shang, called Taigong Wang, the Grand Duke's Hope, and known best as Jiang Ziya; the names are titles and readings of one man and no second record is made of them. At the bottom there is a historical or half-historical figure, the old strategist whom King Wen of Zhou is said to have found fishing and taken into his counsel, and who helped Wu overthrow the last of the Shang at Muye and was rewarded with the state of Qi. That is the layer the histories carry, and it is where his agency lies: he is the mind behind the founding of a dynasty. On top of that the Fengshen Yanyi, a novel of the Ming and not a chronicle, built the Jiang Ziya everyone knows, who fights the Shang with gods and immortals on both sides and who at the end takes the list and reads out the names of the dead and installs them as the gods of heaven. It should be said flatly that the historical strategist did not appoint anybody's gods; the investiture is the novel's. He is set down as a deified human because the man himself became an object of worship, with temples and offerings and a place in the state cult, and it is the human identity that was raised, which is what the category is for.

gods.name: Bai Suzhen
gods.description: The white snake of the legend, a spirit of a thousand years' cultivation who took a woman's shape and came down to the world to find the man who had saved her when he was a boy and she was an animal. She is not catalogued as a monster: she does no evil in the story that is now told, she keeps a pharmacy and heals the poor of Hangzhou, and she is the wife and the protagonist and not the thing that must be killed. Her choices are all in the direction of being human. She marries Xu Xian; and when the monk Fahai tells him what she is and gives him the wine that will show it, and he sees her true shape and dies of the fright, she goes to the mountain and steals the herb of life and brings him back. And when Fahai takes him and shuts him in the Jinshan temple, she raises the river against it to get him out, and the water drowns the country round about, and the versions differ as to how much she is blamed for it and whether it is that flood or her nature that condemns her. She is beaten in the end and shut under the Leifeng Pagoda. The story is older than its present shape and its early forms are harsher to her; she is one figure here and not every white snake in China. Fahai is not catalogued in this batch.

gods.name: Hua Mulan
gods.description: The Ballad of Mulan is a poem of a few hundred characters and it is where she begins, and it is not a life; there is no secure history behind her and none is claimed. In the ballad the conscription lists come round and her father's name is on them and he is old and there is no grown son in the house, so she buys a horse and goes in his place. She serves ten years or twelve. She is not found out. And when it is over and the Khan offers her office and reward, she asks instead for a camel to carry her home, and goes back, and puts on her old clothes and does her hair, and comes out to her comrades, who had campaigned beside her for a decade and had not known. That is the poem and that is her decision, and everything else is later: the Ming plays and the Qing novels gave her a surname and a suicide and a betrothal and a rebellion, the operas gave her more, and the films of the last century gave her others again, and none of them is the original and none is treated here as the canonical one.

notable_mentions.name: Aegeus
notable_mentions.note: King of Athens. Threw himself into the sea named for him when he wrongly believed Theseus dead.

notable_mentions.name: Atalanta
notable_mentions.note: Swift huntress. Only woman on the Calydonian Boar hunt; outran every suitor until one dropped golden apples.

notable_mentions.name: Ganymede
notable_mentions.note: Trojan prince abducted by Zeus to serve as cupbearer of the gods. Immortalized as Aquarius.

notable_mentions.name: Narcissus
notable_mentions.note: Pined away staring at his own reflection. Became the flower that bears his name.

notable_mentions.name: Echo
notable_mentions.note: Nymph reduced to repeating others' words. Loved Narcissus from afar until only her voice remained.

notable_mentions.name: Pygmalion
notable_mentions.note: Sculptor whose ivory statue of Galatea was brought to life by Aphrodite.

notable_mentions.name: Midas
notable_mentions.note: Phrygian king who asked that all he touched turn to gold — and regretted it.

notable_mentions.name: Sarpedon
notable_mentions.note: Son of Zeus and Europa. King of Lycia; died at Troy.

notable_mentions.name: Meleager
notable_mentions.note: Leader of the Calydonian Boar hunt. His life was tied to a log his mother burned.

notable_mentions.name: Cadmus
notable_mentions.note: Covered in the main Cadmus entry — founder of Thebes.

notable_mentions.name: Jocasta
notable_mentions.note: Theban queen; Oedipus's mother-wife. Hanged herself on discovering the truth.

notable_mentions.name: Creon
notable_mentions.note: Theban regent. Forbade burial of Polyneices, setting Antigone's tragedy.

notable_mentions.name: Peleus
notable_mentions.note: Mortal husband of Thetis; father of Achilles.

notable_mentions.name: Rhadamanthus
notable_mentions.note: Brother of Minos; second judge of the underworld.

notable_mentions.name: Triptolemus
notable_mentions.note: Demeter's protégé. Taught humanity agriculture; rode a dragon-drawn chariot.

notable_mentions.name: Iris
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued separately — rainbow messenger of Hera.

notable_mentions.name: Flora
notable_mentions.note: Goddess of flowers and spring. Her Floralia festival was famously licentious.

notable_mentions.name: Pax
notable_mentions.note: Personified peace; cult of the Ara Pacis Augustae.

notable_mentions.name: Silvanus
notable_mentions.note: God of woods and uncultivated fields.

notable_mentions.name: Hygieia
notable_mentions.note: Greek/Roman goddess of health — daughter of Asclepius, catalogued in that entry.

notable_mentions.name: Vertumnus
notable_mentions.note: Shape-shifter god of seasons and plant growth. Wooed Pomona in disguise.

notable_mentions.name: Concordia
notable_mentions.note: Personified civic harmony.

notable_mentions.name: Victoria
notable_mentions.note: Roman Nike — goddess of victory.

notable_mentions.name: Anhur
notable_mentions.note: War-god of This and Lower Egypt; 'Skybearer'.

notable_mentions.name: Banebdjedet
notable_mentions.note: Ram-god of Mendes. Souls of Osiris were said to inhabit him.

notable_mentions.name: Kuk
notable_mentions.note: One of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, personifying primeval darkness.

notable_mentions.name: Meskhenet
notable_mentions.note: Goddess of childbirth bricks — women squatted over her bricks to give birth.

notable_mentions.name: Nehebkau
notable_mentions.note: Two-headed serpent-guardian of the underworld.

notable_mentions.name: Pakhet
notable_mentions.note: Lion-goddess of the eastern desert; 'she who scratches'.

notable_mentions.name: Tatenen
notable_mentions.note: Primordial earth-god; the risen mound of creation at Memphis.

notable_mentions.name: Dellingr
notable_mentions.note: Personified dawn; father of Dagr (day).

notable_mentions.name: Gefn
notable_mentions.note: Alternate name for Freyja as 'giver'.

notable_mentions.name: Hlín
notable_mentions.note: Guardian-goddess attending Frigg; protects those Frigg wishes to save.

notable_mentions.name: Sága
notable_mentions.note: Goddess of histories; drinks daily with Odin from golden cups.

notable_mentions.name: Þjálfi and Röskva
notable_mentions.note: Thor's mortal servants — a brother and sister bonded to him after Thjalfi damaged one of his goats.

notable_mentions.name: Haya
notable_mentions.note: Grain-god; husband of Nisaba.

notable_mentions.name: Ishum
notable_mentions.note: Mild attendant of Nergal; fire-brother to Gibil.

notable_mentions.name: Nungal
notable_mentions.note: Goddess of prisons in Sumerian tradition.

notable_mentions.name: Ninisina
notable_mentions.note: Healing-goddess of Isin. Often merged with Gula.

notable_mentions.name: Mitra (Vedic)
notable_mentions.note: Vedic god of contracts; cognate with Iranian Mithra.

notable_mentions.name: Aryaman
notable_mentions.note: Aditya of hospitality and the milky way.

notable_mentions.name: Bhaga
notable_mentions.note: Aditya of wealth and shares.

notable_mentions.name: Shantanu
notable_mentions.note: Ancestor-king of the Kurus; father of Bhishma by Ganga.

notable_mentions.name: Duryodhana
notable_mentions.note: Eldest Kaurava prince; chief antagonist of the Mahabharata war.

notable_mentions.name: Karna (Mahabharata)
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — son of Surya, tragic Kaurava warrior.

notable_mentions.name: Kunti
notable_mentions.note: Mother of the first three Pandavas and Karna.

notable_mentions.name: Gandhari
notable_mentions.note: Mother of the Kauravas; blindfolded herself for life to share her blind husband's world.

notable_mentions.name: Ao Guang
notable_mentions.note: Dragon King of the Eastern Sea.

notable_mentions.name: Bixia Yuanjun
notable_mentions.note: Goddess of Mount Tai, dawn, and childbirth.

notable_mentions.name: Cangjie
notable_mentions.note: Four-eyed official credited with inventing Chinese characters.

notable_mentions.name: Xuannu
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued as Jiuqian Xuannü above.

notable_mentions.name: Omoikane
notable_mentions.note: Kami of wisdom and counsel; advised the other kami during Amaterasu's hiding.

notable_mentions.name: Ōwatatsumi
notable_mentions.note: Dragon-king of the sea; father of Toyotama-hime.

notable_mentions.name: Sarutahiko
notable_mentions.note: Kami who guided Ninigi's descent to earth.

notable_mentions.name: Belisama
notable_mentions.note: Gallic goddess of fire and forge; consort of Belenus.

notable_mentions.name: Lenus
notable_mentions.note: Treveran healer-god; equated with Mars.

notable_mentions.name: Lugus
notable_mentions.note: Gallic continental form of Lugh; triple-aspected.

notable_mentions.name: Epona
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — Gallic horse-goddess adopted by Roman cavalry.

notable_mentions.name: Jarilo (alt)
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued as Yarilo.

notable_mentions.name: Rusalki
notable_mentions.note: Water-nymphs — spirits of drowned women.

notable_mentions.name: Centeotl
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — god of maize.

notable_mentions.name: Teteo Innan
notable_mentions.note: 'Mother of the Gods' — earth aspect of Coatlicue.

notable_mentions.name: Tlazolteotl
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — 'filth-eater' of confession and purification.

notable_mentions.name: Orula
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued as Orunmila.

notable_mentions.name: Nana Buluku
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — primordial grandmother of Mawu and Lisa.

notable_mentions.name: Laka
notable_mentions.note: Hawaiian goddess of hula; younger sister of Pele.

notable_mentions.name: Kamapua'a
notable_mentions.note: Hawaiian pig-man demigod; lover of Pele.

notable_mentions.name: Pariacaca
notable_mentions.note: Pre-Inca mountain-falcon god of Huarochirí.

notable_mentions.name: Shekhinah
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued as Malkhut/Shekhinah in the Kabbalistic tree; the indwelling divine presence in Judaism generally.

notable_mentions.name: Prometheus (mentioned)
notable_mentions.note: Fully catalogued.

notable_mentions.name: Wotan
notable_mentions.note: Continental Germanic form of Odin; known via Tacitus's Mercury.

notable_mentions.name: Donar
notable_mentions.note: Continental Germanic form of Thor.

notable_mentions.name: Saxnōt
notable_mentions.note: Continental Saxon god named alongside Wotan and Donar in Christianization oaths.

notable_mentions.name: Nerthus
notable_mentions.note: Catalogued — Germanic earth-goddess described by Tacitus.

notable_mentions.name: Vayu (as Dikpala)
notable_mentions.note: Wind-god Vayu also serves as Dikpala of the northwest — see his main entry.

notable_mentions.name: Anahit-Tir-Mihr Triad
notable_mentions.note: Armenian late-pagan devotional triad venerated together; each figure is catalogued.
